【187】**Differential Diagnosis of Vasculitis Neuropathy by Signs and Symptoms**

【188】**The suspicion of a systemic vasculitic neuropathy occurring in the face of known vasculitis is raised with the onset of an asymmetric neuropathy that may evolve over time into a symmetric distal motor sensory neuropathy due to overlap-ping infarction or inflammation of specific peripheral nerves.**

【189】**Trigeminal nerve involvement early and mononeuritis multi-plex are seminal feature of these diseases. The specific fea-tures of each entity lead to the underlying cause of the vas-culitis.**

【190】**In SLE the neuropathy occurs in the face of established disease. Central nervous system features usually predominate with stroke， seizures， psychosis as major signs. Transverse myelitis usually at T4-T6 (dropped cervical level) in many in-stances may be confused with neuropathy if bladder involve-ment is not prominent. Serosal surface， arthralgia， joint and skin manifestations are usually prominent when sensorimo-tor neuropathy begins. The major differential points at this stage are ruling out toxic metabolic or nutritional causes (and usually immune suppressive drugs such as D-penicillamine or cyclosporine. A GBS picture that may emerge in this con-text is more characteristic of PAN. The differential consid-erations are cervical myelitis or severe vasculitic neuroDa-thy. In later stages of the illness a CIDP presentation may be noted and has to be differentiated from lymphoma， HIV， Castleman’s disease， graft versus host disease， osteosclerotic myeloma and monoclonal neuropathy. The vasculitic sensori-motor neuropathy is suggested by an asymmetric onset， stut-tering course and significant motor involvement.**

【191】**The major differential features that are problematic for making the diagnosis of Sjogren’s syndrome are distinguish-ing it from other processes associated with the SICCA com-plex. These are sarcoid， graft versus host disease， amyloido-sis； hepatitis C， HIV and HTLV-1 disease. In sarcoid， bilat-eral VIIth nerve involvement rather than Vth nerve is clas-sic. Dural enhancement associated with intracranial lesions in the posterior hypothalamus and pituitary regions are di-agnostic. Severe mucous ulcerative inflammation is charac-teristic of graft versus host disease whereas Sjogren’s is pri-marily glossitic and conjunctival symptomatology. Dissoci-ated sensory loss (small fiber modality loss) and autonomic neuropathy in association with a primary uveal veil， cardiac and renal disease suggests amyloid neuropathy. HTLV-1 is a long standing myelopathy with prominent spasticity and bladder involvement associated with neuropathy. Hepatitis C is suspected in the face of a cryoglobulinemic neuropathy. HIV most commonly has parotid hypertrophy (cyst forma-tion on MRI) prominent myelin atrophy on CNS MRI with distal burning symmetrical neuropath (late stages).**

【192】**Paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy can present with a severe sensory ataxia. Prominent dorsal column large fiber proprioceptive and vibratory defects are common. Many paraneoplastic neuropathies have some small fiber burning components associated with autonomic features. Idiopathic chronie ataxic neuropathy does not have autonomic involve-ment which is common in both Sjogren's and paraneoplastic neuropathy. Anti-Hu antibodies are found in the majority of paraneoplastic syndromes. Other immune mediated ataxic sensory polyneuropathies are：**

【193】**1\. Miller Fisher variant of GBS**

【194】**2\. MAG (myelin associated glycoprotein)**

【195】**3\. Pure sensory CIDP**

【196】**4\. Immunoglobulin associated paraproteinemias**

【197】**5\. Anti-sulfatide antibodies**

【198】6\. Syphilis

【199】**7.HZ**

【200】8\. SICCA complex

【201】**The hypersensitivity vasculitides are diagnosed by their characteristic leukocytoclastic skin reactions. Most cryoglob-ulinemic neuropathies are secondary to hepatitis C and B or are in association with other collagen vascular diseases. Patients have severe Raynaud’s phenomenon and extreme cyanosis of the extremities often associated with bleeding that is clearly temperature dependent. Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs primarily in children in association with GI pain and arthralgias as well as the seminal purpura. The sensorimo-tor neuropathy is a minor part of the complex. Hypersensi-tivity vasculitis most often occurs from an autoimmune re-action to sulfa drugs or penicillin and may present with dra-matic swelling and burning of the fingers and toes. Temporal arteritis usually presents with headache and involvement of the external carotid vascular system affecting the watershed of the posterior ciliary arteries and the central retinal artery with concomitant loss of vision. Elderly patients with several months of fatigue， polymyalgia rheumatica and weight loss are usually affected. Rarely the arch of the aorta， carotid and subclavian arteries may be affected. Sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy and mononeuritis multiplex may be seen in this context.**

【202】**Polyarteritis nodosa in the majority of patients strikes the peripheral nervous system. It should always be suspected in a middle aged man who has developed late onset asthma， eosinophilia， liver， kidney or testicular infarction. Microa-neurysms of the long medullary arteries of the kidney are di-agnostic. In this setting vasculitic involvement of the brachial and lumbosacral plexus presents as subacute GBS. Raised palpable infarction of skin arterioles of the quadriceps should be sought. Mononeuritis multiplex is common. Central ner-vous systems stroke is rare. Microscopic polyangiitis is a sub-variant of PAN and strikes the kidneys primarily， but vasculi-tis may also be seen in the eyes， lung， muscle and rarely the brain. ANCA antibodies (p>c) are seen in up to 90% of pa-tients. A sensorimotor neuropathy in the face of severe renal involvement should suggest this diagnosis. Decreased com-plement and increased rheumatoid factor are supportive. The lungs are involved in approximately 50% of patients and the neuropathy is not buring in the feet， which separates it from uremic neuropathy.**

【203】**Churg-Strauss sensorimotor neuropathy is suggested in patients with eosinophilia and interstitial lung disease. The pituitary may be involved. IgE is increased in the serum in75% of patients and ANCA antibodies are present (p>c) in50-75%) of patients.**

【204】**Wegener’s granulomatosis invariably attacks the sinuses(greater than 90% of patients). It is also associated with gran-ulomatous lung disease and chronic sinusitis. Orbital and**

【205】**Vth nerve involvement occur. Mononeuritis multiplex is more common than an asymmetric， stuttering， slowly progressive distal predominant sensorimotor neuropathy.**

【206】**Rheumatoid arthritis invariably involves the carpal tunnel and less commonly the tarsal tunnel. Differential diagnosis must entertain hand paresthesias from subluxation at C1-C2. Severe intrinsic hand muscle atrophy out of proportion to the arthropathy is common. High sed rate and RF are seen in greater than 90% of patients. Low level eosinophilic ANA and ANCA antibody response with decreased complement are supportive. Rarely mononeuritis and asymmetric periph-eral vasculitis occurs.**

【207】**Scleroderma is easily diagnosed from its distinctive physi-cal findings. Often not recognized is its penchant for trigemi-nal involvement which may be bilateral. Carpal tunnel syn-drome is common in its early inflammatory stages. Later a subtle sensorimotor neuropathy develops. It should al-ways be suspected in patients with early severe Raynaud's phenomena. The CREST syndrome (calcinosis， Raynaud's， esophageal dysmotility， sclerodactyly and telangiectasia is as-sociated with a sensorimotor neuropathy. Raynaud's is often severe in SLE and rheumatoid arthritis. Scleroderma presents no difficulty in differentiation from other CTD or vasculitic neuropathies. Realizing that Vth nerve， carpal tunnel， tarsal tunnel and a vasculitic neuropathy may occur is what is over-looked.**

【208】**Mixed connective disease has features of scleroderma， SLE and polymyositis. It is the most common connective tis-sue disease that presents with trigeminal neuropathy. Rarely， a sensorimotor neuropathy is present. High (antibody titers of ANA antibodies to extractable nuclear RNP ribonuclease-V1are present).**

【209】**Behcet’s disease primarily affects the CNS with anterior and posterior uveitis， optic neuritis， a brainstem syndrome or vasculitic stroke. Its seminal feature is aphthous ulceration of the mouth and genitals. Occasionally patients have a well de-marcated extra genital， erythematous ulcer on the body that is extremely painful. Large joint and GI involvement occurs. Venous thrombosis of the cortical veins is increasingly recog-nized. Rarely， patients have a concomitant distal predominant sensorimotor polyneuropathy.**

【210】**Relapsing polychondritis may presentVwith a painful swollen ears. Ochronosis and uremia may also involve the pinna. This inflammatory autoimmune disease of cartilage causes tracheal stenosis， saddle nose deformity and heart valve inflammation. The central nervous system features of optic neuritis， vestibulopathy and conductive hearing loss from eustachian tube involvement are the seminal central features. Rarely mononeuritis multiplex and a sensorimotor polyneuropathy are seen concomitantly.**

**The major differential diagnostic problems occurring in the diagnosis of vasculitic neuropathy is not in differen-tiating one connective diseases from another in which it|删除0换行|may occur， but rather diagnosing it in the absence of sys-temic features. The differential diagnosis includes an infec-tious etiology such as Lyme disease， multifocal demyelinat-ing neuropathy， multiple lumbar plexopathy， neuralgic amy-otrophy and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy. The non systemic vasculitic neuropathies may present as mononeuropathy， multiple mononeuropathy or mononeu-ropathy multiplex in addition to an asymmetric distal senso-rimotor polyneuropathy which may occur from overlap of in-farction of large nerves.**

**clinical judgment. It is well known that the use of statistical or actuarial formulas， and not unassisted clinical judgment， provides the highest rates of diagnostic accuracy in a variety of tasks 删除1:<u>(Grove & Meehl， 1996)</u>. Demonstrations of the failure of clinicians to employ predictor informa-tion accurately in neuropsychology are not difficult to find. For exam-ple， Kareken and Williams (1994) had clinical neuropsychologists estimate the IQs of cases using the demographic variables employed by Barona and colleagues (1984) to develop their prediction equations. They found that the clinicians greatly overemphasized education in making predictions and substantially underestimated the error in predic-tion. Kareken (1997) has reviewed this literature from the perspective of neuropsychology and has listed several factors that can contribute to inaccuracy in clinical prediction. We will briefly discuss two of the fac-tors identified by Kareken that we believe are particularly robust， and actually represent two extremes in the prediction process. The first fac-tor is overrepresenting the size of the relationship between a predictor variable and the dependent variable. The Kareken and Williams (1994) study provided an excellent example of this problem. Their clinicians believed that the correlation between education and WAIS-R VIQ was.85 (the actual valuc is .56) and their clinicians'predictions revealed an rof .83 between education and estimated VIQ. Overrepresentation of a predictor-dependent variable relationship can thus lead to heavy reliance|删除0换行|on a single predictor. At the other extreme， however， is the problem of reliance on multiple predictors， some of which may not contribute to accuracy. Thus， clinicians run the risk of losing accuracy when they incorporate too many variables in their predictions. For example， it may be tempting to consider a patient's national region of origin (e.g.， the South)， in addition to education and occupation， to refine further an estimated IQ. Region of origin， however， has been shown to have only a negligible relationship to IQ 删除1:<u>(Vanderploeg & Schinka， 1995)</u> and its inclusion in clinical estimation would likely contribute only to error.**

**Are there situations in which clinical judgment should be used in esti-mating premorbid cognitive status? We believe clinical judgment can play an important role in the application of statistical/actuarial methods in premorbid estimation， primarily in determining the exceptions to straightforward application of the formulas. To illustrate， we cite a recent example from our own practices. The case involved estimation for a 45-year-old white male that sustained a head injury in a motor vehi-cle accident several months prior to evaluation. He had completed 11years of education in the public school system and had been employed as an appliance repairman for the past twenty years. Application of the WTAR/demographic approach 删除1:<u>(Psychological Corporation， 2001)</u> sug-gests a WAIS-R FSIQ of 96. Information from a detailed clinical inter-view， however， revealed information suggesting that the formula might be an underestimate， This individual had been an A to B+ student when his father dicd， forcing him to leave school to help support his family. For several years he worked in unskilled factory jobs until a family friend hired him as an apprentice in appliance repair. He learned these skills easily and made a reasonable living therealter， marrying young and sup-porting a family with several children. In addition to meeting the demands of his job and family， be had developed a strong interest in personal computers and was responsible for establishing and maintain-ing the computer services of his large church， including software for full bookkeeping system， membership maintenance， newsletter produc-tion， and so forth. He was also responsible for training and supervising church office staff. He saw this activity， performed on evenings and wcek-ends， as an avocation and an opportunity to contribute to his church. In addition， his WAIS-IN performance on the current evaluation revealed Vocabulary and Picture Completion scaled scores of 12， although his Information scaled score was 9. Given the details of this individual's admittedly unusual history， the WTAR demographic approach would appear to underestimate substantially his preinorbid level. We assumed that he would have completed a four-year college education， i he had|删除0换行|had the opportunity to do so， and that his volunteer work at church was equivalent to that of an office manager. Using those adjusted demograph-ic values in the WTAR demographic approach resulted in a predicted WAIS-III FSIQ of 113. Using the BEST-3 approach with the adjusted demographic values and the adjustments shown in Table 2.7 resulted in a predicted WAIS-IU FSIQ of 114. Thus we adjusted our estimate of his premorbid WAIS-III FSIQ from 96 to within the range of 110 to 118.**

【8】**Algorithm for Estimating Premorbid Level of Cognitive Ability**

【9】**Based on our review of the extant literature， we have developed an algo-rithm for selecting a method to estimate premorbid level(s) of function-ing. Use of the algorithm is straightforward； instructions are provided at each step.**

【10】**1\. Use the results from an individually administered battery of cogni-tive tests administered prior to any suspected neurological impairment(e.g.， WAIS-R or WAIS-Il). Use the 90% confidence interval to develop a "window of expected performance" for the neuropsychological evalu-ation. Go to step 5 to determine if modifications to the estimated win-dow of performance should be considered. If step 1 data are not available， go to step 2.**

【11】**2\. Use the results from prior tests or batteries of academic aptitude or achievement， whether administered individually or in a group for-mat. Use percentile scores (or standard score equivalents， e.g.， scaled scores， T-scores， or IQ score equivalents) to provide an estimated win~dow of performance for the neuropsychological evaluation. Go to step 5to determine if modifications to the estimated window of performance should be considered. Ifstep 2 data are not available， go to step 3.**

【12】**3\. If the WAIS-R is being used in the neuropsychological evaluation， use the “BEST3” method 删除1:<u>(Vanderploeg， Schinka， & Axelrod， 1996)</u> to calculate separately VIQ and PIQ. These formulas， and the method for determining VIQand PIQ. are provided in Tables 2.5 and 2.6. Go to step5 to determine if modifications to the estimpated window of performance shoul be considered. If step 3 data are not available， go to step 4.**

**There is a caveat to step 3. In normal individuals the BEST-3 approach is knowu to overestimate IQ by 5 to 6 points. In addition， research has shown that there is recovery of function over time following cerebral insults， Therefore， the BEST-3 may overestimate premorbid function-ing in several cases： (a) individuals suspected of having a brain injury but who in fact do not， (b) individuais with minor or mild brain injuries，|删除0换行|and (c) individuals with mild to moderate brain injuries who are a year or more post-insult. In these cases it may be prudent to proceed to step4.b， or at least to cross-check the results of step 3 by comparison with step 4.b.**

【14】**4\. If the WAIS-III is being used in the neuropsychological evaluation， use step 4.a and/or step 4.b.**

【15】**a. Use the BEST-3 (see Tables 2.5 and 2.6 and adjust WAIS-III scores based on data in Table 2.7 as one choice. The same caveat applies to step 4.1 as applies to step 3， as described immediately above.**

【16】**b. Use the WTAR/demographic approach to estimate WAIS-III VIQ.**

【17】**The Best-3 approach is still superior for estimating WAIS-IITPIQ Go to step 5 to determine if modifications to the estimated window of performance should be considered.**

【18】**5\. Examine details of the clinical history to determine if there are strong reasons to adjust the estimated window of performance. Pay par ticular attention to cases in which there are indications that the individ-ual has not been able to achieve in the educational and occupational arena because of limited opportunity. Table 2.3 provides data of WAIS-R IQ equivalents for levels of academic and occupational achievement that can be used as reference points， or adjusted demographic values can be used to recalculate regression formulas.**

【19】**METHODS OF ESTIMATING PREMORBID COGNITIVE ABILITY IN CHILDREN**

【20】**Approaches to preniorbid estimation in children have received far less research attention than has been the case for adults. Estimation of premorbid function in children has encompassed only two of the meth-ods used with adults： regression methods using demographic data and regression methods using both demographic variables and current abil-ity measures.**

**Reynolds and Gutkin (1979) used dernographic variables from the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children -Revised 删除1:<u>(WISC-R， Wechsler，1974)</u> standardization data to develop regression equations to predict children\`s premorbid IQ scores. A stepwise regression procedure using the demographic variables of father’s occupational status， and child's gender， ethnicity， urban versus rural residence， and geographic region resulted in three equations with multiple correlations of .44， .44， and.37， with FSIQ， VIQ and PIQ. respectively. Kendall and Jablensky (2003) raise serious questions as to the validity of categorical diagnoses in schizophrenia (the same may likely is true for other categorical diagnoses). These symptoms emerge either from unusual physiological conditions or as result of extraordi-nary experiences or circumstances .

Pilowsky considers night terrors(Pavor nocturnus) as parahallucinatory experiences. Determining if a child is hallucinating or not， is not always simple .

【24】**The brain and the senses are entrained to receive and to process information； when that does not occur， the brain stimulates itselfand“makes things happen”by creating false perceptions. These experiences are reported in persons who are under prolonged deprivation of food or fluids. “Phantom limb"experiences fall within this category.**

【28】Functional hallucinations are defined as those occurring when the patient simultaneously receives a real stimulus in the concerned perceptual field； for example， a hallucinated voice heard simultaneously with and specific to real water sound. 【30】Hypnagogic and Hypnopompic Hallucinations

【31】Hypnagogic phenomena occur when the person is falling asleep. Hypnopompic phenomena occur when the person is awakening. These definitions do not have universal consensus. For instance， Reddy， Smith， and Robinson (2005) defined hypnagogic sleep phenomena as occurring upon awakening， and is experienced in a semiconscious state. According to these authors， the sleep phenomena involve vivid， auditory， visual， and tactile misperceptions or hal-lucinations. These disturbances need to be differentiated from hallucinatory phenomena fol-lowing a prolonged cataleptic attack . Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations are also associated with narcolepsy . 【52】**DELIRIUM**

【53】Wise and Brandt (1992) defined delirium as a transient and usually reversible dysfunction ofthe cerebral metabolism that has an acute or subacute onset and is manifested by an array of neuropsychiatric abnormalities. Even in its most protean manifestations， it is likely that delirium is underrecognized in child-hood； the diagnosis of delirium is even more difficult in preschoolers. Schieveld and Leentjens (2005) state， “We fear that this child psychiatric emergency often goes unrecognized and is undertreated； the complex combination of a seri-ous illness and polypharmacy in a young child often results in reluctance and delayed decision to add yet another medication to treat delirium . The authors illustrated two cases in children younger than 42 months in a PICU.

【54】Martini (2005) affirms that the hypoactive subtype of delirium is less likely to be recognized and is frequently misdiagnosed as depression . Martini calls attention to delirium secondary to anesthesia with sevoflurane， and to anticholinergic delirium secondary to orphenadrine. Delirium should be considered when there are regressive and chaotic behaviors， anxiety and moaning in severely ill children (pp. 396-397). Children are not as prone to delirium states as are adults following a heart transplant. Delirium in children is sometimes confused with regressive and provocative behaviors (Williams，1996， p. 345).

【55】**Delirium entails：**

【56】1\. Disturbance of the level of consciousness (diminished awareness of the environment， and reduced attention and concentration) that cannot be ac-counted for by a preexisting medical condition or a dementing process.

【57】_2\._ Cognitive deficits (attention and recent memory impairments， disorienta-tion， language and perceptual disturbances-threatening hallucinations or transient delusions-not related to previous deficits).

【58】3.A rapid onset of the disturbance and a fluctuation of symptoms during the day， "sun-downing， that is， progressive decrement of sensorium as the day moves on.

【59】_4.Evidence by history physical examination， laboratory， or other tests that_ indicate that the disturbance is a direct physiological consequence of an identifiable medical condition.

Delirum is frequently associated with a disturbance of the sleep-wake cycle，disturbances of the psychomotor behavior (restlessness or hyperactivity， or decrease of psychomotor activity， reaching sluggishness and lethargy)； or|删除0换行|evidence of emotional disturbance (anxiety， fear， depression， irritability， anger， euphoria， or apathy). These disturbances are particularly prevalent at night. The EEG usually shows generalized slowing 删除1:<u>(modified from DSM-IV-TR， APA，2000)</u>.

【62】Differential Diagnosis of Delirium

【63】**The psychotic features associated with delirium are commonly of an acute nature， except when delirium evolves out of a chronic psychotic background. Wise and Brandt (1992) created an evocative mnemonic device for the different causes of delirium，“I WATCH DEATH”.**

【64】Occasionally， there is a prominent confusional state in the presentation of primary psychoses： the patient appears disoriented to time， place， and even to person； he may also appear incoherent and contradictory in the responses to the examiner. The patient looks as if she or he were delirious. However， there is no fluctuation of the clinical state and， above all， there is no impairment of the autonomic nervous system (no impairment of pulse， blood pressure， no diaphoresis， and no sun-downing). The psychiatrist will also observe find-ings consistent with schizophrenia (i.e.， stereotypes， negativism， or persistent negative and positive symptoms)， or of a mood disorder (fluctuating mood， grandiosity， elation， irritability， pressure of speech， catatonia， etc). Moreover， in distinction to delirium， the neurological examination is noncontributory， EEGs and neuroimaging are negative.

Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the ratio of clinical subjects with the diagnostically significant test sign to all subjects with the diagnostically significant sign. Negative Predictive Value (NPV) is the ratio of persons without the clinical condition who have a non-significant test sign， to all subjects who have a negative sigu.**

【3】**Glaros and Kline (1988) observed that higher sensitivity and specificity values are generally associated with higher predictive values. Predictive values are also affected， however， by the baserate of the clinical condition. When the base rate of a clinical condition is low， the predictive value of a negative test result is greater than the predictive value of a positive test result. Conversely， when the base rate of a clinical condition is high， the predictive value of a positive test result is greater than the predictive power of a negative test result. As Glaros and Kline observed， when a con-dition is relatively rare， a positive test finding is typically not useful in confirming its presence； yet when a condition is prevalent， a positive test finding warrants more confidence than a negative test finding.**

【4】**Hence， in low base rate conditions， the task of differential diagnosis is particularly important， as the clinician is at greater risk of making a false positive diagnosis. False positive or “over-diagnosis” is particularly prevalent in forensic applications， due to a failure to appreciate issles of baserates， sensitivity， specificity， PPV and NPV， and failure to perforin scientific and logical differential diagnosis 删除1:<u>(Faust， Ziskin， & Hiers， 1991； Larrabee，1990，2000)</u>.**

【5】**Baserates and Predictive Values in Relation to MAI Symptoms and Outcome**

【6】**Recently， Binder ane colleagues (1997) completed a meta-analytic investigation of the effects of MHI. Meta-analysis requires calculations of individual effect sizes for each clinical subject (MHI) sainple and each control group sample， computed as the distance between the sam-ple means in standard deviation units. This can be based on the control group standard deviation， d， or on g. the pooled standard deviation of both groups 删除1:<u>(Cohen， 1988； Rosenthal，1991)</u>.**

【7】**The Binder and associates (1997) meta-analysis included neuropsy-chological data from eight published prospective or quasi-prospective MHI studies， with 3-month or longer follow-up， and less than 50% attri-tion. Altogether， 11 samples totaling 314 MHI and 308 control subjects comprised the data. Average general neuropsychological effect sizes， weighted for sample size， were quite small， with mean d of .12 (p<.03) and mean gof .07 (p<.12). These effect sizes were equivalent to a two-point change on either the WAIS-R Full Scale IQ or the WMS-R General Memory Index. Analyzed by neuropsychological domain， attention yielded a significant effect size， with mean d of .20 and mean gof.17， equivalent to a three-point change in WMS-R Attention/Concentration. Both the general effect size and attention effect size for MHI were less than the measurement errors for the WAIS-R and WMS-R index scores.**

【8】**Utilizing a variety of techniques， including the degree of shift of the MHI relative to control distribution， and Cohen’s (1988) Ul statistic， Binder and colleagues (1997) estimated a 5% prevalence of small， per-sistent neuropsychological impairment in persons sustaining MHI. They then conducted a predictive value analysis， using this 5% baserate of persistent impairment and a variety of hypothetica sensitivity and specificity values for neuropsychological tests. As can be seen in Table7.1， the greatest PPV was .32， when sensitivity and specificity were both.90； by contrast， NPV was .99. The authors observed that these data sug-gested a clinician assessing a case of MHI for persistent deficits is more likely to be correct when diagnosing no deficits， and less likely to be cor-rect when diagnosing permanent neuropsychological dysfunction.**

【9】**Although some may argue that the baserates of impairment after MHI may differ in clinical settings， since those who fully recover will not seek neuropsychological evaluation， this must be tempered by consideration of the baserate of motivational impairment in sampies of litigating MHI subjects. Binder and Kelly (1996) found that up to 47% of MHIs showed evidence of motivational impairment on the Portland Digit Recognition Test (PDRT) when employing a performance cutoff of the bottom 2% of a non-litigating bonafide brain damage group. Millis (1992) found that on a forced-choice verbal recognition memory task 50% of MHIs per-formed below the poorest performance of patients who had severe head injury. Greiffenstein， Baker， and Gola (1994) reported a malingering base rate of 60% in chrouic post-concussion patients.**

【10】**Symptomatic Complaint**

【11】**Post-concussive syndrome (PCS) refers to a constellation of somatic， cognitive， and emotional symptoms following MHI 删除1:<u>(Alexander， 1995)</u>.**

【15】**There is longstanding controversy over whether PCS results from phys-iogenic vs. psychogenic factors 删除1:<u>(Lishman，1988)</u>. Physiogenic factors are likely operative in the first one to three months post-trauma， whereas psychogenic factors are more likely related to chronic PCS， persisting several months after MHI 删除1:<u>(Alexander， 1995； Binder， 1997)</u>. For exam-ple， Dikmen， McLean， and Temkin (1986) found that one month after trauma， three of 12 PCS symptoms (bothered by noise， insomnia， and memory difficulties) discriminated MHI from control subjects， but at one year， there were no differences in syinptom endorsement. There is increasing evidence that raises questions about the validity of the PCS symptom constellation. To qualify as a syndrome， a condition must demonstrate a set of specifically associated symptoms that are broadly present in persons who have the condition and absent in those who do not have it (note the relevance of sensitivity and specificity). Moreover， if PCS reflects neurological factors， it should correlate with other neurolog-ical factors， including injury severity and neuropsychological test scores.**

【16】**There are accumulated data for a variety of clinical samples demon-strating a poor association between symptomatic complaints and actual neuropsychological test performance. Patients with severe head injury， Alzheimer’s disease， and non-traumatic focal hemispheric brain disease frequently demonstrate anosognosia or denial or minimization of deficit 删除1:<u>(Feher， Larrabee， Sudilovsky， &： Crook， 1994； Prigatano， 1996； Prigatano & Altman， 1990)</u>. Conversely， persons without neuropsycho-logical deficit may misreport memory dysfunction secondary to depres sion 删除1:<u>(Larrabee & Levin， 1986； Larrabee， West， & Crook， 1991；Williams， Little， Scates， & Blockman， 1987)</u> or somatization (Hanninen et al.，**

【17】**1994). In a more recent investigation of the validity of MMPI-2 neuro-correction items (i.e.， those items purportedly related to neurological dysfunction)， Brulot， Strauss， and Spellacy (1997) found no correlation between the neuro-correction items and initial GCS， duration of PTA， or neuropsychological test performance. Rather， these purported neu-rocorrection items were significantly associated with elevations on the MMPI-2 Depression content scale.**

【18】**Symptoms thought to be representative of PCS， such as headache， memory difficulty， and irritability， are also seen in persons with suspect-ed neurotoxic exposure 删除1:<u>(Larrabee， 1990， Lees-Haley & Brown， 1993)</u>. Hence， these symptoms are not specific to head trauma. More impor-tantly， these symptoms occur frequently in the non-injured population； for example， Lees-Haley and Brown (1993) found that 62% of outpa tient family practice patients report headache， 20% report memory problems， and 38% report irritability. These symptoms increase in rela-tion to stress， independent of presence or absence of MHI 删除1:<u>(Gouvier， Cubic， Jones， Brantley， & Cutlip，1992)</u>. Indeed， Lees-Haley and Brown found that in a group of 120 personal injury claimants in litigation for emotional distress or industrial stress but without neurological claims or injuries， 89% reported headaches， 53% reported memory problems， and 77% reported irritability.**

【19】**Mittenberg， Digiulio，Perrin， and Bass (1992) demonstrated that head trauma-naive normal subjects， asked to imagine they sustained an MHI， endorsed the same set of PCS symptoms as did persons with actual MHI. Moreover， the MHI subjects underestimated the frequency at which these symptoms occurred prior to their trauma. The authors relat-ed their results to selective attentional bias to common internal states， stress， and arousal. Putnam and Millis (1994) offer a similar explana-tion， characterize persistent PCS as somatoform disorder， and draw par-allels between selective attentional bias in MHl and the sell-directed selective attention to bodily sensations in persons with elevated health concerns 删除1:<u>(Watson & Pennebaker， 1989)</u>.**

【20】**Considering the above， failure to appreciate the non-specificity of PCS symptoms can lead to misdiagnosis， and iatrogenesis of persistent complaints 删除1:<u>(Larrabee， 1997； Newcombe， Rabbitt， & Briggs， 1994)</u>. If a patient is prone to selectively attend to conmon phenomena， and incorrectly attribute these to brain injury， "diagnosing"these symptoms as PCS can be quite damaging. Although headache (59.1%)， irritability (65.9%)， and memory problems (50.6%) are frequent in MHI， they are more frequent in non-head-injured persons suing for non-neurologic psychological dis-tress， with headache endorsed by 88%， irritability endorsed by 77%，and poor memory endorsed by 53% of the Lees-Haley and Brown litigants.**

【28】**The data in Table 7.2 clearly demonstrate the poor specificity for pur-ported PCS symptomatic complaints， which can occur with high fre-quency in non-concussed persons. Hence， relying on these symptoins as indicative of PCS would result in abnorinally high false-positive diag noses. These data， as well as the data published by Brulot and colleagues(1997)， raise serious questions as to whether PCS qualifies as a true syn-drome. In this vein， it is interesting to note that of the eight symptoms proposed in DSM-IV 删除1:<u>(American Psychiatric Association， 1994)</u> as part of the research criteria for PCS， only one， disordered sleep， discriminated MHI from control subjects one month post-trauma in the Dikinen and associates (1986) investigation. All eight DSM-IVPCS symptoms aiso had high rates of occurrence in the Lees-Haley and Browr n nigon-head-injured litigants， ranging from 44%(dizziness) to over 80% (disordered sleep， 92%； headache， 88%； anxiety， 93%).**

【29】**Interimn Summary**

【30】**The low baserate of persistent neuropsychological dysfunction estimated at 5% 删除1:<u>(Binder et al.， 1997)</u>， the low baserate of persistent symptomatic complaints， estimated at 7-8% 删除1:<u>(Binder， 1997)</u>， and the poor specificity(i.e.， high false positive rate) of PCS complaints， call for significant cau-tion in the differential diagnosis of MHI in patients with persistent symptomatic complaints. In the following sections， neurological factors potentially related to poorer outcome following MHI are reviewed， as well as other considerations， including non-neurological psychological factors such as somatization disorder， pain， and malingering.**

【31】**NEUROLOGICAL FACTORS POTENTIALLY RELATED TO PERSISTENT PROBLEMS FOLLOWING MHI**

【32】**Data published by Wilson， Teasdale， Hadley， Wiedman， and Lang(1994) dcmonstrate the necessity of considering GCS and duration of post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) in evaluation of MHI. These investigators found a close association between GCS and PTA for persons who expe-rienced six hours or more of coma following closed head injury. Eight patients had coma less than six hours with PTA greater than seven days， and three of these eight were only briefly unconscious， if at all. These findings demonstrate the importance of basing diagnosis of MHI on both brief loss of consciousness and limited post-traumatic amnesia.**

【33】**MRI is more sensitive than CT scan in detecting lesions following mild to moderate head injury 删除1:<u>(Levin et al.，1987； Levin， Williams， Eisen berg， High， & Guinto， 1992)</u>， Levin and colleagues (1992) found that although MRI Icsions were more prevalent than CT in mild/modcrate head injury， and more prominent in moderate (GCS 9-12) relative to mild (GCS 13-15) head injury， these lesions resolved over one-to three-month follow-up， paralleling the recovery seen in neuropsychological test scores. For some of the subiects with acute MRI lesions， however， neuropsychological impairment persisted， despite resolution of the lesion on MRI.**

【34】**In an earlier investigation， Williams， Levin， and Eisenberg (1990) found that subjects with GCS of 13-15 and CT evidence of structural Iesion were more similar in neuropsychological outcome to moderate head injured patients (GCS of 9-12)， than they were similar to MHI(GCS 13-15 without CT scan abnormalities). The GCS group with CT iden-tified lesions was identified as mild/complicated by these investigators.**

【35】**Based on the research of Levin and colleagues， persons with GCS in the 13-15 range may not have a truly mild injury if they have accompa-nying CT or MRI abnormalities. These conclusions are tempered somewhat by the results of Dikmen， Machamer， Winn， and Temkin(1995)， who found that head-injured subjects who took up to one hour to follow a doctor's commands， some of whom had CT scan abnormali-ties， did not differ on neuropsychological testing as a group from non-head-injured orthopedic trauma controls， one year post-injury.**

【36】**Some investigators have presented data suggesting that MHI results in reduced cerebral reserve . Ewing，McCarthy， Gronwall， and Wrightson (1980) found evidence for persisting cognitive deficits in apparently recovered MHI subjects who were subjected to hypoxic stress. This finding appears con~sistent with evidence from the same laboratory demonstrating a longer recovery time for persons following MHI if there is history of a previous concussion 删除1:<u>(Gronwall，1989； Gronwall & Wrightson，1975)</u>.**

【37】**Data also exist that challenge the hypothesis of reduced cerebral reserve. Alterman， Goldstein， Shelly and Bober (1985) found no signifi-cant neurological performance differences between alcoholic subjects with and without history of MHI. Dikinen， Donovan， Loberg， Machamer， and Temkin (1993)， studying the full spectrum of head trauma severity. found no significant interactions between alcohol use and head trauma severity in relation to neuropsychological outcome. Bornstein and associ-ates (1993) found no significant neuropsychological differences between HIVpositive subiects with and without history of MHI. In a study of chil-dren with MHI， Bijur， Haslum， and Golding (1996) did not find evidence for cumulative effect of MHI， comparing children with 1， 2， or 3 MHI with non-head-injured orthopedic controls with 1，2， or 3 orthopedic injuries. Bijur and colleagues suggested that cognitive deficits associated with mul-tiple MHI were secondary to social and personal factors related to multi-ple injuries， rather than resulting from damage to the head.**

【38】参考删除-1:<u>**Age may also be a moderating variable in determining outcome fol lowing MHI. Patients with moderate head injury younger than 65 years of age were reported to have better outcome than patients older than65 删除1:<u>(Pentland， Jones， Roy， & Miller， 1986)</u>. Goldstein and colleagues删除1:<u>(1994， 1996)</u> have found persisting reduction in neuropsychological test performance at one month 删除1:<u>(Goldstein etal.，1996)</u> and two months删除1:<u>(Goldstein et al.， 1994)</u> post-trauma. These data are somewhat non-representative of MHI， however， in that the majority of subjects studied by Goldstein and colleagues had moderate head injury 删除1:<u>(6 of 22 had MHI in Goldstein et al.， 1994；only 2 of 14 had MHI in Goldstein et al.， 1996)</u>.**</u>

【39】**Recently， Goldstein， Levin， Goldman， Clark， and Altonen (2001) compared the neuropsychological test performance of 18 elderly with MHI to test scores of 17 elderly with moderate CHI and 14 community-residing elderly controls. Patients were followed prospectively， over the two months following their trauma (an average follow-up of about one month). The moderate CHI group performed consistently more poorly than mild CHI and controls， who essentially did not differ from one another on the neuropsychological measuires (only 1 of 10 scores was significant，p<.05). Both the mild and moderate CHI groups reported significantly more affective distress， anxiety and somatic concern than did the control groups. The researchers concluded that their results extended the findings of prior investigations in young adults by demon-strating a relatively good cognitive outcome in elderly persons following a single uncomplicated MHI， despite continuing subjective complaints.**

【40】**Some have contended that the inability to find objective evidence for persistent effects of MHI relates to inadequate characterization of ini-tial severity， and/or to insensitive measures of outcome. As I have argued in another paper 删除1:<u>(Larrabee， 1999)</u>， any attempt at improving assess-ment of initial trauma severity or outcome should show statistical advan-tages over current methodologies， in particular， in relation to dose effects. In other words， any proposed improvement in assessment of severity

【32】**Data published by Wilson， Teasdale， Hadley， Wiedman， and Lang(1994) dcmonstrate the necessity of considering GCS and duration of post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) in evaluation of MHI. These investigators found a close association between GCS and PTA for persons who expe-rienced six hours or more of coma following closed head injury. Eight patients had coma less than six hours with PTA greater than seven days， and three of these eight were only briefly unconscious， if at all. These findings demonstrate the importance of basing diagnosis of MHI on both brief loss of consciousness and limited post-traumatic amnesia.**

【29】**Interimn Summary**

【30】**The low baserate of persistent neuropsychological dysfunction estimated at 5% 删除1:<u>(Binder et al.， 1997)</u>， the low baserate of persistent symptomatic complaints， estimated at 7-8% 删除1:<u>(Binder， 1997)</u>， and the poor specificity(i.e.， high false positive rate) of PCS complaints， call for significant cau-tion in the differential diagnosis of MHI in patients with persistent symptomatic complaints. In the following sections， neurological factors potentially related to poorer outcome following MHI are reviewed， as well as other considerations， including non-neurological psychological factors such as somatization disorder， pain， and malingering.**

【31】**NEUROLOGICAL FACTORS POTENTIALLY RELATED TO PERSISTENT PROBLEMS FOLLOWING MHI**

【32】**Data published by Wilson， Teasdale， Hadley， Wiedman， and Lang(1994) dcmonstrate the necessity of considering GCS and duration of post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) in evaluation of MHI. These investigators found a close association between GCS and PTA for persons who expe-rienced six hours or more of coma following closed head injury. Eight patients had coma less than six hours with PTA greater than seven days， and three of these eight were only briefly unconscious， if at all. These findings demonstrate the importance of basing diagnosis of MHI on both brief loss of consciousness and limited post-traumatic amnesia.**

【33】**MRI is more sensitive than CT scan in detecting lesions following mild to moderate head injury 删除1:<u>(Levin et al.，1987； Levin， Williams， Eisen berg， High， & Guinto， 1992)</u>， Levin and colleagues (1992) found that although MRI Icsions were more prevalent than CT in mild/modcrate head injury， and more prominent in moderate (GCS 9-12) relative to mild (GCS 13-15) head injury， these lesions resolved over one-to three-month follow-up， paralleling the recovery seen in neuropsychological test scores. For some of the subiects with acute MRI lesions， however， neuropsychological impairment persisted， despite resolution of the lesion on MRI.**

【34】**In an earlier investigation， Williams， Levin， and Eisenberg (1990) found that subjects with GCS of 13-15 and CT evidence of structural Iesion were more similar in neuropsychological outcome to moderate head injured patients (GCS of 9-12)， than they were similar to MHI(GCS 13-15 without CT scan abnormalities). The GCS group with CT iden-tified lesions was identified as mild/complicated by these investigators.**

【35】**Based on the research of Levin and colleagues， persons with GCS in the 13-15 range may not have a truly mild injury if they have accompa-nying CT or MRI abnormalities. These conclusions are tempered somewhat by the results of Dikmen， Machamer， Winn， and Temkin(1995)， who found that head-injured subjects who took up to one hour to follow a doctor's commands， some of whom had CT scan abnormali-ties， did not differ on neuropsychological testing as a group from non-head-injured orthopedic trauma controls， one year post-injury.**

【36】**Some investigators have presented data suggesting that MHI results in reduced cerebral reserve . Ewing，McCarthy， Gronwall， and Wrightson (1980) found evidence for persisting cognitive deficits in apparently recovered MHI subjects who were subjected to hypoxic stress. This finding appears con~sistent with evidence from the same laboratory demonstrating a longer recovery time for persons following MHI if there is history of a previous concussion 删除1:<u>(Gronwall，1989； Gronwall & Wrightson，1975)</u>.**

【37】**Data also exist that challenge the hypothesis of reduced cerebral reserve. Alterman， Goldstein， Shelly and Bober (1985) found no signifi-cant neurological performance differences between alcoholic subjects with and without history of MHI. Dikinen， Donovan， Loberg， Machamer， and Temkin (1993)， studying the full spectrum of head trauma severity. found no significant interactions between alcohol use and head trauma severity in relation to neuropsychological outcome. Bornstein and associ-ates (1993) found no significant neuropsychological differences between HIVpositive subiects with and without history of MHI. In a study of chil-dren with MHI， Bijur， Haslum， and Golding (1996) did not find evidence for cumulative effect of MHI， comparing children with 1， 2， or 3 MHI with non-head-injured orthopedic controls with 1，2， or 3 orthopedic injuries. Bijur and colleagues suggested that cognitive deficits associated with mul-tiple MHI were secondary to social and personal factors related to multi-ple injuries， rather than resulting from damage to the head.**

【38】参考删除-1:<u>**Age may also be a moderating variable in determining outcome fol lowing MHI. Patients with moderate head injury younger than 65 years of age were reported to have better outcome than patients older than65 删除1:<u>(Pentland， Jones， Roy， & Miller， 1986)</u>. Goldstein and colleagues删除1:<u>(1994， 1996)</u> have found persisting reduction in neuropsychological test performance at one month 删除1:<u>(Goldstein etal.，1996)</u> and two months删除1:<u>(Goldstein et al.， 1994)</u> post-trauma. These data are somewhat non-representative of MHI， however， in that the majority of subjects studied by Goldstein and colleagues had moderate head injury 删除1:<u>(6 of 22 had MHI in Goldstein et al.， 1994；only 2 of 14 had MHI in Goldstein et al.， 1996)</u>.**</u>

【39】**Recently， Goldstein， Levin， Goldman， Clark， and Altonen (2001) compared the neuropsychological test performance of 18 elderly with MHI to test scores of 17 elderly with moderate CHI and 14 community-residing elderly controls. Patients were followed prospectively， over the two months following their trauma (an average follow-up of about one month). Both the mild and moderate CHI groups reported significantly more affective distress， anxiety and somatic concern than did the control groups. The researchers concluded that their results extended the findings of prior investigations in young adults by demon-strating a relatively good cognitive outcome in elderly persons following a single uncomplicated MHI， despite continuing subjective complaints.**

Weight gain may result from hyperorality and increased consumption of carbohydrates 删除1:<u>(Mendez， Selwood， Mastri， &Frey， 1993)</u>. The neurobehavioral changes associated with FTD are often compared with those of Kliver-Bucy syndrome (first produced in animals by surgical ablation of the temporal lobes， amygdalae， and hip-pocampi)， which also include apathy， hyperorality， exploration behav iors， and alterations in sexual behavior 删除1:<u>(Cummings & Benson， 1992)</u>.**

【1】**Neuropsychological deficits are those expected from frontal degen-eration； executive dysfunction and language disturbance (commonly. reduced speech). Difficulty generating responses， inhibiting inappro-priate responses， manipulating information within working memory shifting attention， and abstracting ideas are common findings. A recent meta-analysis 删除1:<u>(Zakzanis et al.， 1999)</u> found that measures of cognitive flexibility and abstraction (e.g.， Wisconsin Card Sorting Test categories achieved) were best at differentiating FTD patients from control sub-jects， FTD patients with more prominent left-sided degeneration tend to exhibit progressive reduction in speech 删除1:<u>(Mesulam，1982)</u> with preser-vation in visuoconstruction， motor skills， naming， and comprehension.**

【2】**In a recent study， Levy and colleagues (1996) found that FTD was best differentiated from AD by the presence of hyperorality， motor com-pulsions， apathy， disinhibition， and irritability. From a neuropsychologi-cal standpoint， FTD patients tend to exhibit more perseverative errors and better verbal and visual recognition memory than do AD patients.**

**The category of frontotemporal dementias has been further subdi-vided based on the most prominent location of atrophy. The frontal variant of FTD has been labeled dementia of frontal type (DFT) and the temporal variant has been labeled semantic dementia 删除1:<u>(Hodges et al.，1999)</u>. The semantic dementia subtype is characterized by surface dyslexia and loss of semantic memory， with deficits in naming， category fluency， and semantic knowledge， but preservation of phonological and grammar skills， visuospatial function， working memory cpisodic memo-ry， and nonverbal problem solving. The DFT subtype， in contrast， is characterized by executive dysfunction 删除1:<u>(e.g.， impaired planning on copying the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure； Hodges et al.， 1999)</u>.DFT is believed to begin in the ventromedial frontal lobe， a region associated|删除0换行|with the social aspects of behavior； executive functions， which are asso-ciated with dorsolateral prefrontal regions， may be relatively intact until later in the course of DFT 删除1:<u>(Hodges et al.， 1999)</u>.**

【4】**Corticobasal Degeneration**

【5】**CBD， also called extrapyramidal apraxic disorder， is a rare discase that begins insidiously， frequentty with bradykinesia and unilateral onset of upper extremity tremor， clumsiness， stiffness， and myoclonus. Later in the course， rigidity of the arm is seen， with a dystonic， jerky， useless hand. Alien hand syndrome develops in about half of CBD patients删除1:<u>(Rinne， Lee， Thompson， & Marsden， 1994)</u>. Less frequently， the lower extremities are affected. Supranuclear gaze palsy often is present， but unlike PSP patients， those with CBD have prominent parietal lobe fea-tures. Death， usually due to iminobility complications， occurs five to ten years following symptom onset. About 60% of patients have a positive family histor y of CBD syrnptoms.**

【6】**Global dementia is not a feature of CBD， but ideomotor apraxia and limb-kinetic apraxia are common. Neuropsychological deficits tend to be within the realm of executive functioning and construction 删除1:<u>(Massman， Kreiter， Jankovic， & Doody， 1996； Pillon et al.， 1995)</u>. Thus， CBD patients tend to exhibit both cortical and subcortical deficits.**

【7】**Frontotemporal Dementia with Parkinsonism**

【8】**Frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17) is an autosomal dominant disease that has been mapped to the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) gene on chromosome 17. Genetic testing is avail-able for patients who have frontotemporal dementia and a positive fam-ily history of dementia. Mutations in the MAPT gene appear to promote abnormal microtubule assembly and produce abundant tau protein deposits in brain tissue 删除1:<u>(Spillantini et al.，1998)</u>.**

【9】**FTDP-17 is a neurodegenerative condition with a typical onset between age 40 and 60， insidious behavioral changes， language dysfunc-tion， and extrapyramidal syinptoms. As is the case with Lewy Body Disease ， rigidity， bradykinesia， and masked facies occur more frequently than does tremor； supranuclear palsy and saccadic eye movenient disturbances may be present also. The course of the disease usually lasts five to ten years and progresses to mutism in the middle stages 删除1:<u>(Foster et al.，1997)</u>.**

【10】**Similar to other diseases falling under the rubric of Pick Complex， the most common presenting symptoms of FTDP-17 are behavior changes， which often include apathy and disinhibition. Obsessive-compulsive behavior， hyperorality， restlessress， aggressiveness， and psychosis may also occur early in the course of the disease. If psychotic symptoms are present， they are usually persecutory delusions and visual or auditory hallucinations 删除1:<u>(Sumi， Bird，Nochlin， & Raskind，1992)</u>.**

【11】**Early cognitive symptoms in FTDP-17 include word-finding difficul-ties and semantic paraphasias； eventually， patients develop perseverative speech， echolalia， and mutism. Executive dysfunction， attention diffi-culties， and impaired abstract reasoning also develop. After a few years， profound dementia， with marked memory impairment， is present.**

【12】**Although some of the initial symptoms of FTDP-17 are similar to those presenting in AD， presence of frontotemporal atrophy on imag-ing， decreased anterior cerebral perfusion on SPECT， profound disinhi-bition， and parkinsonian symptoms should raise suspicion ofFTDP-17.**

【13】**DEMENTING LEWY BODY DISEASE**

【14】**Lewy Body Disease (LBD) may be the second most common dementing disorder 删除1:<u>(Sparks， Lukas， & Drumm， 1998)</u>， accounting for between 7and 26% of dementias 删除1:<u>(Fields， 1998)</u>. Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions composed of ubiquitin and neurofilament pro teins， and can exist in both cortical and subcortical regions. They tend to have the highest densities in parahippocampal cortex， cingulate， ncocortex， temporal pole， substantia nigra， locus coeruleus， nucleus basalis of Meynert， and amygdala. Upon neuropathological examina-tion， they are found in about 20% of dementia cases， but may also occur in the absence of dementia. Their pathogenesis is unknown. Because the neuropathology of LBD includes cortical and subcortical changes， patients with the discase tend to exhibit features of both cortical and subcortical dementing syndromes.**

【15】**Cortical Lewy bodies can occur in PD (both with and without demen-tia)， AD， AD with diffuse LBD， the Lewy Body variant of AD， and pure diffuse LBD. Controversy regarding the nature of LBD as a variant of AD or as an entity unto itself continues. When pathological markers of both AD and LBD are present， the “Lewy body variant of Alzheimer's disease” is typically diagrosed 删除1:<u>(Hansen et al.， 1990)</u>. About 20% of AD patients are believed to fall into this category 删除1:<u>(Fields，1998)</u>. Pure dif fuse LBD， without AD-like pathology， accounts for about 20% of cortical**

【16】**Lewy body cases， however. Diagnostic guidelines recommend that any dementing disorder in which Lewy bodies are present be called “Dementia with Lewy Bodies，" regardless of other neuropathological markers删除1:<u>(McKeith et al.， 1996)</u>.**

【17】**The onset of Lewy Body Disease is similar to that of AD， but LBD may progress more rapidly in terms of both cognitive decline and time to death 删除1:<u>(Olichney et al.， 1998)</u>. Patients with LBD may present with psy-chiatric disturbances (most commonly， depressive symptoms) before cognitive symptoms appear. The hallsnarks of LBD that help differenti-ate it from AD include parkinsonian symptoms， hallucinations， and fluctuations in cognitive functioning (i.e.， “good” and “bad" days). Parkinsonian symptoms tend to be more mild than those in PD. Gait abnormality， masked facies， and bradykinesia are common， but tremor and extreme rigidity are not 删除1:<u>(Fields， 1998)</u>. Visual hallucinations early in the course of the disease commonly differentiate LBD from AD and PD. Compared to AD patients， those with LBD tend to exhibit greater impairments in attention， fluency， visuospatial processing， and psy-chomotor speed 删除1:<u>(Hansen et al.， 1990；McKeith & O'Brien， 1996；Sparks et al.， 1998)</u>， features commonly noted as consistent with subcortical dementia. LBD and AD patients tend to present with the same types of cortical deficits， however. Depression and REM sleep behavior disorder have recently been included as supporting features of LBD 删除1:<u>(McKeith et al.， 1999)</u>. Of note， neuroleptic mnedications， even administered in low doses， teiid to exacerbate the dementia associated with LBD and can increase parkinsonian symptoms and hasten death 删除1:<u>(McKeith， Fairbairu， Perry， Thompson， & Perry， 1992)</u>. Antiparkinsonian medica-tions， though effective in controlling motor symptoms， may precipitate hallucinations and delusions.**

【18】**CREUTZFELDT-IAKOB DISEASE**

**A rare prion disease， Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) occurs in only one in one inillion individuals， but is of interest because it is an infec-tious disease (“prion”being an abbreviation for proteinaceous infectious particle). It occurs in sporadic and familial forms and pri-marily affects middle-aged adults. Forgetfulness， poor concentration， and depression， along with vague somatic complaints and fatigue， may be presenting symptoms. The rate of progression varies， but the disease results in global dementia fairly quickly， with death occurring usually within a few months to one year. Aphasia， agnosia， apraxia，|删除0换行|amnesia， psychosis， visual disturbances， myoclonus， cerebellar signs， and other motor disturbances usually are prominent 删除1:<u>(Cummings &Benson，1992)</u>.**

【20】**SUBSTANCE-INDUCED PERSISTING DEMENTIA**

【21】**A large number of non-prescription and prescription medications， as well as recreational drugs， can produce cognitive deficits. Excess con-sumption of almost any substance may result in reversible or irreversible CNS neurotoxicity， but on occasion， therapeutic levels or small amounts of a substance can yield unusual reactions in susceptible individuals. Careful questioning regarding both medication and substance abuse history is therefore essential when interviewing patients referred for suspected dementia. Below we review the neuropsychological conse-quences of long-term alcohol abuse， which is the most common cause of Substance-Induced Persisting Dementia. For a more extensive review of the neurotoxic effects of medications and recrcational drugs， we refer the interested reader to Cummings and Benson’s 1992 chapter. More recent reviews of the neuropsychological effects of drugs of abuse(Bates & Convit1999)andprescription medications删除1:<u>(Stein &Strickland，1998)</u> are also available.**

【22】**Frank dementia caused by alcohol abuse is rare. Acute alcohol abuse can affect neuropsychological performance considerably 删除1:<u>(sce Rourke &Loberg， 1996)</u>， so we recommend scheduling neuropsychological test-ing after at least two weeks of abstinence from alcohol. Many of the neu-ropsychological deficits associated with alcohol abuse can be reversed upon cessation of alcohol consumption， but long-term alcohol abuse can result in irreversible dementia syndromes， including Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-induced persisting dementia.**

【23】**Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome， characterized by a severe amnestic dis-order， is caused by extended malnutrition (thiamine deficiency)， not merely excessive use of alcohol. The thiamine deficiency results in white matter hemorrhages， which in turn cause both motor and cognitive deficits. An acute episode of Wernicke's encephalopathy， characterized by acute onset of ataxic gait， nystagmus， ophthalmoplegia， and confusion， typically heralds the disease； these symptoms resolve within about a month upon receiving thiamine therapy. The residual deficits that com-prise Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome include severe retrograde and anterograde amnesia and other cognitive deficits (particularly executive dysfunction). General intellectual abilities and semantic knowledge are usually preserved in these patients .**

【24】**Alcohol-induced persisting dementia is usually mild and typically includes executive dysfunction and visuospatial deficits， along with memory disturbance. Unlike AD， patients with alcoholic dementia usu-ally have intact language abilities. The onset of dementia appears gradu-ally and may reflect not only heavy long-term alcohol use， but also the cognitive disturbances associated with cirrhosis of the liver 删除1:<u>(e.g.， atten-tion， coordination， memory， motor， information processing speed， and language dysfunction； see Cummings & Benson， 1992)</u>.**

【25】**DIFFERENTIATION OF DEMENTIA**

【26】**FROM NON-DEMENTING CONDITIONS**

【27】**Historically， defining the boundaries between normal age-related changes and the very earliest signs of dementia has been difficult， primar-ily because many of the early cognitive and functional changes of AD overlap with changes observed in normal aging (e.g.，complaints of mem-ory decline among older adults， less efficient learning and recall of new information， and slowed processing speed). Yet the increasing availability of pharmacologic treatments for dementia makes imperative the identifi-cation of accurate early markers that reliably differentiate dementia from normal aging or non-dementing conditions 删除1:<u>(Thal，1999)</u>. Clearly， the ear-liest detection of dementia will be of maximnal benefit when considering neuroprotective agents designed to impede the onset of dementia by slowing or preventing the degenerative neuropathologic processes.**

【28】**Normal Aging or the Preclinical Period of Dementia?**

**Biologic evidence suggests that Alzheimer’s disease may involve a long preclinical period of neuropathologic changes prior to the appearance of the full dementia syndrome . Katzman (1994) proposed a chronic disease model of AD， which holds that genetic factors， traumatic events， or other unknown factors predis-pose one to developing AD. An initiating factor (such as age) then trig-gers intracellular events that lead to neuritic degeneration， the formation of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles， and the loss of synapses and neurons. Over a period of time the neural degeneration is thought to gradually accumulate and reach a level that initiates the clinical symptoms of the dementia syndrome. This framework for understanding the development of AD suggests that cognitive deficits， structural volume loss， or functional (i.e.，cerebral metabolic or blood|删除0换行|flow) brain changes associaled with the disease also appear gradually. Thus， these changes might be identified before the degree of neural degeneration has reached a level necessary to produce clinically diag-nosable dementia (i.e.， when both cognitive and functional impairments are evident， as required by both DSM \[American Psychiatric Association，1994\] and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria \[McKhann et al.， 1984\]).**

【30】此段无关页码删除:<u>参考删除-1:<u>**Consistent with this framework， a growing body of evidence demon-strates that cognitive decrements can be detected several years or more prior to clinical diagnosis in nondemented individuals who subsequent-ly develop dementia 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.， 1994，1995，1999； Fuld， Masur， Blau， Crystal， & Aronson， 1990； Grober & Kawas， 1997； Howieson et al.， 1997； Katzman et al.， 1989； La Rue &Jarvik， 1980， 1987； Linn et al.， 1995； Masur， Fuld， Blau， Crystal，& Aronson， 1990， 1994；Petersen et al.， 1995)</u>， and the majority of these reeent studies indicate that measures of leatn-ing and memory are particularly effective in this regard 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.，1994，1995； Fuld et al.， 1990； Grober & Kawas， 1997； Howieson et al.， 1997； Linn et al.， 1995； Masur， Sliwinski， Lipton， Blau， & Crystal， 1994； Small， Basun， & Backman， 1998； Smith et al.， 1998； Zonderman et al.， 1995)</u>. This latter finding is not surprising， given that failure of recent memory is nsually the tnost prominent neuropsychologic feature during the early stages of AD 删除1:<u>(Welsh et al.，1991； Welsh， Butters， Hughes， Mohs， &Heyman 1992)</u>. 【31】**Milld Cognitive Impairment**

参考删除-1:<u>**Another recent diagnostic classification that attempts to define the bor-derland between normal aging and dementia has been forwarded by Petersen and colleagues， which they term Mild Cognitive Impairment删除1:<u>(MCI； Petersen et al.， 1995， 1996， 1999； Smith et al， 1998)</u>. By defini-tion， MCl involves a significant memory impairment (1.5 standard devi-ations below the mean for age)， the absence of impairment in other cognitive domains， and a lack of significant functional declines in activi-ties of daily living. Petersen and colleagues (1995) have longitudinally followed individuals who met criteria for MCI， but not for dementia， and have found that over several years of follow-up， these MCI patients evolved to dementia at a rate of approximately 15% per year. One of the factors that has been most useful in predicting which of these MCI|删除0换行|patients will subsequently develop dementia has been the presence of the apolipoprotein E E4 gene (ApoE-e4 allele； see Bondi， Salmon， &Kaszniak， 1996， for review). The results of Petersen and associates(1995)， as well as those of other investigators 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.， 1995，1999； Small et al.， 1998； Smith et al.， 1998)</u>， indicate that ApoE is an important risk factor for AD that may be useful in predicting which patients with MCl are more likely to progress to dementia. However， a consensus workgroup convened to examine the diagnostic utility of ApoE genotyp-ing cautioned that the predictive value of ApoE genotype is marginal， especially given that some 35-40% of AD patients do not carry an ApoE-E4 allele 删除1:<u>(Mayeux et al.， 1998)</u>.**</u>

【33】**Depression**

【34】**One of the more difficult and challenging of differential diagnostic considerations in older adults is that of dementia versus depression. The neuropsychologist is often asked to determine whether an individ-ual is experiencing cognitive difficulty secondary to a mood disturbance or dementia. Further confounding this distinction is the realization that， in perhaps 20-30% of cases 删除1:<u>(Teri & Wagner， 1992)</u>， depression often co-exists in patients with dementia. We briefly describe some of the contributions of neuropsychological assessment to differential diag-nosis of depression. Thorough reviews can be found in LaRue (1992) and Kaszniak and Christensen (1994).**

【35】**Despite the large nunber of symptoms that can overlap between depression and dementia (e.g.， memory complaints， agitation， personali ty change， sleep disturbance， fatigue， increased dependency poor con-centration， diminished interest)， there are both cognitive and behavioral features that are helpful in differentiating， for example， Alzheimer’s dis-ease from depression. Kaszniak and Christensen (1994) describe a num-ber of history and behavioral features that can provide some utility in differentiation. They include (1) symptom duration (long in AD vs. short in depression)， (2) previous psychiatric history (unusual in AD vs. usual int depression)， (3) progression of symptoms (slow in AD vs. rapid in depression)， (4) patient’s own complaints of d

An acute episode of Wernicke's encephalopathy， characterized by acute onset of ataxic gait， nystagmus， ophthalmoplegia， and confusion， typically heralds the disease； these symptoms resolve within about a month upon receiving thiamine therapy. The residual deficits that com-prise Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome include severe retrograde and anterograde amnesia and other cognitive deficits (particularly executive dysfunction). General intellectual abilities and semantic knowledge are usually preserved in these patients .**

【24】**Alcohol-induced persisting dementia is usually mild and typically includes executive dysfunction and visuospatial deficits， along with memory disturbance. Unlike AD， patients with alcoholic dementia usu-ally have intact language abilities. The onset of dementia appears gradu-ally and may reflect not only heavy long-term alcohol use， but also the cognitive disturbances associated with cirrhosis of the liver 删除1:<u>(e.g.， atten-tion， coordination， memory， motor， information processing speed， and language dysfunction； see Cummings & Benson， 1992)</u>.**

【25】**DIFFERENTIATION OF DEMENTIA**

【26】**FROM NON-DEMENTING CONDITIONS**

【27】**Historically， defining the boundaries between normal age-related changes and the very earliest signs of dementia has been difficult， primar-ily because many of the early cognitive and functional changes of AD overlap with changes observed in normal aging (e.g.，complaints of mem-ory decline among older adults， less efficient learning and recall of new information， and slowed processing speed). Yet the increasing availability of pharmacologic treatments for dementia makes imperative the identifi-cation of accurate early markers that reliably differentiate dementia from normal aging or non-dementing conditions 删除1:<u>(Thal，1999)</u>. Clearly， the ear-liest detection of dementia will be of maximnal benefit when considering neuroprotective agents designed to impede the onset of dementia by slowing or preventing the degenerative neuropathologic processes.**

【28】**Normal Aging or the Preclinical Period of Dementia?**

**Biologic evidence suggests that Alzheimer’s disease may involve a long preclinical period of neuropathologic changes prior to the appearance of the full dementia syndrome . Katzman (1994) proposed a chronic disease model of AD， which holds that genetic factors， traumatic events， or other unknown factors predis-pose one to developing AD. An initiating factor (such as age) then trig-gers intracellular events that lead to neuritic degeneration， the formation of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles， and the loss of synapses and neurons. Over a period of time the neural degeneration is thought to gradually accumulate and reach a level that initiates the clinical symptoms of the dementia syndrome. This framework for understanding the development of AD suggests that cognitive deficits， structural volume loss， or functional (i.e.，cerebral metabolic or blood|删除0换行|flow) brain changes associaled with the disease also appear gradually. Thus， these changes might be identified before the degree of neural degeneration has reached a level necessary to produce clinically diag-nosable dementia (i.e.， when both cognitive and functional impairments are evident， as required by both DSM \[American Psychiatric Association，1994\] and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria \[McKhann et al.， 1984\]).**

【30】此段无关页码删除:<u>参考删除-1:<u>**Consistent with this framework， a growing body of evidence demon-strates that cognitive decrements can be detected several years or more prior to clinical diagnosis in nondemented individuals who subsequent-ly develop dementia 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.， 1994，1995，1999； Fuld， Masur， Blau， Crystal， & Aronson， 1990； Grober & Kawas， 1997； Howieson et al.， 1997； Katzman et al.， 1989； La Rue &Jarvik， 1980， 1987； Linn et al.， 1995； Masur， Fuld， Blau， Crystal，& Aronson， 1990， 1994；Petersen et al.， 1995)</u>， and the majority of these reeent studies indicate that measures of leatn-ing and memory are particularly effective in this regard 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.，1994，1995； Fuld et al.， 1990； Grober & Kawas， 1997； Howieson et al.， 1997； Linn et al.， 1995； Masur， Sliwinski， Lipton， Blau， & Crystal， 1994； Small， Basun， & Backman， 1998； Smith et al.， 1998； Zonderman et al.， 1995)</u>. This latter finding is not surprising， given that failure of recent memory is nsually the tnost prominent neuropsychologic feature during the early stages of AD 删除1:<u>(Welsh et al.，1991； Welsh， Butters， Hughes， Mohs， &Heyman 1992)</u>. Furthermore， numerous studies have shown that mea-sures of the ability to learn and retain new information are quite sensi-tive in differentiating between mild AD patients and normal older adults删除1:<u>(e.g.， Delis et al.， 1991； Kaszniak et al.， 1986； Petersen， Smith， Ivnik， Kokmen， & Tangalos， 1994； Storandt et al.， 1984； Welsh et al.，1991)</u>.**</u></u>

【31】**Milld Cognitive Impairment**

参考删除-1:<u>**Another recent diagnostic classification that attempts to define the bor-derland between normal aging and dementia has been forwarded by Petersen and colleagues， which they term Mild Cognitive Impairment删除1:<u>(MCI； Petersen et al.， 1995， 1996， 1999； Smith et al， 1998)</u>. By defini-tion， MCl involves a significant memory impairment (1.5 standard devi-ations below the mean for age)， the absence of impairment in other cognitive domains， and a lack of significant functional declines in activi-ties of daily living. Petersen and colleagues (1995) have longitudinally followed individuals who met criteria for MCI， but not for dementia， and have found that over several years of follow-up， these MCI patients evolved to dementia at a rate of approximately 15% per year. One of the factors that has been most useful in predicting which of these MCI|删除0换行|patients will subsequently develop dementia has been the presence of the apolipoprotein E E4 gene (ApoE-e4 allele； see Bondi， Salmon， &Kaszniak， 1996， for review). The results of Petersen and associates(1995)， as well as those of other investigators 删除1:<u>(Bondi et al.， 1995，1999； Small et al.， 1998； Smith et al.， 1998)</u>， indicate that ApoE is an important risk factor for AD that may be useful in predicting which patients with MCl are more likely to progress to dementia. However， a consensus workgroup convened to examine the diagnostic utility of ApoE genotyp-ing cautioned that the predictive value of ApoE genotype is marginal， especially given that some 35-40% of AD patients do not carry an ApoE-E4 allele 删除1:<u>(Mayeux et al.， 1998)</u>.**</u>

【33】**Depression**

【34】**One of the more difficult and challenging of differential diagnostic considerations in older adults is that of dementia versus depression. The neuropsychologist is often asked to determine whether an individ-ual is experiencing cognitive difficulty secondary to a mood disturbance or dementia. Further confounding this distinction is the realization that， in perhaps 20-30% of cases 删除1:<u>(Teri & Wagner， 1992)</u>， depression often co-exists in patients with dementia. We briefly describe some of the contributions of neuropsychological assessment to differential diag-nosis of depression. Thorough reviews can be found in LaRue (1992) and Kaszniak and Christensen (1994).**

【140】What makes a good doctor? One of many essential attributes is the ability to take a good history， appropriately examine， and apply sound clinical judgement to reach the correct diagnosis.

All 19 chapters in this book have the same format. Each starts with a patient’s history concerning a common complaint and asks you， the reader， to generate a differential diagnosis based upon the information supplied. This is then followed by the examination findings， thus helping you refine the diagnostic|删除0换行|process so that you are able to arrive at a single principal working diagnosis. The emergency management of this condition is then discussed.

【142】Our hope is that working through these cases will be enjoyable， and that you will refine your diagnostic skills.

【143】**Francis Morris Alan Fletcher**

【144】**Unconsciousness and Coma**

【145】_Roger Dalton_

【146】**CASE HISTORY**

【147】A 57-year-old man is found in an unconscious state at home. He was in bed when his wife left at 7.00 a.m. that morning to go to work. On her return home at 3.45 p.m.， he was still in the same position in bed， unrousable， incontinent of urine， and the cup of tea she had left for him was untouched. He has been unwell recently， and prescribed a course of antibiotics and co-codamol from his General Practitioner for a discharging ear infection. He suffers from hypertension， type 2 diabetes mellitus and long-standing depression. His medication list shows that he has been prescribed gliclazide 80 mg twice daily， atenolol 25 mg once daily， ramipril 5mg once daily and amitriptyline 25 mg once daily. He has no known allergies. His wife informs you that he has had bad headaches recently， but that no-one else at home has been unwell.

【148】This man is in a coma， which is defined as unrousable unrespon-siveness. Using the objective clinical assessment tool， the Glasgow Coma Score ， coma is defined as a score of 8 or less. Those patients with a score between 14 and 9 are defined as having altered consciousness and those with a top score of 15 are normal， alert and orientated. When considering a differential diagnosis for the cause of a patient's unresponsiveness it is important to consider those conditions that are easily reversible first.

【149】**Hypoglycaemia**

【150】The patient is a known diabetic. Hypoglycaemia or， less commonly， hyperglycaemia can result in altered consciousness and must be actively diagnosed and promptly treated. A simple bedside glu-cose test will identify abnormalities in blood glucose levels and will guide appropriate therapy.

【151】It is essential that any patient with confusion， altered conscious-ness， coma or focal neurological signs has their blood glucose esti-mated as part of the initial assessment. Neurological signs resulting from hypoglycaemia usually resolve quickly with treatment， though
