【6】etiology. However， the pediatric inherited metabolic disorders may be unmasked by stresses such as fever， illness， and trauma 删除2:<u>(Chapter 13)</u>， confounding the diagnosis.

【7】A common type of sudden-onset chorea in childhood is Sydenham chorea， seen following a streptococcal throat infection 删除2:<u>(Chapter 17)</u>. Cases usually resolve after a few weeks， but symptoms may be debilitating.

【8】**Subacute Onset**

【9】Development of chorea over days to weeks may suggest a metabolic process删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>， such as nonketotic hyperglycemia in a non-insulin-dependent dia-betic patient， although these patients can present quite acutely. Other metabolic disorders which present with this time frame include a range of electrolyte distur-bances such as hyper- 删除1:<u>(Sparacio et al.， 1976)</u> and hyponatremia 删除1:<u>(Piccolo et al.，2003； Tang et al.， 1981)</u>， hyper-删除1:<u>(Matsis et al.， 1989)</u> and hypocalcemia 删除1:<u>(Howdle et al.， 1979； Topakian et al.， 2006)</u>， or hypomagnesemia.

【10】Endocrine abnormalities related to thyroid or parathyroid disease may cause chorea 删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>， specifically hyperthyroidism 删除1:<u>(Fidler et al.， 1971； Fischbeck and Layzer， 1979； Lucantoni et al.， 1994)</u>. Hypo- and hyperparathyroidism have also been associated with chorea， which may be paroxysmal，likely due to distur-bances of calcium 删除1:<u>(Hattori and Yorifuji， 2000； Soffer et al.， 1977)</u>.

【11】A subacute presentation may be seen with prion diseases， specifically new vari-ant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease， related to bovine spongiform encephalopathy删除1:<u>(Bowen et al.， 2000； McKee and Talbot， 2003)</u> 删除2:<u>(Chapter 11)</u>， or with slowly grow-ing mass lesions 删除2:<u>(Chapter 16)</u>.

【12】A similar time course can be seen with paraneoplastic syndromes 删除1:<u>(Albin et al.，1988； Batchelor et al.， 1998； Dorban et al.， 2004； Kujawa et al.， 2001； Tani et al.，2000； Vernino et al.， 2002)</u> 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u> and has been reported with a variety of tumors， including renal， small cell lung， breast， and Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lym-phoma. The causative autoantibodies include anti-CRMP-5/CV2 删除1:<u>(Muehlschlegel et al.， 2005； Vernino et al.， 2002)</u>， anti-Hu 删除1:<u>(Dorban et al.， 2004)</u>， anti-Yo 删除1:<u>(Krolak-Salmon et al.， 2006)</u>， anti-NMDA receptor， and others.

【13】**Chronic Progressive Course**

【14】A slow disease course， progressing over a number of years， particularly when accompanied by cognitive or psychiatric findings， is likely to indicate a neurode-generative process， for example， due to HD 删除2:<u>(Chapter 3)</u>， the AD inherited ataxias删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>， a neuroacanthocytosis syndrome (Chapters 6，7)， or a neurodegen-eration with iron accumulation syndrome (Chapters 8-10).

【15】**Chronic Stable Chorea**

Choreiform movements which develop gradually but do not progress can some-times be attributed to use of a medication. either as a direct side effect or as a tardive syndrome 删除2:<u>(Chapter 14)</u>. Benign hereditary chorea 删除2:<u>(Chapter 4)</u> should also|删除0换行|be considered， particularly if there is childhood onset and an AD family history. This condition is due to mutations of thyroid transcription factor 1 (TITF-1)删除1:<u>(Breedveld et al.， 2002； Devos et al.， 2006； Mahajnah et al.， 2007； Willemsen et al.， 2005)</u>， also known as NKX2.1， although it may be genetically heterogeneous删除1:<u>(Bauer et al.， 2006)</u>. The chorea may respond to L-dopa 删除1:<u>(Asmus et al.，2005)</u>.

【17】A similar， relatively stable， temporal presentation may also be due to auto-immune processes， as in lupus 删除1:<u>(Font et al.， 1998； Watanabe and Onda， 2004)</u>， Sjogren syndrome 删除1:<u>(Venegas et al.， 2005)</u>， and antiphospholipid antibody syn-drome 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u>.

【18】**Episodic Chorea**

【19】The paroxysmal hyperkinetic disorders are more typically dystonic in nature， and thus， they have been classified with the genetic dystonias， although chorea can be a component 删除2:<u>(Chapter 19)</u>. The diagnosis of these disorders was previously based upon their phenomenology and precipitating factors， but this is being replaced by molecular identification. Many appear to be due to mutations of ion channels and to respond to anticonvulsants. More rarely， episodic chorea may be psychogenic in etiology 删除2:<u>(Chapter 21)</u>.

Episodes of dystonia and/or chorea typically occur at rest and may be precipitated by alcohol， caffeine， stress， extremes of temperature， fatigue， or fasting. Episodes are much less frequent than those of paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia， and only a few may occur in a month； but they tend to be more long-lasting and severe.

Episodes in these patients were precipitated by exercise， stress， alcohol consumption， and sleep deprivation and consisted of dystonia， choreoatherosis， and dysarthria. Spasticity also occurs and can persist between attacks.</u>

Episodes often resolve with age. Treatment with anticonvulsants is usually beneficial删除1:<u>(Chatterjee et al.， 2002； Huang et al.， 2005； Picard et al.， 1998； Tsao， 2004)</u>， sug-gesting a channelopathy. 【26】Patients with episodic ataxia 1 may sometimes manifest choreoathetosis during ataxic episodes 删除1:<u>(Gancher and Nutt， 1986)</u>. More typical features are dysarthria and persistent myokymia 删除1:<u>(Litt et al.， 1994； Lubbers et al.， 1995)</u>. Treatment with acetazolamide can be helpful.

【27】**Medical History**

【28】The medical history may be informative in the patient with chorea. In pediatric cases nonneurological features can be very helpful in indicating a specific inher-ited metabolic disorder 删除2:<u>(Chapter 13)</u>.

【29】Patients with endocrine disorders， especially diabetic patients with nonketotic hyperglycemia 删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>， and autoimmune disorders 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u> may develop chorea， in some cases as the presenting symptom. Patients with aceruloplasmin-emia typically have diabetes mellitus due to deposition of iron in the pancreas删除2:<u>(Chapter 10)</u>. One-third of patients with Friedreich ataxia also develop diabetes， which is thought to be due to mitochondrial dysfunction 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【30】Women of childbearing age should be evaluated for pregnancy (chorea gravi-darum) or may develop chorea related to estrogen-/progesterone-containing med-ications 删除1:<u>(Caviness and Muenter， 1991； Miranda et al.， 2004； Nausieda et al.，1979； Suchowersky and Muthipeedika， 2005)</u>. However， contradictorily， suppression of estrogen with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone may also result in chorea 删除1:<u>(Gironell et al.， 2008)</u>.

Correction of the hypothyroidism did not prevent development of the other features， including the chorea， suggesting that these were primary effects of the mutation rather than secondary to the hypothyroidism. Differences in the mutations in these two disorders may account for the varying severity.

【32】Polycythemia vera may be a cause of chorea 删除1:<u>(Cohen et al.， 1989； Nazabal et al.，2000)</u>， although it is unclear whether this is due to the presence of autoantibodies or to hyperviscosity resulting in basal ganglia ischemia.

【33】Celiac disease has been associated with a number of neurological complica-tions， most likely due to an autoimmune mechanism. Chorea may occasionally respond to a gluten-free diet 删除1:<u>(Pereira et al.， 2004)</u>.

【38】Abnormal susceptibility to infection and a predilection to develop cancers is seen in AT 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>. The gene for chronic granulomatous disease is adjacent to the gene for McLeod syndrome on the X chromosome. With improved thera-pies for the chronic， recurrent infections to which these boys are susceptible， it is likely that some of them with large X-chromosome deletions could later develop McLeod syndrome.

【39】A variety of movement disorders including chorea have been associated with human immunodeficiency viral (HIV) infection 删除1:<u>(Tse et al.， 2004)</u>. Sometimes these are due to a mass lesion， such as lymphoma or abscess 删除2:<u>(Chapter 16)</u>， whereas

【44】**Medication and Drug Use**

【45】A number of medications may cause chorea 删除2:<u>(Chapter 14)</u>， either as a direct， and often predictable， function of their action， as seen following L-dopa in Parkinson disease， or as a side effect.

【46】The effects of specific medications may suggest a relationship to the patho-physiology of chorea in other conditions， as information from animal models of L-dopa-induced dyskinesias may be used to further our understanding of mecha-nisms in other hyperkinetic disorders. The etiology of L-dopa-induced dyskine-sias in Parkinson disease， namely， an increase in dopaminergic stimulation within the putamen， can be inferred from the relationship to dosing with dopaminergic medications. However， to date， alterations have been observed in a large number of parameters related to different neurotransmitters involved in striatal function-ing， and agents with a variety of mechanisms of actions have been reported to reduce dyskinesias in animal models 删除1:<u>(Blandini， 2003； Brotchie et al.， 2005； Monville et al.， 2005； Papa and Chase， 1996)</u>.

【47】Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is more accurately described as “chorea”and appears after an interval of 3 months following the initiation of a dopamine-blocking med-ication 删除2:<u>(Chapter 14)</u>. In addition to the classic neuroleptics， TD has been reported with the atypical antipsychotics， including risperidone 删除1:<u>(Harrison and Goa， 2004)</u> and olanzapine 删除1:<u>(Bella and Piccoli， 2003； Bressan et al.，2004)</u>. The newer agents quetiapine， clozapine， aripiprazole， and ziprasidone may occasionally cause TD. Other dopaminergic antagonists， such as compazine and metoclopramide， may also be responsible.

【48】The timing of the emergence of the symptoms and the fact that TD often does not resolve (and may even worsen) with discontinuation of the medication make it hard to confirm or refute the association of other medications with this disorder， but selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)， lithium， and anticonvulsant medications have also been implicated.

【49】Chorea may be seen as a direct side effect of other medications， including gabapentin 删除1:<u>(Lai et al.， 2008； Twardowschy et al.， 2008； Zesiewicz et al.，2008)</u>， lamotrigine 删除1:<u>(Miller and Levsky，2008)</u>， and lithium 删除1:<u>(Stemper et al.， 2003)</u>.

【50】Stimulants in particular， including those used therapeutically 删除1:<u>(Weiner et al.， 1978)</u> as well as those used recreationally， such as amphetamine， cocaine， and specifi-cally “crack”cocaine， may result in chorea (“crack-dancing"). The mechanism of action of these agents， namely the release of dopamine， is probably the explana-tion for the appearance of the movement disorder. Usually the timing and the resolution of the movements with discontinuation of the offending agent make the diagnosis and treatment straightforward.

【51】**ASSOCIATED NEUROLOGICAL FEATURES**

【52】**Distribution of Chorea**

【53】Chorea typically looks identical regardless of the etiology. The exceptions to this are when the facial and lingual muscles are markedly involved or when there is asymmetric involvement of the limbs.

【54】Facial muscles alone are most commonly affected in neuroleptic-induced TD. Prominent orofacial and lingual involvement can be seen in ChAc and PKAN. In ChAc the tongue movements are dystonic and specifically induced by eating删除2:<u>(Chapter 6)</u>.

【55】Structural lesions are a common cause of unilateral chorea in adults， often due to a focal lesion involving the basal ganglia 删除2:<u>(Chapter 16)</u>. Another cause may be non-ketotic hyperglycemia， which is typically unilateral， for unknown reasons删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>.

【56】**Peripheral Neuropathy**

【57】参考删除-1:<u>Hyporeflexia and peripheral sensory changes suggestive of a peripheral neuro-pathic process are characteristic of the two core neuroacanthocytosis syndromes， ChAc (Rampoldi et al.， 2002； Walker et al.， 2006a，b) and McLeod syndrome. The other disorders in which peripheral neuropathy may be present in addition to chorea are some of the inherited ataxias， both AR (Friedreich ataxia \[Hanna et al.，1998； Spacey et al.， 2004； Zhu et al.， 2002\]，AOA1 \[Le Ber et al.， 2003b； Shahwan et al.， 2006\]， and AOA2 \[Moreira et al.， 2004\]) and AD (SCA 1， 2 and3 \[Geschwind et al.， 1997； Namekawa et al.， 2001\]) 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.</u>

【58】**Hyperreflexia**

【59】Hyperreflexia is seen in neurodegenerative disorders in which the cortex is also affected， for example， HD， HDL2， and the SCAs. Reflex asymmetry may serve to localize a focal lesion.

【61】**Ataxia**

【62】Ataxia and abnormal eye movements also suggest the inherited ataxias， which may be both AD and AR in inheritance 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>. Ataxia and hyperreflexia suggest SCA17 删除1:<u>(Schneider et al.， 2006； Stevanin et al.， 2003； Zuhlke et al.，2003； Zuhlke and Burk， 2007)</u> and DRPLA. However， the phenotype may be remark-ably variable， both within and between families， and ataxia may be absent.

【63】**Cognitive and Psychiatric Symptoms**

【64】Neurodegenerative causes of chorea are frequently associated with personality changes， subcortical dementia， and frank psychiatric disease 删除2:<u>(Chapter 20)</u>. This may be due to degenerative processes affecting the frontal cortex but also to involvement of the caudate nucleus in cortical-subcortical loops. These findings are being increasingly recognized as harbingers of frank neurological disease and can often be detected even when subtle by detailed neuropsychological testing.

【65】The use of neuroleptics for psychiatric symptoms preceding the appearance of a movement disorder may mask the diagnosis as neurological signs and symptoms may be erroneously attributed to the medication. Psychiatrists should be attuned to any atypical features of either psychiatric or neurological presentations.

【66】**Ophthalmological Findings**

【67】Abnormal eye movements are found in chorea of a variety of etiologies，including HD and ChAc， with intrusions of square-wave jerks. Impaired smooth pursuit and saccadic gaze， or ophthalmoplegia， may suggest a cerebellar disorder 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【68】Pigmentary retinopathy is indicative of PKAN and is an invariable feature of typical (young-onset) disease 删除2:<u>(Chapter 8)</u>. The characteristic telangiectactic blood vessels seen in the conjunctivae of the eye may be helpful in making the diagnosis of AT but may be absent in atypical， late-onset disease 删除1:<u>(Verhagen et al.， 2009)</u>删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【69】Other localophthalmologicalfindings mayindicate autoimmune disease删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u>.

【71】Seizures are seen in approximately 50% of patients with a neuroacanthocytosis syndrome (Chapters 6， 7). These can predate the appearance of the movement disorder by several years. Seizures can also be present in young-onset HD， although these patients tend to have an akinetic-rigid phenotype rather than chorea. 【17】A similar， relatively stable， temporal presentation may also be due to auto-immune processes， as in lupus 删除1:<u>(Font et al.， 1998； Watanabe and Onda， 2004)</u>， Sjogren syndrome 删除1:<u>(Venegas et al.， 2005)</u>， and antiphospholipid antibody syn-drome 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u>.

【18】**Episodic Chorea**

【19】The paroxysmal hyperkinetic disorders are more typically dystonic in nature， and thus， they have been classified with the genetic dystonias， although chorea can be a component 删除2:<u>(Chapter 19)</u>. The diagnosis of these disorders was previously based upon their phenomenology and precipitating factors， but this is being replaced by molecular identification. Many appear to be due to mutations of ion channels and to respond to anticonvulsants. More rarely， episodic chorea may be psychogenic in etiology 删除2:<u>(Chapter 21)</u>.

【20】Paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia (paroxysmal dystonic choreoathetosis， DYT8) is due to a mutation of the myofibrillogenesis regulator gene located at2q33 删除1:<u>(Friedman et al.， 2008； Rainier et al.， 2004)</u>， which may be involved in detoxifying alcohol and caffeine 删除1:<u>(Lee et al.， 2004)</u>. Episodes of dystonia and/or chorea typically occur at rest and may be precipitated by alcohol， caffeine， stress， extremes of temperature， fatigue， or fasting. Episodes are much less frequent than those of paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia， and only a few may occur in a month； but they tend to be more long-lasting and severe.

【21】参考删除-1:<u>Paroxysmal choreoathetosis with spasticity (DYT9) has been localized to1p.21-p13.3 删除1:<u>(Auburger et al.， 1996)</u>. Episodes in these patients were precipitated by exercise， stress， alcohol consumption， and sleep deprivation and consisted of dystonia， choreoatherosis， and dysarthria. Spasticity also occurs and can persist between attacks.</u>

【22】Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PKD； paroxysmal kinesigenic dystonia， DYT10) of childhood onset may be familial or sporadic and is characterized by very frequent， brief episodes of limb dystonia following movement. Episodes often resolve with age. Treatment with anticonvulsants is usually beneficial删除1:<u>(Chatterjee et al.， 2002； Huang et al.， 2005； Picard et al.， 1998； Tsao， 2004)</u>， sug-gesting a channelopathy. Other cases are associated with features such as seizures删除1:<u>(Cuenca-Leon et al.， 2002； Thiriaux et al.， 2002)</u> and have been termed“benign infantile convulsions and paroxysmal choreoathetosis”删除1:<u>(Szepetowski et al.， 1997)</u>.

【23】Paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia (DYT18) is an intermediate form with invol-untary movements developing following more prolonged exertion than PKD， which can last from minutes to hours. This syndrome is one of several neurological

【25】参考删除-1:<u>conditions， including seizures， due to mutations of the glucose transporter GLUT1删除1:<u>(Suls et al.， 2008； Weber et al.，2008)</u>.</u>

【26】Patients with episodic ataxia 1 may sometimes manifest choreoathetosis during ataxic episodes 删除1:<u>(Gancher and Nutt， 1986)</u>. More typical features are dysarthria and persistent myokymia 删除1:<u>(Litt et al.， 1994； Lubbers et al.， 1995)</u>. Treatment with acetazolamide can be helpful.

【27】**Medical History**

【28】The medical history may be informative in the patient with chorea. In pediatric cases nonneurological features can be very helpful in indicating a specific inher-ited metabolic disorder 删除2:<u>(Chapter 13)</u>.

【29】Patients with endocrine disorders， especially diabetic patients with nonketotic hyperglycemia 删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>， and autoimmune disorders 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u> may develop chorea， in some cases as the presenting symptom. Patients with aceruloplasmin-emia typically have diabetes mellitus due to deposition of iron in the pancreas删除2:<u>(Chapter 10)</u>. One-third of patients with Friedreich ataxia also develop diabetes， which is thought to be due to mitochondrial dysfunction 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【30】Women of childbearing age should be evaluated for pregnancy (chorea gravi-darum) or may develop chorea related to estrogen-/progesterone-containing med-ications 删除1:<u>(Caviness and Muenter， 1991； Miranda et al.， 2004； Nausieda et al.，1979； Suchowersky and Muthipeedika， 2005)</u>. Hormone replacement therapy may similarly be responsible， possibly due to sensitization of dopamine receptors by estrogens. However， contradictorily， suppression of estrogen with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone may also result in chorea 删除1:<u>(Gironell et al.， 2008)</u>.

【31】The gene identified as causing benign hereditary chorea has been reported as part of a multisystem disorder due to a mutation of the gene TITF-I 删除1:<u>(Breedveld et al.， 2002； Devos et al.， 2006； Mahajnah et al.， 2007； Willemsen et al.， 2005)</u>， which causes congenital hypothyroidism， hypotonia， and pulmonary problems删除1:<u>(Doyle et al.， 2004； Ferrara et al.， 2008； Glik et al.， 2008； Krude et al.， 2002)</u>删除2:<u>(Chapter 4)</u>. Correction of the hypothyroidism did not prevent development of the other features， including the chorea， suggesting that these were primary effects of the mutation rather than secondary to the hypothyroidism. Differences in the mutations in these two disorders may account for the varying severity.

【32】Polycythemia vera may be a cause of chorea 删除1:<u>(Cohen et al.， 1989； Nazabal et al.，2000)</u>， although it is unclear whether this is due to the presence of autoantibodies or to hyperviscosity resulting in basal ganglia ischemia.

【33】Celiac disease has been associated with a number of neurological complica-tions， most likely due to an autoimmune mechanism. Chorea may occasionally respond to a gluten-free diet 删除1:<u>(Pereira et al.， 2004)</u>.

Patients with hepatic disease and chorea should be evaluated for the only treat-able genetic movement disorder， Wilson disease. Chorea may occasionally be seen|删除0换行|删除1:<u>(Machado et al.， 2006)</u> but is not commonly reported as a presenting symptom. More typically， there is an asymmetric， coarse flapping tremor present at rest， with posture holding or with action. Dystonia， parkinsonism， and ataxia can be seen. A thorough evaluation is required， including ophthalmological slit-lamp examina-tion. It is unusual for patients to present with neurological disease in the absence of hepatic findings. Ceruloplasmin levels are typically decreased but may be deceptively raised as it is an acute-phase reactant. Twenty-four-hour copper excretion is elevated. Rarely， Kayser-Fleischer rings may be absent in late-onset disease 删除1:<u>(Ross et al.， 1985)</u>. If ceruloplasmin and 24-hour copper excretion are normal， hepatosplenomegaly in a patient with chorea suggests a neuroacantho-cytosis syndrome， either ChAc 删除1:<u>(Rampoldi et al.， 2002； Walker et al.， 2006a)</u>删除2:<u>(Chapter 6)</u> or McLeod syndrome 删除1:<u>(Rampoldi et al.， 2002)</u> 删除2:<u>(Chapter 7)</u>. Liver dis-ease due to a variety of etiologies may also cause acquired hepatocerebral degeneration， likely due to manganese deposition in the basal ganglia， which may be seen in brain MRI.

【35】A condition of poorly-defined etiology known as “post-pump chorea”may occur in children after undergoing open-heart surgery or cardiopulmonary bypass. This may be due to microemboli or a hyperviscosity syndrome and appears to reduce in incidence with improvements in technology and experience 删除1:<u>(Menache et al.， 2002)</u> 删除2:<u>(Chapter 13)</u>.

【36】Cardiac disease， specifically cardiomyopathy， is frequently found in Friedreich ataxia 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>. Similar findings， along with arrhythmias， are seen in McLeod syndrome 删除2:<u>(Chapter 7)</u>.

【37】In children with acute onset of chorea， evaluation for a recent upper respiratory tract infection by streptococcus group A， in consideration of Sydenham chorea删除2:<u>(Chapter 17)</u>， is essential. However， much more rarely， striatal necrosis may occur as a complication of measles encephalitis 删除1:<u>(Cambonie et al.， 2000)</u> or following undefined febrile illness 删除1:<u>(Yamamoto et al.， 1997)</u>. A similar picture can be seen after Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection 删除1:<u>(Zambrino et al.， 2000)</u>， with a mixture of chorea and dystonia， hyperreflexia， and encephalopathy. Chorea has also been reported in the setting of encephalopathy due to parvoviral infection 删除1:<u>(Fong and de Sousa， 2006)</u> and following herpes simplex encephalitis 删除1:<u>(Kullnat and Morse，2008)</u>.

【38】Abnormal susceptibility to infection and a predilection to develop cancers is seen in AT 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>. The gene for chronic granulomatous disease is adjacent to the gene for McLeod syndrome on the X chromosome. With improved thera-pies for the chronic， recurrent infections to which these boys are susceptible， it is likely that some of them with large X-chromosome deletions could later develop McLeod syndrome.

【39】A variety of movement disorders including chorea have been associated with human immunodeficiency viral (HIV) infection 删除1:<u>(Tse et al.， 2004)</u>. Sometimes these are due to a mass lesion， such as lymphoma or abscess 删除2:<u>(Chapter 16)</u>， whereas

【41】参考删除-1:in other cases they may be a direct result of HIV encephalopathy</mark>encephalopathy 删除1:<u>(Passarin et al.，2005； Sporer et al.， 2005)</u>.</u>

【42】Chorea has been reported following correction of hyponatremia causing central pontine myelinolysis 删除1:<u>(Tison et al.， 1991)</u>.

【43】Medical findings suggestive of cancer， such as weight loss， lymphadenopathy， chronic cough， and change in bowel habit， may be indicative of a paraneoplastic syndrome 删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u>， although the absence of these does not rule out this diag-nosis as tumor growth may be suppressed by the autoantibodies which are respon-sible for the paraneoplastic syndromes.

【44】**Medication and Drug Use**

【45】A number of medications may cause chorea 删除2:<u>(Chapter 14)</u>， either as a direct， and often predictable， function of their action， as seen following L-dopa in Parkinson disease， or as a side effect.

【46】The effects of specific medications may suggest a relationship to the patho-physiology of chorea in other conditions， as information from animal models of L-dopa-induced dyskinesias may be used to further our understanding of mecha-nisms in other hyperkinetic disorders. The etiology of L-dopa-induced dyskine-sias in Parkinson disease， namely， an increase in dopaminergic stimulation within the putamen， can be inferred from the relationship to dosing with dopaminergic medications. However， to date， alterations have been observed in a large number of parameters related to different neurotransmitters involved in striatal function-ing， and agents with a variety of mechanisms of actions have been reported to reduce dyskinesias in animal models 删除1:<u>(Blandini， 2003； Brotchie et al.， 2005； Monville et al.， 2005； Papa and Chase， 1996)</u>.

【47】Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is more accurately described as “chorea”and appears after an interval of 3 months following the initiation of a dopamine-blocking med-ication 删除2:<u>(Chapter 14)</u>. In addition to the classic neuroleptics， TD has been reported with the atypical antipsychotics， including risperidone 删除1:<u>(Harrison and Goa， 2004)</u> and olanzapine 删除1:<u>(Bella and Piccoli， 2003； Bressan et al.，2004)</u>. The newer agents quetiapine， clozapine， aripiprazole， and ziprasidone may occasionally cause TD. Other dopaminergic antagonists， such as compazine and metoclopramide， may also be responsible.

【48】The timing of the emergence of the symptoms and the fact that TD often does not resolve (and may even worsen) with discontinuation of the medication make it hard to confirm or refute the association of other medications with this disorder， but selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)， lithium， and anticonvulsant medications have also been implicated.

【49】Chorea may be seen as a direct side effect of other medications， including gabapentin 删除1:<u>(Lai et al.， 2008； Twardowschy et al.， 2008； Zesiewicz et al.，2008)</u>， lamotrigine 删除1:<u>(Miller and Levsky，2008)</u>， and lithium 删除1:<u>(Stemper et al.， 2003)</u>.

【50】Stimulants in particular， including those used therapeutically 删除1:<u>(Weiner et al.， 1978)</u> as well as those used recreationally， such as amphetamine， cocaine， and specifi-cally “crack”cocaine， may result in chorea (“crack-dancing"). The mechanism of action of these agents， namely the release of dopamine， is probably the explana-tion for the appearance of the movement disorder. Usually the timing and the resolution of the movements with discontinuation of the offending agent make the diagnosis and treatment straightforward.

【51】**ASSOCIATED NEUROLOGICAL FEATURES**

【52】**Distribution of Chorea**

【53】Chorea typically looks identical regardless of the etiology. The exceptions to this are when the facial and lingual muscles are markedly involved or when there is asymmetric involvement of the limbs.

【54】Facial muscles alone are most commonly affected in neuroleptic-induced TD. Prominent orofacial and lingual involvement can be seen in ChAc and PKAN. In ChAc the tongue movements are dystonic and specifically induced by eating删除2:<u>(Chapter 6)</u>.

【55】Structural lesions are a common cause of unilateral chorea in adults， often due to a focal lesion involving the basal ganglia 删除2:<u>(Chapter 16)</u>. Another cause may be non-ketotic hyperglycemia， which is typically unilateral， for unknown reasons删除2:<u>(Chapter 15)</u>.

【56】**Peripheral Neuropathy**

【57】参考删除-1:<u>Hyporeflexia and peripheral sensory changes suggestive of a peripheral neuro-pathic process are characteristic of the two core neuroacanthocytosis syndromes， ChAc (Rampoldi et al.， 2002； Walker et al.， 2006a，b) and McLeod syndrome. The other disorders in which peripheral neuropathy may be present in addition to chorea are some of the inherited ataxias， both AR (Friedreich ataxia \[Hanna et al.，1998； Spacey et al.， 2004； Zhu et al.， 2002\]，AOA1 \[Le Ber et al.， 2003b； Shahwan et al.， 2006\]， and AOA2 \[Moreira et al.， 2004\]) and AD (SCA 1， 2 and3 \[Geschwind et al.， 1997； Namekawa et al.， 2001\]) 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.</u>

【58】**Hyperreflexia**

【59】Hyperreflexia is seen in neurodegenerative disorders in which the cortex is also affected， for example， HD， HDL2， and the SCAs. Reflex asymmetry may serve to localize a focal lesion.

【60】删除5:<u>**I. INTRODUCTION**</u>

【61】**Ataxia**

【62】Ataxia and abnormal eye movements also suggest the inherited ataxias， which may be both AD and AR in inheritance 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>. Ataxia and hyperreflexia suggest SCA17 删除1:<u>(Schneider et al.， 2006； Stevanin et al.， 2003； Zuhlke et al.，2003； Zuhlke and Burk， 2007)</u> and DRPLA. However， the phenotype may be remark-ably variable， both within and between families， and ataxia may be absent.

【63】**Cognitive and Psychiatric Symptoms**

【64】Neurodegenerative causes of chorea are frequently associated with personality changes， subcortical dementia， and frank psychiatric disease 删除2:<u>(Chapter 20)</u>. This may be due to degenerative processes affecting the frontal cortex but also to involvement of the caudate nucleus in cortical-subcortical loops. These findings are being increasingly recognized as harbingers of frank neurological disease and can often be detected even when subtle by detailed neuropsychological testing.

【65】The use of neuroleptics for psychiatric symptoms preceding the appearance of a movement disorder may mask the diagnosis as neurological signs and symptoms may be erroneously attributed to the medication. Psychiatrists should be attuned to any atypical features of either psychiatric or neurological presentations.

【66】**Ophthalmological Findings**

【67】Abnormal eye movements are found in chorea of a variety of etiologies，including HD and ChAc， with intrusions of square-wave jerks. Impaired smooth pursuit and saccadic gaze， or ophthalmoplegia， may suggest a cerebellar disorder 删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【68】Pigmentary retinopathy is indicative of PKAN and is an invariable feature of typical (young-onset) disease 删除2:<u>(Chapter 8)</u>. The characteristic telangiectactic blood vessels seen in the conjunctivae of the eye may be helpful in making the diagnosis of AT but may be absent in atypical， late-onset disease 删除1:<u>(Verhagen et al.， 2009)</u>删除2:<u>(Chapter 12)</u>.

【69】Other localophthalmologicalfindings mayindicate autoimmune disease删除2:<u>(Chapter 18)</u>.

【70】**Seizures**

【71】Seizures are seen in approximately 50% of patients with a neuroacanthocytosis syndrome (Chapters 6， 7). These can predate the appearance of the movement disorder by several years. Seizures can also be present in young-onset HD， although these patients tend to have an akinetic-rigid phenotype rather than chorea. Diagnosis of a bone lesion as originating from cartilage is usually a simple task for the radiologist. The lesion’s|删除0换行|radiolucent matrix， scalloped margin， and annular， punctate， or comma-shaped calcifications usually suf-fice to establish its chondrogenic nature . However， whether a cartilage tumor is benign or malig-nant is sometimes extremely difficult for the radiologist and the pathologist to determine (33，49，62，70).

【87】All cartilage tumors， whether benign or malignant， exhibit a positive reaction for S-100 protein (54). This is sometimes diagnostically useful， as most other bone tumors do not display this reaction. Histologically， carti-lage tumors are usually recognized by the features of their intercellular matrix， which has a uniformly translu-cent appearance and contains less collagen compared with the intercellular matrix of osteoblastic tumors， such as osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The tumor cells themselves are usually located in rounded spaces (lacu-nae)， as in normal cartilage. In benign cartilage tumors， such as enchondroma， the tissue is sparsely cellular . The cells， typically with small， dark-staining nuclei， fail to show the cytologic features that are characteristic of chondrosarcoma， such as large nuclei； pleomor-phism；large， swollen chondroblastic and double nuclei； and mitoses. The tumor tissue is usually avascular， and areas of degenerate and calcified matrix are common. Calcification is sometimes followed by vascularization and replacement by bone， as in normal endochondral ossification. Because of their slow growth， enchondro-mas erode and expand the overlying cortical bone  but do not invade it， unlike chondrosarcomas. Nevertheless， some slow-growing， low-grade chondrosar-

【89】通用删除16(英):<u>Figure 3-2 Histopathology of a benign cartilage lesion. Sparsely cellular tissue and uniform-sized chondrocytes lo-cated in rounded lacunae are characteristic features of en-chondroma (hematoxylin and eosin， original magnification×235).</u>

【90】comas can masquerade as enchondromas， and some aggressive-looking benign cartilage lesions may be mis-takenly diagnosed as chondrosarcomas. Moreover， it is important to be aware of the capricious biological behav- _1or_ ior displayed by cartilage tumors. Some benign-appear-ing lesions of cartilage may behave in an aggressive or malignant manner， whereas tumors that present an omi-nous appearance on radiologic or histologic examina-tion may show limited progression.

【91】Clinically， malignancy is suggested by a variety of signs， including development of pain in a previously asymptomatic lesion (e.g.， malignant transtormation of enchondroma to chondrosarcoma)， development of swelling or a mass at the site of a lesion， or rapid growth of a lesion (e.g.， malignant transformation of osteochon-droma to chondrosarcoma). Radiologically， the pres-ence of a periosteal reaction， destruction of the cortex， and a soft tissue mass are almost pathognomonic fea-tures of malignancy (25). The histopathologic features of a malignant cartilage tumor include the presence of hypercellular and pleomorphic tumor tissue， apprecia-ble numbers of plump cells with large or double nuclei， invasion (permeation) of bone trabeculae， and infiltra-tion of Haversian systems and bone marrow . However， these obvious features of malignancy may be not so prominent in biopsy specimen， or only a few areas in such a specimen may reveal the diagnostic features of malignancy. As Dahlin and Unni (13) pointed out， in the pathologic evaluation it is necessary to examine many fields in these tumors to be certain that there is sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of malignancy be-cause evidence that a tumor is a chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma is frequently found in iso-lated areas within the mass. Therefore， it is of para-mount importance to obtain biopsy specimens from several areas of a tumor. Close cooperation among the clinician， the radiologist， and the pathologist in review-ing the history， the radiologic examination， and the biopsy specimens is crucial to reaching a conclusion on the exact nature of a cartilage lesion.

【93】From the radiologic standpoint， the differential diagnosis of cartilage lesions should focus on the fol-lowing three points：

【94】1\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from the noncartilaginous lesions (e.g.， calcifying enchon-droma from bone infarct； enchondroma located near the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor， osteoarthritic geode， or intraosseous gan-glion； or chondromyxoid fibroma from aneurys-mal bone cyst).

【95】2\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from a malignant one (e.g.， enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma； osteochondroma from exostotic chondrosarcoma； periosteal chondroma from periosteal chondrosarcoma； orsynovial chondromatosis from synovial chondrosarcoma).

【96】3.Distinguishing a malignant cartilage tumor from a noncartilaginous lesion \[e.g.， chondrosarcoma at the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor or from malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH)； or periosteal chondrosarcomafroomm periostealOS-teosarcoma.

【97】From the histopathologic standpoint，because the mi-croscopic features of cartilage lesions are obvious and characteristic， focus should be directed to the following：

【98】1\. Recognition of the varieties of benign cartilage tu-mors (e.g.， enchondroma， periosteal chondroma， chondroblastoma， chondromyxoid fibroma) and various subtypes of chondrosarcoma (e.g.， clear cell， mesenchymal， or periosteal).

【99】2\. Recognition of benign versus malignant tumor(e.g.， enchondroma vs. well-differentiated chon-drosarcoma； chondromyxoid fibroma vs. myxoid chondrosarcoma； or chondroblastoma vs. mes-enchymal chondrosarcoma).

【100】**3\. Differentiation of chondrosarcoma from other malignant tumors that contain cartilage (e.g. from chondroblastic osteosarcoma or periosteal osteosarcoma).**

【101】Benign Lesions

【102】**Enchondroma**

Enchondroma is the second most common benign tu-mor of bone and is characterized by the formation of mature hyaline cartilage. It constitutes about 10% of all benign bone tumors and represents the most common tumor of the phalanges of the hand. Several theories have been postulated regarding its etiology. Among these is that the enchondroma develops from abnor-mal zones of dysplastic chondrocytes in the growth plate. These abnormal foci fail to undergo normal en-dochondral ossification； instead， they are deposited within the metaphysis and， as the bone grows， are dis-placed into the diaphysis (49). Customarily， a lesion lo-cated centrally in the bone is called an enchondroma， whereas one located outside the cortex is called a chon-droma (periosteal or juxtacortical). Separate groups|删除0换行|consist of lesions (a) located in the soft tissues and (b) located in the joint， bursa， or in the tendon sheath. The former are called soft tissue chondromas and the latter synovial chondromatosis (69)

【104】**_Clinical Presentation_**

【105】Although the tumor may occur at any age， most cases arise between the second and fourth decades； there is no sex predilection. The short， tubular bones of the hand and foot (phalanges， metacarpals， and metatarsals) are preferred sites， followed in frequency by the femur， humerus， tibia， and ribs . The lesion is often asymptomatic and usually is discovered incidentally due to a pathologic fracture through the tumor.

【106】The single most important complication of the le-sion is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. In a solitary enchondroma this occurs predominantly in a long or flat bone and almost never in a short tubu-lar bone. An important clinical sign is development of pain at the site of the lesion in a previously asympto-matic patient and in the absence of a fracture.

【107】**_Imaging_**

【108】Radiography is usually sufficient to demonstrate the le-sion and to establish its chondroid character. In short. tubular bones， the lesion is often entirely radiolucent， but in long bones it may display visible calcifi-cations(24). This flocculent mineralization usually assumes the form of dots， rings， and arcs， giving a“pop-corn”appearance . If the calcifications are ex-tensive， the lesion is called a calcifying enchondroma. The cortex is usually thinned and expanded in a symmetric， fusiform fashion. The often cloudy or hazy appearance of a lesion provides a clue to its chon-droid composition (18). The lesion can also be recog nized by scalloped inner cortical margins， reflecting the lobular growth pattern of cartilage . Computedtomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (aMnRoIe) ramnaayy ffaurrtthheerr daelineate the tumor and more pre-cisely localize it in the bone . Because in long bones enchondroma may present as a radiolucent lesion with poorly defined margins， particularly in areas where trabeculae are sparse or absent (diaphysis)， MRI may be extremely helpful in revealing the exact size and extent of the tumor  (74). Like most cartilaginous and fibrous lesions， enchondroma exhibits low to inter-mediate signal intensity on Tl-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. Diagnosis of a bone lesion as originating from cartilage is usually a simple task for the radiologist. The lesion’s|删除0换行|radiolucent matrix， scalloped margin， and annular， punctate， or comma-shaped calcifications usually suf-fice to establish its chondrogenic nature . However， whether a cartilage tumor is benign or malig-nant is sometimes extremely difficult for the radiologist and the pathologist to determine (33，49，62，70).

【87】All cartilage tumors， whether benign or malignant， exhibit a positive reaction for S-100 protein (54). This is sometimes diagnostically useful， as most other bone tumors do not display this reaction. Histologically， carti-lage tumors are usually recognized by the features of their intercellular matrix， which has a uniformly translu-cent appearance and contains less collagen compared with the intercellular matrix of osteoblastic tumors， such as osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The tumor cells themselves are usually located in rounded spaces (lacu-nae)， as in normal cartilage. In benign cartilage tumors， such as enchondroma， the tissue is sparsely cellular . The cells， typically with small， dark-staining nuclei， fail to show the cytologic features that are characteristic of chondrosarcoma， such as large nuclei； pleomor-phism；large， swollen chondroblastic and double nuclei； and mitoses. The tumor tissue is usually avascular， and areas of degenerate and calcified matrix are common. Calcification is sometimes followed by vascularization and replacement by bone， as in normal endochondral ossification. Because of their slow growth， enchondro-mas erode and expand the overlying cortical bone  but do not invade it， unlike chondrosarcomas. Nevertheless， some slow-growing， low-grade chondrosar-

Moreover， it is important to be aware of the capricious biological behav- _1or_ ior displayed by cartilage tumors. Some benign-appear-ing lesions of cartilage may behave in an aggressive or malignant manner， whereas tumors that present an omi-nous appearance on radiologic or histologic examina-tion may show limited progression.

【91】Clinically， malignancy is suggested by a variety of signs， including development of pain in a previously asymptomatic lesion (e.g.， malignant transtormation of enchondroma to chondrosarcoma)， development of swelling or a mass at the site of a lesion， or rapid growth of a lesion (e.g.， malignant transformation of osteochon-droma to chondrosarcoma). Radiologically， the pres-ence of a periosteal reaction， destruction of the cortex， and a soft tissue mass are almost pathognomonic fea-tures of malignancy (25). The histopathologic features of a malignant cartilage tumor include the presence of hypercellular and pleomorphic tumor tissue， apprecia-ble numbers of plump cells with large or double nuclei， invasion (permeation) of bone trabeculae， and infiltra-tion of Haversian systems and bone marrow . However， these obvious features of malignancy may be not so prominent in biopsy specimen， or only a few areas in such a specimen may reveal the diagnostic features of malignancy. As Dahlin and Unni (13) pointed out， in the pathologic evaluation it is necessary to examine many fields in these tumors to be certain that there is sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of malignancy be-cause evidence that a tumor is a chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma is frequently found in iso-lated areas within the mass. Therefore， it is of para-mount importance to obtain biopsy specimens from several areas of a tumor. Close cooperation among the clinician， the radiologist， and the pathologist in review-ing the history， the radiologic examination， and the biopsy specimens is crucial to reaching a conclusion on the exact nature of a cartilage lesion.

【94】1\. 【95】2\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from a malignant one (e.g.， enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma； osteochondroma from exostotic chondrosarcoma； periosteal chondroma from periosteal chondrosarcoma； orsynovial chondromatosis from synovial chondrosarcoma).

【97】From the histopathologic standpoint，because the mi-croscopic features of cartilage lesions are obvious and characteristic， focus should be directed to the following：

【98】1\. Recognition of the varieties of benign cartilage tu-mors (e.g.， enchondroma， periosteal chondroma， chondroblastoma， chondromyxoid fibroma) and various subtypes of chondrosarcoma (e.g.， clear cell， mesenchymal， or periosteal).

【99】2\. Recognition of benign versus malignant tumor(e.g.， enchondroma vs. well-differentiated chon-drosarcoma； chondromyxoid fibroma vs. myxoid chondrosarcoma； or chondroblastoma vs. mes-enchymal chondrosarcoma).

【100】**3\. Differentiation of chondrosarcoma from other malignant tumors that contain cartilage (e.g. from chondroblastic osteosarcoma or periosteal osteosarcoma).**

【101】Benign Lesions

【102】**Enchondroma**

Enchondroma is the second most common benign tu-mor of bone and is characterized by the formation of mature hyaline cartilage. It constitutes about 10% of all benign bone tumors and represents the most common tumor of the phalanges of the hand. Several theories have been postulated regarding its etiology. Among these is that the enchondroma develops from abnor-mal zones of dysplastic chondrocytes in the growth plate. These abnormal foci fail to undergo normal en-dochondral ossification； instead， they are deposited within the metaphysis and， as the bone grows， are dis-placed into the diaphysis (49). Customarily， a lesion lo-cated centrally in the bone is called an enchondroma， whereas one located outside the cortex is called a chon-droma (periosteal or juxtacortical). Separate groups|删除0换行|consist of lesions (a) located in the soft tissues and (b) located in the joint， bursa， or in the tendon sheath. The former are called soft tissue chondromas and the latter synovial chondromatosis (69)

【104】**_Clinical Presentation_**

【105】Although the tumor may occur at any age， most cases arise between the second and fourth decades； there is no sex predilection. The short， tubular bones of the hand and foot (phalanges， metacarpals， and metatarsals) are preferred sites， followed in frequency by the femur， humerus， tibia， and ribs . The lesion is often asymptomatic and usually is discovered incidentally due to a pathologic fracture through the tumor.

【106】The single most important complication of the le-sion is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. In a solitary enchondroma this occurs predominantly in a long or flat bone and almost never in a short tubu-lar bone. An important clinical sign is development of pain at the site of the lesion in a previously asympto-matic patient and in the absence of a fracture.

【107】**_Imaging_**

【108】Radiography is usually sufficient to demonstrate the le-sion and to establish its chondroid character. In short. tubular bones， the lesion is often entirely radiolucent， but in long bones it may display visible calcifi-cations(24). This flocculent mineralization usually assumes the form of dots， rings， and arcs， giving a“pop-corn”appearance . If the calcifications are ex-tensive， the lesion is called a calcifying enchondroma. The cortex is usually thinned and expanded in a symmetric， fusiform fashion. The often cloudy or hazy appearance of a lesion provides a clue to its chon-droid composition (18). The lesion can also be recog nized by scalloped inner cortical margins， reflecting the lobular growth pattern of cartilage . Computedtomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (aMnRoIe) ramnaayy ffaurrtthheerr daelineate the tumor and more pre-cisely localize it in the bone . Because in long bones enchondroma may present as a radiolucent lesion with poorly defined margins， particularly in areas where trabeculae are sparse or absent (diaphysis)， MRI may be extremely helpful in revealing the exact size and extent of the tumor  (74). Like most cartilaginous and fibrous lesions， enchondroma exhibits low to inter-mediate signal intensity on Tl-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. Diagnosis of a bone lesion as originating from cartilage is usually a simple task for the radiologist. The lesion’s|删除0换行|radiolucent matrix， scalloped margin， and annular， punctate， or comma-shaped calcifications usually suf-fice to establish its chondrogenic nature . However， whether a cartilage tumor is benign or malig-nant is sometimes extremely difficult for the radiologist and the pathologist to determine (33，49，62，70).

【87】All cartilage tumors， whether benign or malignant， exhibit a positive reaction for S-100 protein (54). This is sometimes diagnostically useful， as most other bone tumors do not display this reaction. Histologically， carti-lage tumors are usually recognized by the features of their intercellular matrix， which has a uniformly translu-cent appearance and contains less collagen compared with the intercellular matrix of osteoblastic tumors， such as osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The tumor cells themselves are usually located in rounded spaces (lacu-nae)， as in normal cartilage. In benign cartilage tumors， such as enchondroma， the tissue is sparsely cellular . The cells， typically with small， dark-staining nuclei， fail to show the cytologic features that are characteristic of chondrosarcoma， such as large nuclei； pleomor-phism；large， swollen chondroblastic and double nuclei； and mitoses. The tumor tissue is usually avascular， and areas of degenerate and calcified matrix are common. Calcification is sometimes followed by vascularization and replacement by bone， as in normal endochondral ossification. Because of their slow growth， enchondro-mas erode and expand the overlying cortical bone  but do not invade it， unlike chondrosarcomas. Nevertheless， some slow-growing， low-grade chondrosar-

Moreover， it is important to be aware of the capricious biological behav- _1or_ ior displayed by cartilage tumors. Some benign-appear-ing lesions of cartilage may behave in an aggressive or malignant manner， whereas tumors that present an omi-nous appearance on radiologic or histologic examina-tion may show limited progression.

【91】Clinically， malignancy is suggested by a variety of signs， including development of pain in a previously asymptomatic lesion (e.g.， malignant transtormation of enchondroma to chondrosarcoma)， development of swelling or a mass at the site of a lesion， or rapid growth of a lesion (e.g.， malignant transformation of osteochon-droma to chondrosarcoma). Radiologically， the pres-ence of a periosteal reaction， destruction of the cortex， and a soft tissue mass are almost pathognomonic fea-tures of malignancy (25). The histopathologic features of a malignant cartilage tumor include the presence of hypercellular and pleomorphic tumor tissue， apprecia-ble numbers of plump cells with large or double nuclei， invasion (permeation) of bone trabeculae， and infiltra-tion of Haversian systems and bone marrow . However， these obvious features of malignancy may be not so prominent in biopsy specimen， or only a few areas in such a specimen may reveal the diagnostic features of malignancy. As Dahlin and Unni (13) pointed out， in the pathologic evaluation it is necessary to examine many fields in these tumors to be certain that there is sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of malignancy be-cause evidence that a tumor is a chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma is frequently found in iso-lated areas within the mass. Therefore， it is of para-mount importance to obtain biopsy specimens from several areas of a tumor. Close cooperation among the clinician， the radiologist， and the pathologist in review-ing the history， the radiologic examination， and the biopsy specimens is crucial to reaching a conclusion on the exact nature of a cartilage lesion.

【94】1\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from the noncartilaginous lesions (e.g.， calcifying enchon-droma from bone infarct； enchondroma located near the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor， osteoarthritic geode， or intraosseous gan-glion； or chondromyxoid fibroma from aneurys-mal bone cyst).

【95】2\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from a malignant one (e.g.， enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma； osteochondroma from exostotic chondrosarcoma； periosteal chondroma from periosteal chondrosarcoma； orsynovial chondromatosis from synovial chondrosarcoma).

【96】3.Distinguishing a malignant cartilage tumor from a noncartilaginous lesion \[e.g.， chondrosarcoma at the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor or from malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH)； or periosteal chondrosarcomafroomm periostealOS-teosarcoma.

【97】From the histopathologic standpoint，because the mi-croscopic features of cartilage lesions are obvious and characteristic， focus should be directed to the following：

【98】1\. Recognition of the varieties of benign cartilage tu-mors (e.g.， enchondroma， periosteal chondroma， chondroblastoma， chondromyxoid fibroma) and various subtypes of chondrosarcoma (e.g.， clear cell， mesenchymal， or periosteal).

【99】2\. Recognition of benign versus malignant tumor(e.g.， enchondroma vs. well-differentiated chon-drosarcoma； chondromyxoid fibroma vs. myxoid chondrosarcoma； or chondroblastoma vs. mes-enchymal chondrosarcoma).

【100】**3\. Differentiation of chondrosarcoma from other malignant tumors that contain cartilage (e.g. from chondroblastic osteosarcoma or periosteal osteosarcoma).**

【101】Benign Lesions

【102】**Enchondroma**

Enchondroma is the second most common benign tu-mor of bone and is characterized by the formation of mature hyaline cartilage. It constitutes about 10% of all benign bone tumors and represents the most common tumor of the phalanges of the hand. Several theories have been postulated regarding its etiology. Among these is that the enchondroma develops from abnor-mal zones of dysplastic chondrocytes in the growth plate. These abnormal foci fail to undergo normal en-dochondral ossification； instead， they are deposited within the metaphysis and， as the bone grows， are dis-placed into the diaphysis (49). Customarily， a lesion lo-cated centrally in the bone is called an enchondroma， whereas one located outside the cortex is called a chon-droma (periosteal or juxtacortical). Separate groups|删除0换行|consist of lesions (a) located in the soft tissues and (b) located in the joint， bursa， or in the tendon sheath. The former are called soft tissue chondromas and the latter synovial chondromatosis (69)

【104】**_Clinical Presentation_**

【105】Although the tumor may occur at any age， most cases arise between the second and fourth decades； there is no sex predilection. The short， tubular bones of the hand and foot (phalanges， metacarpals， and metatarsals) are preferred sites， followed in frequency by the femur， humerus， tibia， and ribs . The lesion is often asymptomatic and usually is discovered incidentally due to a pathologic fracture through the tumor.

【106】The single most important complication of the le-sion is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. In a solitary enchondroma this occurs predominantly in a long or flat bone and almost never in a short tubu-lar bone. An important clinical sign is development of pain at the site of the lesion in a previously asympto-matic patient and in the absence of a fracture.

【107】**_Imaging_**

【108】Radiography is usually sufficient to demonstrate the le-sion and to establish its chondroid character. In short. tubular bones， the lesion is often entirely radiolucent， but in long bones it may display visible calcifi-cations(24). This flocculent mineralization usually assumes the form of dots， rings， and arcs， giving a“pop-corn”appearance . If the calcifications are ex-tensive， the lesion is called a calcifying enchondroma. The cortex is usually thinned and expanded in a symmetric， fusiform fashion. The often cloudy or hazy appearance of a lesion provides a clue to its chon-droid composition (18). The lesion can also be recog nized by scalloped inner cortical margins， reflecting the lobular growth pattern of cartilage . Computedtomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (aMnRoIe) ramnaayy ffaurrtthheerr daelineate the tumor and more pre-cisely localize it in the bone . Because in long bones enchondroma may present as a radiolucent lesion with poorly defined margins， particularly in areas where trabeculae are sparse or absent (diaphysis)， MRI may be extremely helpful in revealing the exact size and extent of the tumor  (74). Like most cartilaginous and fibrous lesions， enchondroma exhibits low to inter-mediate signal intensity on Tl-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. Diagnosis of a bone lesion as originating from cartilage is usually a simple task for the radiologist. The lesion’s|删除0换行|radiolucent matrix， scalloped margin， and annular， punctate， or comma-shaped calcifications usually suf-fice to establish its chondrogenic nature . However， whether a cartilage tumor is benign or malig-nant is sometimes extremely difficult for the radiologist and the pathologist to determine <mark>(33，49，62，70).</mark>

【87】All cartilage tumors， whether benign or malignant， exhibit a positive reaction for S-100 protein (54). This is sometimes diagnostically useful， as most other bone tumors do not display this reaction. Histologically， carti-lage tumors are usually recognized by the features of their intercellular matrix， which has a uniformly translu-cent appearance and contains less collagen compared with the intercellular matrix of osteoblastic tumors， such as osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The tumor cells themselves are usually located in rounded spaces (lacu-nae)， as in normal cartilage. In benign cartilage tumors， such as enchondroma， the tissue is sparsely cellular . The cells， typically with small， dark-staining nuclei， fail to show the cytologic features that are characteristic of chondrosarcoma， such as large nuclei； pleomor-phism；large， swollen chondroblastic and double nuclei； and mitoses. The tumor tissue is usually avascular， and areas of degenerate and calcified matrix are common. Calcification is sometimes followed by vascularization and replacement by bone， as in normal endochondral ossification. Because of their slow growth， enchondro-mas erode and expand the overlying cortical bone  but do not invade it， unlike chondrosarcomas. Nevertheless， some slow-growing， low-grade chondrosar-

Moreover， it is important to be aware of the capricious biological behav- _1or_ ior displayed by cartilage tumors. Some benign-appear-ing lesions of cartilage may behave in an aggressive or malignant manner， whereas tumors that present an omi-nous appearance on radiologic or histologic examina-tion may show limited progression.

【91】Clinically， malignancy is suggested by a variety of signs， including development of pain in a previously asymptomatic lesion (e.g.， malignant transtormation of enchondroma to chondrosarcoma)， development of swelling or a mass at the site of a lesion， or rapid growth of a lesion (e.g.， malignant transformation of osteochon-droma to chondrosarcoma). Radiologically， the pres-ence of a periosteal reaction， destruction of the cortex， and a soft tissue mass are almost pathognomonic fea-tures of malignancy (25). The histopathologic features of a malignant cartilage tumor include the presence of hypercellular and pleomorphic tumor tissue， apprecia-ble numbers of plump cells with large or double nuclei， invasion (permeation) of bone trabeculae， and infiltra-tion of Haversian systems and bone marrow . However， these obvious features of malignancy may be not so prominent in biopsy specimen， or only a few areas in such a specimen may reveal the diagnostic features of malignancy. As Dahlin and Unni (13) pointed out， in the pathologic evaluation it is necessary to examine many fields in these tumors to be certain that there is sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of malignancy be-cause evidence that a tumor is a chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma is frequently found in iso-lated areas within the mass. Therefore， it is of para-mount importance to obtain biopsy specimens from several areas of a tumor. Close cooperation among the clinician， the radiologist， and the pathologist in review-ing the history， the radiologic examination， and the biopsy specimens is crucial to reaching a conclusion on the exact nature of a cartilage lesion.

【93】From the radiologic standpoint， the differential diagnosis of cartilage lesions should focus on the fol-lowing three points：

【94】1\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from the noncartilaginous lesions (e.g.， calcifying enchon-droma from bone infarct； enchondroma located near the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor， osteoarthritic geode， or intraosseous gan-glion； or chondromyxoid fibroma from aneurys-mal bone cyst).

【95】2\. Distinguishing a benign cartilage tumor from a malignant one (e.g.， enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma； osteochondroma from exostotic chondrosarcoma； periosteal chondroma from periosteal chondrosarcoma； orsynovial chondromatosis from synovial chondrosarcoma).

【96】3.Distinguishing a malignant cartilage tumor from a noncartilaginous lesion \[e.g.， chondrosarcoma at the articular end of bone from giant cell tumor or from malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH)； or periosteal chondrosarcomafroomm periostealOS-teosarcoma.

【97】From the histopathologic standpoint，because the mi-croscopic features of cartilage lesions are obvious and characteristic， focus should be directed to the following：

【98】1\. Recognition of the varieties of benign cartilage tu-mors (e.g.， enchondroma， periosteal chondroma， chondroblastoma， chondromyxoid fibroma) and various subtypes of chondrosarcoma (e.g.， clear cell， mesenchymal， or periosteal).

【99】2\. Recognition of benign versus malignant tumor(e.g.， enchondroma vs. well-differentiated chon-drosarcoma； chondromyxoid fibroma vs. myxoid chondrosarcoma； or chondroblastoma vs. mes-enchymal chondrosarcoma).

【100】**3\. Differentiation of chondrosarcoma from other malignant tumors that contain cartilage (e.g. from chondroblastic osteosarcoma or periosteal osteosarcoma).**

【101】Benign Lesions

【102】**Enchondroma**

Enchondroma is the second most common benign tu-mor of bone and is characterized by the formation of mature hyaline cartilage. It constitutes about 10% of all benign bone tumors and represents the most common tumor of the phalanges of the hand. Several theories have been postulated regarding its etiology. Among these is that the enchondroma develops from abnor-mal zones of dysplastic chondrocytes in the growth plate. These abnormal foci fail to undergo normal en-dochondral ossification； instead， they are deposited within the metaphysis and， as the bone grows， are dis-placed into the diaphysis (49). Customarily， a lesion lo-cated centrally in the bone is called an enchondroma， whereas one located outside the cortex is called a chon-droma (periosteal or juxtacortical). Separate groups|删除0换行|consist of lesions (a) located in the soft tissues and (b) located in the joint， bursa， or in the tendon sheath. The former are called soft tissue chondromas and the latter synovial chondromatosis (69)

【104】**_Clinical Presentation_**

【105】Although the tumor may occur at any age， most cases arise between the second and fourth decades； there is no sex predilection. The short， tubular bones of the hand and foot (phalanges， metacarpals， and metatarsals) are preferred sites， followed in frequency by the femur， humerus， tibia， and ribs . The lesion is often asymptomatic and usually is discovered incidentally due to a pathologic fracture through the tumor.

【106】The single most important complication of the le-sion is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. In a solitary enchondroma this occurs predominantly in a long or flat bone and almost never in a short tubu-lar bone. An important clinical sign is development of pain at the site of the lesion in a previously asympto-matic patient and in the absence of a fracture.

【107】**_Imaging_**

【108】Radiography is usually sufficient to demonstrate the le-sion and to establish its chondroid character. In short. tubular bones， the lesion is often entirely radiolucent， but in long bones it may display visible calcifi-cations(24). This flocculent mineralization usually assumes the form of dots， rings， and arcs， giving a“pop-corn”appearance . If the calcifications are ex-tensive， the lesion is called a calcifying enchondroma. The cortex is usually thinned and expanded in a symmetric， fusiform fashion. The often cloudy or hazy appearance of a lesion provides a clue to its chon-droid composition (18). The lesion can also be recog nized by scalloped inner cortical margins， reflecting the lobular growth pattern of cartilage . Computedtomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (aMnRoIe) ramnaayy ffaurrtthheerr daelineate the tumor and more pre-cisely localize it in the bone . Because in long bones enchondroma may present as a radiolucent lesion with poorly defined margins， particularly in areas where trabeculae are sparse or absent (diaphysis)， MRI may be extremely helpful in revealing the exact size and extent of the tumor  (74). Like most cartilaginous and fibrous lesions， enchondroma exhibits low to inter-mediate signal intensity on Tl-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. 【87】All cartilage tumors， whether benign or malignant， exhibit a positive reaction for S-100 protein <mark>(54)</mark>. This is sometimes diagnostically useful， as most other bone tumors do not display this reaction. Histologically， carti-lage tumors are usually recognized by the features of their intercellular matrix， which has a uniformly translu-cent appearance and contains less collagen compared with the intercellular matrix of osteoblastic tumors， such as osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The tumor cells themselves are usually located in rounded spaces (lacu-nae)， as in normal cartilage. In benign cartilage tumors， such as enchondroma， the tissue is sparsely cellular . The cells， typically with small， dark-staining nuclei， fail to show the cytologic features that are characteristic of chondrosarcoma， such as large nuclei； pleomor-phism；large， swollen chondroblastic and double nuclei； and mitoses. The tumor tissue is usually avascular， and areas of degenerate and calcified matrix are common. Calcification is sometimes followed by vascularization and replacement by bone， as in normal endochondral ossification. 【91】Clinically， malignancy is suggested by a variety of signs， including development of pain in a previously asymptomatic lesion (e.g.， malignant transtormation of enchondroma to chondrosarcoma)， development of swelling or a mass at the site of a lesion， or rapid growth of a lesion (e.g.， malignant transformation of osteochon-droma to chondrosarcoma). Radiologically， the pres-ence of a periosteal reaction， destruction of the cortex， and a soft tissue mass are almost pathognomonic fea-tures of malignancy (25). The histopathologic features of a malignant cartilage tumor include the presence of hypercellular and pleomorphic tumor tissue， apprecia-ble numbers of plump cells with large or double nuclei， invasion (permeation) of bone trabeculae， and infiltra-tion of Haversian systems and bone marrow . However， these obvious features of malignancy may be not so prominent in biopsy specimen， or only a few areas in such a specimen may reveal the diagnostic features of malignancy. As Dahlin and Unni (13) pointed out， in the pathologic evaluation it is necessary to examine many fields in these tumors to be certain that there is sufficient evidence for a diagnosis of malignancy be-cause evidence that a tumor is a chondrosarcoma rather than a benign enchondroma is frequently found in iso-lated areas within the mass. Therefore， it is of para-mount importance to obtain biopsy specimens from several areas of a tumor. Close cooperation among the clinician， the radiologist， and the pathologist in review-ing the history， the radiologic examination， and the biopsy specimens is crucial to reaching a conclusion on the exact nature of a cartilage lesion.

【101】Benign Lesions

【102】**Enchondroma**

Enchondroma is the second most common benign tu-mor of bone and is characterized by the formation of mature hyaline cartilage. It constitutes about 10% of all benign bone tumors and represents the most common tumor of the phalanges of the hand. Several theories have been postulated regarding its etiology. Among these is that the enchondroma develops from abnor-mal zones of dysplastic chondrocytes in the growth plate. These abnormal foci fail to undergo normal en-dochondral ossification； instead， they are deposited within the metaphysis and， as the bone grows， are dis-placed into the diaphysis (49). Customarily， a lesion lo-cated centrally in the bone is called an enchondroma， whereas one located outside the cortex is called a chon-droma (periosteal or juxtacortical). Separate groups|删除0换行|consist of lesions (a) located in the soft tissues and (b) located in the joint， bursa， or in the tendon sheath. The former are called soft tissue chondromas and the latter synovial chondromatosis (69)

【104】**_Clinical Presentation_**

【105】Although the tumor may occur at any age， most cases arise between the second and fourth decades； there is no sex predilection. The short， tubular bones of the hand and foot (phalanges， metacarpals， and metatarsals) are preferred sites， followed in frequency by the femur， humerus， tibia， and ribs . The lesion is often asymptomatic and usually is discovered incidentally due to a pathologic fracture through the tumor.

【106】The single most important complication of the le-sion is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. In a solitary enchondroma this occurs predominantly in a long or flat bone and almost never in a short tubu-lar bone. An important clinical sign is development of pain at the site of the lesion in a previously asympto-matic patient and in the absence of a fracture.

【107】**_Imaging_**

【108】Radiography is usually sufficient to demonstrate the le-sion and to establish its chondroid character. In short. tubular bones， the lesion is often entirely radiolucent， but in long bones it may display visible calcifi-cations(24). This flocculent mineralization usually assumes the form of dots， rings， and arcs， giving a“pop-corn”appearance . If the calcifications are ex-tensive， the lesion is called a calcifying enchondroma. The cortex is usually thinned and expanded in a symmetric， fusiform fashion. The often cloudy or hazy appearance of a lesion provides a clue to its chon-droid composition (18). The lesion can also be recog nized by scalloped inner cortical margins， reflecting the lobular growth pattern of cartilage . Computedtomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (aMnRoIe) ramnaayy ffaurrtthheerr daelineate the tumor and more pre-cisely localize it in the bone . Because in long bones enchondroma may present as a radiolucent lesion with poorly defined margins， particularly in areas where trabeculae are sparse or absent (diaphysis)， MRI may be extremely helpful in revealing the exact size and extent of the tumor  (74). Like most cartilaginous and fibrous lesions， enchondroma exhibits low to inter-mediate signal intensity on Tl-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. 【235】**Developmental regression**

【236】**· The differential diagnosis for developmental regression in children is very large. It is useful to break down the differential by the following parameters：◆ age of presentation，**

【237】**◆ involvement of CNS only or including other organ systems，**

【238】**◆ involvement of CNS only or including peripheral NS involvement，**

【241】**· Involvement of CNS + PNS suggests lysosomal or mitochondrial disorders.**

【242】**· Involvement of gray matter more often presents with seizures， dementia， and personality change.**

【243】**·Involvement of white matter more often presents with spasticity， focal neurological deficits， and blindness.**

【244】**· Regression can occur in several clinical scenarios. These scenarios can be helpful in narrowing the differential：**

【245】**1 Acute，rapid deterioration**

【246】**2 Acute intermittent attacks with cumulative regression**

【247】**3 Gradual，more chronic loss of milestones.**

【248】**·Chronic nonprogressive conditions (such as cerebral palsy) may seem to evolve as the affected child develops， and must be distinguished from true regression.**

【249】**Developmental regression in infants**

【250】**·No single entity is predominant in this age range， and specific differential diagnosis is based on clinical characteristics of the patient's presentation.**

【251】**·Rare but potentially treatable disorders that result in acute episodes of regression/neurological dysfunction include disorders of amino acid metabolism.**

【252】**·Other potentially treatable conditions include progressive hydrocephalus， hypothyroidism，and AIDS.**

【253】**· It is still important to diagnose the many rare but untreatable conditions including lysosomal disorders， mitochondrial disorders， and the predominantly white or gray matter disorders. Knowledge of a specific diagnosis may assist in prognosis， genetic counseling， participation in clinical research trials， and long-term care.**

【165】**Developmental disorders**

【166】**Developmental delay**

【167】**·Defined as a static， nonprogressive， significant delay in 22 of the following domains： gross/fine motor，language， cognition， social/personal，and activities of daily living.**

【168】**·Referred to as mental retardation in children over 5 years of age.**

【169】**·Up to 5-10% of children have some developmental disability， 1-3% of all children have global developmental delay.**

【170】**· Important to distinguish from developmental REGRESSION， which is a loss of previously achieved milestones.**

【171】**· Important to distinguish from a predominantly language delay or a predominant motor delay， both of which have narrower， more specific differential diagnoses.**

【172】1 Predominantly language delay

【173】**1.1 Hearing impairment**

【174】1.2 Autism： developmental disorder， usually becomes evident near 1-2 years of age .

【175】·Etiology is likely multifactorial， with a genetic component.

【176】·Characterized by impaired socialization， poor language development， repetitive behaviors， and a desire for sameness.

【177】▪Some demonstrate a relative insensitivity to pain.

【178】1.31Landau-Kleffner syndrome， acquired epileptiform aphasia (usually re-gression).

【179】▪Acquired language regression.

【180】· Epileptiform activity， including status epilepticus， on EEG during sleep.

【181】1.4 Bilateral perisylvian syndrome

【182】2 Predominantly motor delay

【183】**2.1 Cerebral palsy**

【184】·Nonprogressive motor and cerebral impairment due to brain injury acquired during development (almost always prenatal or perinatal).

【185】▪Associated with intrauterine infection， birth asphyxia， cerebral inf-arction， cerebral dysgenesis. In most cases， specific etiology undeter-mined.

【186】Patterns of motor impairment include： hemiplegia， spastic diplegia， quadriplegia， extrapyramidal， and rarely cerebellar/ataxic.

【187】Variable degree of cognitive impairment.

【188】(Greatest impairment) quadriplegia >> spastic diplegia > hemiplegia >extrapyramidal or ataxic (less impairment).

【189】2.2 Myopathy： congenital，metabolic (tend to slowly progress).

【190】2.3 Neuropathy： genetic， metabolic (tend to progress).

【191】3Global developmental delay (GDD)

【192】**3.1 Perinatal or prenatal insult/disorder**

【193】·Perinatal asphyxia， infection， premature birth， intracranial hemor-rhage，hydrocephalus，etc.

【194】3.2 Chromosomal/genetic abnormality： particularly suspect if dysmorphic features or congenital abnormalities in other organs present.

【195】3.2.1 FragileX syndrome： FMR1 gene. Most common GDD in males.

【196】o Triplet repeat expansion at Xq27.

【197】o Characterized by long facies， enlarged ears， macro-orchidism， moderate mental retardation， occasionally autistic behavior.

【198】3.2.2 Rett syndrome： MECP2 gene. Major etiology in females.

【199】o Mutation at Xq28， only manifest in females. Onset at 1 year of age.

【200】o Clinical signs include acquired microcephaly， developmental ar-rest/regression， hypotonia， ataxia， seizures， autistic behavior.

【201】o Other findings include breathing irregularities with hyperpnea and loss of purposeful hand movements (constant hand wring-ing movements).

【202】**3.2.3 Down syndrome： Trisomy 21.**

【203】o Characteristics：lhypotonia， round/flat(Mongoloid)facies， Brushfield spots， flat nape of neck.

【204】o Associated congenital cardiac disease.

【234】3.7 Progressive encephalopathy： see Developmental regression.

【235】**Developmental regression**

【236】**· The differential diagnosis for developmental regression in children is very large. It is useful to break down the differential by the following parameters：◆ age of presentation，**

【237】**◆ involvement of CNS only or including other organ systems，**

【238】**◆ involvement of CNS only or including peripheral NS involvement，**

【239】**◆ primarily gray matter or white matter disease.**

【240】**·Involvement of CNS+ other organ systems suggests lysosomal， peroxisomal， or mitochondrial disease.**

【241】**· Involvement of CNS + PNS suggests lysosomal or mitochondrial disorders.**

【242】**· Involvement of gray matter more often presents with seizures， dementia， and personality change.**

【243】**·Involvement of white matter more often presents with spasticity， focal neurological deficits， and blindness.**

【244】**· Regression can occur in several clinical scenarios. These scenarios can be helpful in narrowing the differential：**

【245】**1 Acute，rapid deterioration**

【246】**2 Acute intermittent attacks with cumulative regression**

【247】**3 Gradual，more chronic loss of milestones.**

【248】**·Chronic nonprogressive conditions (such as cerebral palsy) may seem to evolve as the affected child develops， and must be distinguished from true regression.**

【249】**Developmental regression in infants**

【250】**·No single entity is predominant in this age range， and specific differential diagnosis is based on clinical characteristics of the patient's presentation.**

【251】**·Rare but potentially treatable disorders that result in acute episodes of regression/neurological dysfunction include disorders of amino acid metabolism.**

【252】**·Other potentially treatable conditions include progressive hydrocephalus， hypothyroidism，and AIDS.**

【253】**· It is still important to diagnose the many rare but untreatable conditions including lysosomal disorders， mitochondrial disorders， and the predominantly white or gray matter disorders. Knowledge of a specific diagnosis may assist in prognosis， genetic counseling， participation in clinical research trials， and long-term care.**
