【110】**OWENOIDpapulosis and Bowen’s disease are both examples of squamous-cell carcinomas in situ histologically， i.e.， they may have atypical keratinocytes at all levels of the epithelium， dyskeratotic cells， mitotic figures， and multinucleated cells. Both may have epidermal proliferation with thinning of the suprapapillary plates； parakeratosis； di-lated， tortuous vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Both lesions may be pigmented and have melanophages.**

【111】**In bowenoid1papulosis， the most striking features are the numerous mitotic figures and numerous necrotic cells (with karyorrhexis)； in Bowen’s disease， the most eye-catching abnormalities are striking nuclear atypia(often“monster"nuclei)， multinucleated cells， andFpallid or pagetoid cells. In addition， the architectural patterns differ. Bowenoid papulosis has many features of condyloma acuminata， namely， small domed lesions with vacuo-lated cells， hypergranulosis， and focal parakeratosis. Nearby， there may be classic verrucae (condylomata). The atypical cells tend to be small and monomorphous and to have areas of normal keratinocytes interposed be-tween them. In contrast， lesions of Bowen’s disease are flat-surfaced， have no contiguous changes suggestive of warts， and have pleomorphic atypical cells devoid of "skip areas.'**

【112】**Bowenoidpapulosis occurs on the glans and shaft of the penis， and on the vulva. The lesions are usually numerous， reddish to violaceous papules， slightly scaly， often verrucoid or velvety， and sometimes pigmented. The papules of bowenoidpapulosis become conflucnt， sometimes forming plaques. Individual lesions range from 2 to 10 mm in diameter and are generally asymptomatic. Bowenoid papulosis seems to be more common in men than in women， and it is found most commonly on the shaft of the penis. Unlike Bowen’s disease， bowenoid papulosis occurs almost always in young adults， and then in circumcisedmen. Often there is a history of previous genital lesions， especially condyloma acuminata， but also herpes simplex and molluscum contagiosum. Usually， lesions of bowenoid papulo-sis are diagnosed clinically as condyloma acuminatum， verruca vulgaris， lichen planus， or psoriasis. The fact that these lesions are frequently numer-ous and verrucous in appearance suggests an infectious cause. Immunoper-oxidase stains for human papilloma virus have been positive in some lesions of bowenoid papulosis， thereby confirming the infectious nature of the con-dition.**

**Bowen’s disease is characterized by a flat， slightly scaly plaque that may be confused clinically with psoriasis， but never with bowenoid papulo-sis， although the two conditions may sometimes be indistinguishable from|删除0换行|one another histologically. Erythroplasia of Queyrat (i.e.， squamous-cell car-cinoma in situ of the mucocutaneous surfaces and of the mucosa) is most common on the glans penis and prepuce. Clinically， the lesion tends to be a single， slightly elevated， sharply defined， bright red， glistening， velvety plaque， similar to that of Bowen’s disease. **SQUAMOUS-CELL carcinoma in situ in the anogeni-|删除0换行|tal region and a condyloma acuminatum biopsied 48 to 72 hours after podo-phyllin treatment have numerous histologic features in common， such as mitotic figures at all levels of a thickened epidermis， some of which are atypical； zones of pallor of keratinocytes； necrotic keratinocytes； parakerato-sis； dilated blood vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Squamous-cell carcinoma in situ is characterized by numerous cells with atypical nuclei throughout the epidermis， disordered maturation of kerati-nocytes， and atypical mitotic figures in all stages of cell division. In contrast， a condyloma biopsied 48 to 72 hours after application of podophyllin retains the hypergranulosis and “owl’s eye"halos around nuclei in the upper part of the epithelium that are so typical of verrucae； confluence of necrotic kerati-nocytes (with ballooning of the necrotic cells) in the upper part of the epi-thelium； few atypical cells and fewer atypical mitoses； and a markedly in-creased number of mitoses that are all arrested in metaphase.**

【183】**Squamous-cell carcinomas in situ in the anogenital region are charac-teristically single， reddish， sharply marginated plaques with a smooth， sometimes glistening surface. Middle-aged and uncircumcised men are usu-ally at risk； women with these lesions sometimes have carcinoma of the vagina， uterus， or utcrine cervix. Although a lesion of squamous-cell carci-noma in situ on the genitalia may be longstanding， it nevertheless has the potential for deep extension locally and eventual metastasis.**

【184】**Clinical history should help to differentiate a podophyllin-treated con-dyloma from squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. The often-asked question of whether podophyllin treatment induces atypia and carcinoma-like changes may be answered emphatically “no.” Podophyllin applied to these numer-ous fleshy excresences induces maximal changes at 48 to 72 hours in the form of superficial necrosis of the epithelium and arrest of keratinocytes in metaphase. If the podophyllin is not removed 4 to 6 hours after it has been applied， severe extensive necrosis and accompanying pain may result.**

【185】**Podophyllin is a resin extracted from the plant Podophyllum peltatum， commonly known as the May apple or mandrake. This resin is apotent cytotoxic agent， arresting dividing cells in metaphase. Ultrastructurally， the affected cells show nuclear destruction with numerous small granules of nuclear debris scattered throughout the cytoplasm. Interestingly， there are unusually large numbers of tonofilaments. The mucous membranes are particularly sensitive to the effects of podophyllin， perhaps explaining why warts on those surfaces are so susceptible to destruction by podophyllin.**

【186】**Many dermatopathologists and dermatologists have incorrectly taught that the histologic changes noted after treatment with podophyllin cannot be differentiated from those of squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. In most cases， this is not true because the changes induced by podophyllin treatment are necrosis and increased numbers of mitoses， whereas in squamous-cell carcinoma in situ there are atypical cells and atypical mitoses. If a lesion were thought to be a condyloma acuminatum clinically， but was histologi-cally bowenoid papulosis (i.e.， squamous-cell carcinoma in situ in a pre-existing condyloma) and the lesion was then treated with podophyllin， its subsequent histologic analysis would demonstrate features both of the un-derlying squamous-cell carcinoma in situ， as well as the changes induced by podophyllin. Such a coincidence must be extremely rare.**

【19】monly as desmoplastic trichoepithelioma or sclerosing epithelial hamar-toma was first clearly described clinically and histologically by Zeligman in1960 under the title solitary trichoepithelioma 删除1:<u>(Arch Dermatol 82： 89-94，1960)</u>. Zeligman commented that a solitary trichoepithelioma makes its appearance anytime from birth to the thirties， grows slowly， and is not associated with a family history of the condition. Furthermore， he wrote， that they‘“have thus far been noted only on the face. They are relatively small， usually not over 2 cm， and are asymptomatic. The lesions are usually round andpapular. At times， they are in aggregate annular with grouped papules on the periphery and have a thread-like elevated border. Microscop-ically， the important problem is that of separating hamartomatous tricho-epithelioma from basal cell carcinoma differentiating towards hair follicles. Though at times this is impossible on microscopic grounds alone， a tricho-epitheliomna tends to have more mature cells， many of which are in narrow strands and nests. Since both contain masses of basal cells and keratinous cysts， in some instances there is no sharp demarcation between them and one may have to rely on clinical data for differentiation.”

【20】The same lesion was discussed by Brownstein and Shapiro in 1977删除1:<u>(Cancer 40：2979-2986，1977)</u>， who called it desmoplastic trichoepithelioma， and by MacDonald， Jones， and Marks， in 1978 删除1:<u>(Clin Exp Dermatol 2： 153-160， 1977)</u>， who named it sclerosing epithelial hamartoma. Both sets of authors commented on the problem of differentiation from morphea-like basal-cell carcinoma. Brownstein and Shapiro listed the following histologic features as being helpful in differentiation of desmoplastic trichoepitheli-oma from morphea-like basal-cell carcinoma：

| **Histologic**  | **Desmoplastic**  | **Basal-Cell**  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Features**  | **Trichoepithelioma**  | **Carcinoma**  |
| **Horn cysts**  | **Constant**  | **Never**  |

【22】MacDonald and coauthors wrote about the problem of differentiation in these words：“Occasionally， histological differentiation (of sclerosing epi-thelial hamartoma) from morphoeic basal cell epithelioma may be difficult.

【23】In the latter， areas showing more typical solid islands of basal-cell epitheli-oma with peripheral palisading or retraction artifact may be found. Horn cysts are unusual. The sclerotic stroma tends to invade the surrounding tissue irregularly. Morphoeic basal-cell epithelioma is not usually symmetri-cal in its overall architecture.”

【24】We attempted to apply these criteria to the differentiation of desmo-plastic trichoepithelioma from morpheiform basal-cell carcinoma and were211C0 unsuccessful. For that reason， we undertook a study that took many months to complete， because desmoplastic trichoepithelioma and morphea-like basal-cell carcinoma have such similar features in common， e.g.， cords of basaloid cells in a fibrotic stroma， and because biopsy specimens are often so superficial or tiny that differentiation between the two neoplasms in point proves to be exceedingly difficult. Shadow cells are not specific for desmoplastic trichoepithelioma， but are seen most often in pilomatricomas； they are not seen， in our experience， in basal-cell carci-nomas，

【110】**OWENOIDpapulosis and Bowen’s disease are both examples of squamous-cell carcinomas in situ histologically， i.e.， they may have atypical keratinocytes at all levels of the epithelium， dyskeratotic cells， mitotic figures， and multinucleated cells. Both may have epidermal proliferation with thinning of the suprapapillary plates； parakeratosis； di-lated， tortuous vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Both lesions may be pigmented and have melanophages.**

【111】**In bowenoid1papulosis， the most striking features are the numerous mitotic figures and numerous necrotic cells (with karyorrhexis)； in Bowen’s disease， the most eye-catching abnormalities are striking nuclear atypia(often“monster"nuclei)， multinucleated cells， andFpallid or pagetoid cells. In addition， the architectural patterns differ. Bowenoid papulosis has many features of condyloma acuminata， namely， small domed lesions with vacuo-lated cells， hypergranulosis， and focal parakeratosis. Nearby， there may be classic verrucae (condylomata). The atypical cells tend to be small and monomorphous and to have areas of normal keratinocytes interposed be-tween them. In contrast， lesions of Bowen’s disease are flat-surfaced， have no contiguous changes suggestive of warts， and have pleomorphic atypical cells devoid of "skip areas.'**

【112】**Bowenoidpapulosis occurs on the glans and shaft of the penis， and on the vulva. The lesions are usually numerous， reddish to violaceous papules， slightly scaly， often verrucoid or velvety， and sometimes pigmented. The papules of bowenoidpapulosis become conflucnt， sometimes forming plaques. Individual lesions range from 2 to 10 mm in diameter and are generally asymptomatic. Bowenoid papulosis seems to be more common in men than in women， and it is found most commonly on the shaft of the penis. Unlike Bowen’s disease， bowenoid papulosis occurs almost always in young adults， and then in circumcisedmen. Often there is a history of previous genital lesions， especially condyloma acuminata， but also herpes simplex and molluscum contagiosum. Usually， lesions of bowenoid papulo-sis are diagnosed clinically as condyloma acuminatum， verruca vulgaris， lichen planus， or psoriasis. The fact that these lesions are frequently numer-ous and verrucous in appearance suggests an infectious cause. Immunoper-oxidase stains for human papilloma virus have been positive in some lesions of bowenoid papulosis， thereby confirming the infectious nature of the con-dition.**

**Bowen’s disease is characterized by a flat， slightly scaly plaque that may be confused clinically with psoriasis， but never with bowenoid papulo-sis， although the two conditions may sometimes be indistinguishable from|删除0换行|one another histologically. Erythroplasia of Queyrat (i.e.， squamous-cell car-cinoma in situ of the mucocutaneous surfaces and of the mucosa) is most common on the glans penis and prepuce. Clinically， the lesion tends to be a single， slightly elevated， sharply defined， bright red， glistening， velvety plaque， similar to that of Bowen’s disease. In contrast， solar keratoses may have identical histologic features to those of radiation keratoses and arsenical keratoses， but they differ from bowenoid papulosis and Bowen’s disease by having atypical keratinocytes mostly in the lower half of the epidermis， foci of suprabasal clefts in some lesions， and acantholytic dyskeratotic cells above the clefts.

Therefore， lesions of bowenoid papulosis should be removed completely but conservatively， even though they commonly regress entirely without treatment.

【110】**OWENOIDpapulosis and Bowen’s disease are both examples of squamous-cell carcinomas in situ histologically， i.e.， they may have atypical keratinocytes at all levels of the epithelium， dyskeratotic cells， mitotic figures， and multinucleated cells. Both may have epidermal proliferation with thinning of the suprapapillary plates； parakeratosis； di-lated， tortuous vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Both lesions may be pigmented and have melanophages.**

【111】**In bowenoid1papulosis， the most striking features are the numerous mitotic figures and numerous necrotic cells (with karyorrhexis)； in Bowen’s disease， the most eye-catching abnormalities are striking nuclear atypia(often“monster"nuclei)， multinucleated cells， andFpallid or pagetoid cells. In addition， the architectural patterns differ. Bowenoid papulosis has many features of condyloma acuminata， namely， small domed lesions with vacuo-lated cells， hypergranulosis， and focal parakeratosis. Nearby， there may be classic verrucae (condylomata). The atypical cells tend to be small and monomorphous and to have areas of normal keratinocytes interposed be-tween them. In contrast， lesions of Bowen’s disease are flat-surfaced， have no contiguous changes suggestive of warts， and have pleomorphic atypical cells devoid of "skip areas.'**

【112】**Bowenoidpapulosis occurs on the glans and shaft of the penis， and on the vulva. The lesions are usually numerous， reddish to violaceous papules， slightly scaly， often verrucoid or velvety， and sometimes pigmented. The papules of bowenoidpapulosis become conflucnt， sometimes forming plaques. Individual lesions range from 2 to 10 mm in diameter and are generally asymptomatic. Bowenoid papulosis seems to be more common in men than in women， and it is found most commonly on the shaft of the penis. Unlike Bowen’s disease， bowenoid papulosis occurs almost always in young adults， and then in circumcisedmen. Often there is a history of previous genital lesions， especially condyloma acuminata， but also herpes simplex and molluscum contagiosum. Usually， lesions of bowenoid papulo-sis are diagnosed clinically as condyloma acuminatum， verruca vulgaris， lichen planus， or psoriasis. The fact that these lesions are frequently numer-ous and verrucous in appearance suggests an infectious cause. Immunoper-oxidase stains for human papilloma virus have been positive in some lesions of bowenoid papulosis， thereby confirming the infectious nature of the con-dition.**

**Bowen’s disease is characterized by a flat， slightly scaly plaque that may be confused clinically with psoriasis， but never with bowenoid papulo-sis， although the two conditions may sometimes be indistinguishable from|删除0换行|one another histologically. Erythroplasia of Queyrat (i.e.， squamous-cell car-cinoma in situ of the mucocutaneous surfaces and of the mucosa) is most common on the glans penis and prepuce. Clinically， the lesion tends to be a single， slightly elevated， sharply defined， bright red， glistening， velvety plaque， similar to that of Bowen’s disease. The process almost always starts on the glans and then may spread onto adjacent skin of the penile shaft or _D11C_ prepuce. Men with erythroplasia are generally middle-aged or older and are uncircumcised. In women， this disease is often associated with squamous-cell carcinoma of the vagina or uterine cervix. The neoplasm may remain in situ for many years， but if left unattended， it may extend beneath the epithe-lium and eventually metastasize to regional lymph nodes and other organs.

【114】Squamous-cell carcinoma in situ is a histologic term describing a set of features shared by bowenoid papulosis and Bowen’s disease， namely， atypi-cal keratinocytes throughout most of the thickness of the epithelium in some foci. In contrast， solar keratoses may have identical histologic features to those of radiation keratoses and arsenical keratoses， but they differ from bowenoid papulosis and Bowen’s disease by having atypical keratinocytes mostly in the lower half of the epidermis， foci of suprabasal clefts in some lesions， and acantholytic dyskeratotic cells above the clefts.

We know of no case of bowenoid papulosis in which the neoplas-tic process has extended beneath the epithelium and metastasized， although we anticipate that， one day， that will happen. **SQUAMOUS-CELL carcinoma in situ in the anogeni-|删除0换行|tal region and a condyloma acuminatum biopsied 48 to 72 hours after podo-phyllin treatment have numerous histologic features in common， such as mitotic figures at all levels of a thickened epidermis， some of which are atypical； zones of pallor of keratinocytes； necrotic keratinocytes； parakerato-sis； dilated blood vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Squamous-cell carcinoma in situ is characterized by numerous cells with atypical nuclei throughout the epidermis， disordered maturation of kerati-nocytes， and atypical mitotic figures in all stages of cell division. In contrast， a condyloma biopsied 48 to 72 hours after application of podophyllin retains the hypergranulosis and “owl’s eye"halos around nuclei in the upper part of the epithelium that are so typical of verrucae； confluence of necrotic kerati-nocytes (with ballooning of the necrotic cells) in the upper part of the epi-thelium； few atypical cells and fewer atypical mitoses； and a markedly in-creased number of mitoses that are all arrested in metaphase.**

【183】**Squamous-cell carcinomas in situ in the anogenital region are charac-teristically single， reddish， sharply marginated plaques with a smooth， sometimes glistening surface. Middle-aged and uncircumcised men are usu-ally at risk； women with these lesions sometimes have carcinoma of the vagina， uterus， or utcrine cervix. Although a lesion of squamous-cell carci-noma in situ on the genitalia may be longstanding， it nevertheless has the potential for deep extension locally and eventual metastasis.**

【184】**Clinical history should help to differentiate a podophyllin-treated con-dyloma from squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. The often-asked question of whether podophyllin treatment induces atypia and carcinoma-like changes may be answered emphatically “no.” Podophyllin applied to these numer-ous fleshy excresences induces maximal changes at 48 to 72 hours in the form of superficial necrosis of the epithelium and arrest of keratinocytes in metaphase. If the podophyllin is not removed 4 to 6 hours after it has been applied， severe extensive necrosis and accompanying pain may result.**

【185】**Podophyllin is a resin extracted from the plant Podophyllum peltatum， commonly known as the May apple or mandrake. This resin is apotent cytotoxic agent， arresting dividing cells in metaphase. Ultrastructurally， the affected cells show nuclear destruction with numerous small granules of nuclear debris scattered throughout the cytoplasm. Interestingly， there are unusually large numbers of tonofilaments. The mucous membranes are particularly sensitive to the effects of podophyllin， perhaps explaining why warts on those surfaces are so susceptible to destruction by podophyllin.**

【186】**Many dermatopathologists and dermatologists have incorrectly taught that the histologic changes noted after treatment with podophyllin cannot be differentiated from those of squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. In most cases， this is not true because the changes induced by podophyllin treatment are necrosis and increased numbers of mitoses， whereas in squamous-cell carcinoma in situ there are atypical cells and atypical mitoses. If a lesion were thought to be a condyloma acuminatum clinically， but was histologi-cally bowenoid papulosis (i.e.， squamous-cell carcinoma in situ in a pre-existing condyloma) and the lesion was then treated with podophyllin， its subsequent histologic analysis would demonstrate features both of the un-derlying squamous-cell carcinoma in situ， as well as the changes induced by podophyllin. Such a coincidence must be extremely rare.**

【110】**OWENOIDpapulosis and Bowen’s disease are both examples of squamous-cell carcinomas in situ histologically， i.e.， they may have atypical keratinocytes at all levels of the epithelium， dyskeratotic cells， mitotic figures， and multinucleated cells. Both may have epidermal proliferation with thinning of the suprapapillary plates； parakeratosis； di-lated， tortuous vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Both lesions may be pigmented and have melanophages.**

【111】**In bowenoid1papulosis， the most striking features are the numerous mitotic figures and numerous necrotic cells (with karyorrhexis)； in Bowen’s disease， the most eye-catching abnormalities are striking nuclear atypia(often“monster"nuclei)， multinucleated cells， andFpallid or pagetoid cells. In addition， the architectural patterns differ. Bowenoid papulosis has many features of condyloma acuminata， namely， small domed lesions with vacuo-lated cells， hypergranulosis， and focal parakeratosis. Nearby， there may be classic verrucae (condylomata). The atypical cells tend to be small and monomorphous and to have areas of normal keratinocytes interposed be-tween them. In contrast， lesions of Bowen’s disease are flat-surfaced， have no contiguous changes suggestive of warts， and have pleomorphic atypical cells devoid of "skip areas.'**

【112】**Bowenoidpapulosis occurs on the glans and shaft of the penis， and on the vulva. The lesions are usually numerous， reddish to violaceous papules， slightly scaly， often verrucoid or velvety， and sometimes pigmented. The papules of bowenoidpapulosis become conflucnt， sometimes forming plaques. Individual lesions range from 2 to 10 mm in diameter and are generally asymptomatic. Bowenoid papulosis seems to be more common in men than in women， and it is found most commonly on the shaft of the penis. Unlike Bowen’s disease， bowenoid papulosis occurs almost always in young adults， and then in circumcisedmen. Often there is a history of previous genital lesions， especially condyloma acuminata， but also herpes simplex and molluscum contagiosum. Usually， lesions of bowenoid papulo-sis are diagnosed clinically as condyloma acuminatum， verruca vulgaris， lichen planus， or psoriasis. The fact that these lesions are frequently numer-ous and verrucous in appearance suggests an infectious cause. Immunoper-oxidase stains for human papilloma virus have been positive in some lesions of bowenoid papulosis， thereby confirming the infectious nature of the con-dition.**

**Bowen’s disease is characterized by a flat， slightly scaly plaque that may be confused clinically with psoriasis， but never with bowenoid papulo-sis， although the two conditions may sometimes be indistinguishable from|删除0换行|one another histologically. Erythroplasia of Queyrat (i.e.， squamous-cell car-cinoma in situ of the mucocutaneous surfaces and of the mucosa) is most common on the glans penis and prepuce. Clinically， the lesion tends to be a single， slightly elevated， sharply defined， bright red， glistening， velvety plaque， similar to that of Bowen’s disease. The process almost always starts on the glans and then may spread onto adjacent skin of the penile shaft or _D11C_ prepuce. Men with erythroplasia are generally middle-aged or older and are uncircumcised. In women， this disease is often associated with squamous-cell carcinoma of the vagina or uterine cervix. The neoplasm may remain in situ for many years， but if left unattended， it may extend beneath the epithe-lium and eventually metastasize to regional lymph nodes and other organs.

【114】Squamous-cell carcinoma in situ is a histologic term describing a set of features shared by bowenoid papulosis and Bowen’s disease， namely， atypi-cal keratinocytes throughout most of the thickness of the epithelium in some foci. In contrast， solar keratoses may have identical histologic features to those of radiation keratoses and arsenical keratoses， but they differ from bowenoid papulosis and Bowen’s disease by having atypical keratinocytes mostly in the lower half of the epidermis， foci of suprabasal clefts in some lesions， and acantholytic dyskeratotic cells above the clefts.

【115】Despite the histologic similarities between bowenoidpapulosis and erythroplasia of Queyrat on the genitals， they seem to vary in their biologic potential. We know of no case of bowenoid papulosis in which the neoplas-tic process has extended beneath the epithelium and metastasized， although we anticipate that， one day， that will happen. Therefore， lesions of bowenoid papulosis should be removed completely but conservatively， even though they commonly regress entirely without treatment.

**SQUAMOUS-CELL carcinoma in situ in the anogeni-|删除0换行|tal region and a condyloma acuminatum biopsied 48 to 72 hours after podo-phyllin treatment have numerous histologic features in common， such as mitotic figures at all levels of a thickened epidermis， some of which are atypical； zones of pallor of keratinocytes； necrotic keratinocytes； parakerato-sis； dilated blood vessels； and an inflammatory-cell infiltrate in the dermis. Squamous-cell carcinoma in situ is characterized by numerous cells with atypical nuclei throughout the epidermis， disordered maturation of kerati-nocytes， and atypical mitotic figures in all stages of cell division. In contrast， a condyloma biopsied 48 to 72 hours after application of podophyllin retains the hypergranulosis and “owl’s eye"halos around nuclei in the upper part of the epithelium that are so typical of verrucae； confluence of necrotic kerati-nocytes (with ballooning of the necrotic cells) in the upper part of the epi-thelium； few atypical cells and fewer atypical mitoses； and a markedly in-creased number of mitoses that are all arrested in metaphase.**

【183】**Squamous-cell carcinomas in situ in the anogenital region are charac-teristically single， reddish， sharply marginated plaques with a smooth， sometimes glistening surface. Middle-aged and uncircumcised men are usu-ally at risk； women with these lesions sometimes have carcinoma of the vagina， uterus， or utcrine cervix. Although a lesion of squamous-cell carci-noma in situ on the genitalia may be longstanding， it nevertheless has the potential for deep extension locally and eventual metastasis.**

【184】**Clinical history should help to differentiate a podophyllin-treated con-dyloma from squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. The often-asked question of whether podophyllin treatment induces atypia and carcinoma-like changes may be answered emphatically “no.” Podophyllin applied to these numer-ous fleshy excresences induces maximal changes at 48 to 72 hours in the form of superficial necrosis of the epithelium and arrest of keratinocytes in metaphase. If the podophyllin is not removed 4 to 6 hours after it has been applied， severe extensive necrosis and accompanying pain may result.**

【185】**Podophyllin is a resin extracted from the plant Podophyllum peltatum， commonly known as the May apple or mandrake. This resin is apotent cytotoxic agent， arresting dividing cells in metaphase. Ultrastructurally， the affected cells show nuclear destruction with numerous small granules of nuclear debris scattered throughout the cytoplasm. Interestingly， there are unusually large numbers of tonofilaments. The mucous membranes are particularly sensitive to the effects of podophyllin， perhaps explaining why warts on those surfaces are so susceptible to destruction by podophyllin.**

【186】**Many dermatopathologists and dermatologists have incorrectly taught that the histologic changes noted after treatment with podophyllin cannot be differentiated from those of squamous-cell carcinoma in situ. In most cases， this is not true because the changes induced by podophyllin treatment are necrosis and increased numbers of mitoses， whereas in squamous-cell carcinoma in situ there are atypical cells and atypical mitoses. If a lesion were thought to be a condyloma acuminatum clinically， but was histologi-cally bowenoid papulosis (i.e.， squamous-cell carcinoma in situ in a pre-existing condyloma) and the lesion was then treated with podophyllin， its subsequent histologic analysis would demonstrate features both of the un-derlying squamous-cell carcinoma in situ， as well as the changes induced by podophyllin. Such a coincidence must be extremely rare.**

【1】**·Nummular (discoid) eczema： Coin-shaped patches and plaques， usually mul-tiple on limbs， which start erythematous and turn dry and scaly.**

【3】**Papulosquamous Group**

【4】**1\. Can this be fungal?**

【5】**·Dermatophyte fungi (tinea， ringworm)： Annular patches with elevated， well-defined， serpiginous borders ± central clearing. This may affect the groin(tinea cruris)， foot (tinea pedis， athlete’s foot)， face (tinea faciale) or elsewhere on the body (tinea corporis) and are usually asymmetrical. Always consider dermato-phyte infection in an itchy patch-skin scraping and potassium hydroxide (KOH) smear may find spores and hyphae.**

【6】**2\. Attempt to identify based on morphology and distribution.**

【7】**·Psoriasis： Skin-coloured or erythematous papules and plaques with silvery scales， classically affecting scalp， elbows and knees. These may be few and large(e.g.， chronic plaque psoriasis) or small and many (e.g.， guttate psoriasis)， and is usually more symmetrical than tinea. Removal of scales reveals small bleeding points (Auspitz sign)， and skin trauma aggravates lesions (Koebner phenomenon). Nails involvement is common (pitting， onycholysis， discoloration)， and there may also be arthritis . This is a chronic long-standing disease.**

【8】**·Nummular (discoid) eczema： Oval， weeping patches and plaques with crusted papulovesicles (exudative acute discoid eczema) or multiple dry， erythematous， well-circumscribed oval plaques (dry discoid eczema).**

【9】**· Pityriasis rosea： This starts as a herald patch on the trunk (resembling tinea). Two to five days later， the patient develops tan or salmon-coloured oval scaly papules and patches with collarette scales (arranged in a ring) on the trunk and proximal limbs， in a 'Christmas tree'distribution (following skin cleavage lines). This is thought to be an immune reaction to herpes viruses 6 and 7， which self-resolves in 6 to 8 weeks.**

【10】**·Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA) and Pityriasis lichenoides chronica (PLC)： Crops of erythematous papules on trunk and limbs appearing over weeks-months； with central necrosis and haemorrhagic crusting (in PLEVA)， or central mica-like scales (in PLC)， or hyper/hypo-pigmentation (post-inflamma-tory) or any combination of lesions.**

【11】**·Seborrheic dermatitis： Ill-defined erythematous patches with course greasy scales， mainly affecting sebaceous gland-rich areas-scalp， eyebrows， creases around the nose and behind the ears； sometimes also the upper trunk and skin folds (axilla， groin， inframammary folds).**

【12】**Lichen planus： Pruritic purple planar polygonal papules and plaques， or white mucosal patches with white lines .**

【13】**3\. Consider systemic disease and sinister causes.**

【14】**·Discoid lupus： These plaques begin purplish-red and scaly， then turn depressed and atrophic (often with a hyperpigmented border). These are usually found on sun-exposed skin (face， trunk， arms). If involving scalp or hairline， it may also cause scarring alopecia. Lupus may be skin-limited or systemic-look for mani-festations of possible systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)， test antinuclear antibody (ANA)， dsDNA and consider biopsy.**

【15】**Malignant and premalignant causes： The first clue is often that the lesion looks atypical'or thick， and does not respond to topical treatment. A biopsy is neces-sary to confirm or exclude.**

【16】**\- Mycosis fungoides： A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma， initially indistinguishable from psoriasis or eczema (may be irregular or look atypical to an experienced eye)， which gradually becomes elevated， indurated， then nodular or ulcerative.**

【17】**\-Extramammary Paget’s disease： Suspect this in a chronic 'eczematous rash'，‘lichen simplex'or ‘psoriatic plaque’in the groin that does not improve with steroids. This is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that may arise from skin cancer or from underlying anorectal or bladder adenocarcinoma.**

【18】**\-Bowen’s disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)： An irregular， asymmet-rical， erythematous scaly or crusted plaque.**

【19】**\- Actinic keratosis： A scaly， erythematous patch or papule on sun-exposed skin(usually face).**

【20】**·Secondary syphilis： A great mimic； consider especially if palms and soles are involved. Take a sexual history， do VDRL and a treponemal test (e.g.， TPPA).**

【21】**·Drug eruptions： For example， antimalarials (chloroquine)，lithium， beta-blockers.**

【22】**Vesicles， Bullae， Pustules**

【23】**Decide if these papules are filled with pus (pustules) or clear fluid. Clear blisters are sorted by size as vesicles (small <0.5 cm) and bullae (larger >0.5 cm).**

【24】**Pustules ± Vesicles**

【25】**Pustules are neutrophil collections representing infection or inflammation. Their dis-tribution is key.**

【26】**Predominantly face：**

【27】**Acne： Usually a young person with papules and pustules， open and closed come-dones (black- and whiteheads) in the face and upper trunk. Rule out secondary causes， for example， cosmetics， drugs (steroids， phenytoin，lithium) and Cushing's disease. A lady with particularly bad acne should be examined for other signs of hirsutism .**

【28】**Rosacea： Often a middle-aged patient with chronic erythema and telangiectasia of the central third of the face (nose and medial cheeks). There may be papules and pustules， blepharitis， conjunctivitis and frequent flushing； comedones are absent.**

【29】**Asymmetrical，localised： More likely an infective cause.**

【30】**Herpes zoster (shingles)： Vesicles and pustules on an erythematous base， in a der-matomal distribution， often with pain and pruritus. Send vesicle smear for varicella-zoster virus (VZV) PCR. Zoster in the CN Vi dermatome can cause sight-threatening corneal involvement-urgent ophthalmology consult is indicated. Zoster in the immunocompromised can be disseminated and life-threatening.**

【31】**·Impetigo (non-bullous)： Staphylococcus aureus skin infection can present any-where as pustules， which quickly break to form a honey-coloured crust. Scraping crust away leaves a non-ulcerated glistening base. Gram stain of the crust finds gram positive cocci.**

【32】**Symmetrical， generalised-angry looking pustules with a background of erythe-matous skin：**

【33】**· Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)： An acute generalised erup-tion of pinpoint superficial non-follicular pustules on a background oferythematous skin， which may coalesce to become lakes of pustules. Triggers include drugs (anti-biotics， e.g.， beta-lactams，carbamazepine， etc.)and viruses.**

【34】**Pustular psoriasis： The morphology is identical to AGEP-but there is usually a history of psoriasis， and often a superimposed trigger (e.g.， steroid withdrawal， sepsis， stress or hypocalcaemia). This is potentially life threatening.**

【35】**Symmetrical， generalised-without angry skin：**

【36】**Varicella zoster (chickenpox)： A generalised pruritic eruption. Lesions develop rapidly from macules， to papules， vesicles， then pustules and crusting； lesions of all stages are present at the same time. This is a disease of childhood， but may occur in adults who have neither had chickenpox nor vaccination.**

【37】**Folliculitis： Papules and pustules formed in hair follicles (hair seen at the centre of lesions). This may be due to Malassezia furfur (pustules appear monomorphic)， gram positive skin commensals or gram negative bacteria (especially in patients on antibiotics). Do gram stain and skin scraping.**

【38】**Pseudofolliculitis barbae： Folliculitis'of a dense beard may not be infective， but an inflammatory response to a curved ingrowing beard.**

【39】**Vesicles Alone**

【40】**The key is to recognise these monomorphic vesicles， filled with clear fluid. Distinguish by their distribution：**

【41】**· Acute contact dermatitis： May present initially as vesicles in the area of contact， before becoming an eczematous rash. Look for classic sites of contact dermatitis and take a contact history .**

【42】**Herpes simplex virus (HSV)： HSV infection presents as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base， affecting the lips (HSV-1)， genitals (HSV-2： screen for other STDs) or hands (herpetic whitlow)； autoinoculation of distant sites can also occur. Primary infection results in more extensive disease + systemic fever and malaise， while recurrent lesions occur in the same site and are milder. HSV infection can be severe in the immunocompromised， or on eczematous skin (eczema herpeticum). Viral swabs can be taken by scraping the base of a fresh blister； virus can be proven by PCR or immunofluorescence， and Tzanck smear may show multinucleated giant cells.**

【43】**Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackievirus and enterovirus)： Erythematous mac-ules， vesicles and ulcers affecting hand， foot and mouth. There may be sore throat and fever.**

【44】**Bullae**

【45】**Bullae arise from disruption of adhesion molecules or epidermal cell injury. Intra-epidermal bullae are flaccid and easily ruptured， but sub-epidermal bullae are tense and less easily broken. Very often， patients present with bullae already broken， leaving the skin with erosions or crusts and the clinician with no clue. Some differentials：**

【46】**Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS-TEN)： This is the first differential to consider in a sick patient-bullae and erosions occur late in its course .**

【47】**Bullous impetigo： While impetigo usually presents with pustules and thick crusts， S. aureus strains that produce exfoliative toxins can present with bullous impetigoflaccid clear or cloudy bullae， which rupture to leave a thin crust. One bulla can become multiple after autoinoculation.**

**Pemphigus vulgaris： Large flaccid blisters， which rupture to leave weeping/crusted erosions. There is extensive mucous membrane involvement， and Nikolsky’s sign is positive (pressure applied laterally to the bulla results in extension). This is an auto-|删除0换行|immune disease occurring in middle-aged to elderly patients， and may rarely be a paraneoplastic syndrome.**

【49】**·Pemphigus foliaceus： Flaccid blisters with positive Nikolsky's sign， similar to pem-phigus vulgaris， but without mucosal involvement.**

【50】**Bullous pemphigoid： Tense pruritic blisters on normal or erythematous skin，neg-ative Nikolsky's sign and mucosal sparing. This is an autoimmune disease occurring in elderly patients， associated with neurologic disease.**

【51】**Workup： Skin biopsy and immunofluorescence is essential for diagnosis of bullous diseases.**

【52】**Erythematous Non-Scaly Rash**

【53】**Erythema is a sign of hyper-vascularity from local inflammation. Broad subgroups are：**

【54】**·(Generalised maculopapular rash： Generalised erythema or erythematous macules and papules， symmetrically distributed over large areas of skin.**

【55】**Localised erythema： Unique morphologies with a specific distribution.**

【56】**IDiscrete erythematous nodules： Isolated subcutaneous nodules.**

【57】**IDiscrete erythematous plaques and patches： Isolated erythematous to dark plaques and patches.**

【58】**Discrete erythematous papules： Small pruritic papules that do not become confluent.**

【59】**Generalised Maculopapular Rashes**

【60】**First rule out Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS-TEN). Drug and viral rashes are hard to tell apart； toxic erythemas and erythroderma look classic.**

【61】**Distinctive：**

【62】**SJS-TEN： Begins as fever + a painful diffuse symmetrical rash (erythema， dusky patches， coalescing erythematous ± purpuric macules； may also include papules and other morphologies)， starting in the face and thorax then spreading elsewhere. Later， bullae form and skin sloughs to give large erosions； the extent of body surface area sloughed distinguishes SJS (<10%)， SJS-TEN overlap (10-30%) and TEN (>30%). Mucous membranes are almost always involved-causing painful mucositis， ulcers， conjunctivitis or urethritis. Patients are systemically ill with fever， anaemia， leuco-cytosis or leukopenia， fluid loss with electrolyte imbalances and secondary bacterial infection. Aetiologies of SJS/TEN are drugs (the same list below) and infection(especially mycoplasma). Biopsy is usually done.**

【63】**Erythema multiforme： Erythematous lesions of multiple forms， including ery-thematous papules and plaques， target lesions， vesicles and bullae. Target lesions are**

【64】**Note： Erythema multiforme major’refers to SJS； this term is discouraged as they are thought to** **be distinct diseases and not a continuum.**

【65】**diagnostic but not always present-these have three zones of colour： an (1) erythe-matous halo around (2) a middle pale area， within which an (3) erythematous or dark centre. Lesions develop acutely (<24 hr)， starting in the peripheries and spreading centripetally， and persist for about 2 weeks. They may be pruritic and involve mucous membranes. Aetiology is most commonly infectious (e.g.， HSV，mycoplasma) or drug-related.**

【66】**Mainly maculopapular rash：**

【67】**Drug rash： Sudden-onset symmetrical rash； may or may not be pruritic， and may _exfoliate. Drugs can cause many rash morphologies； always consider drugs in any_ acute-onset rash. Take a careful drug history (including over-the-counter， traditional medicines and supplements) to assess the likelihood of a drug rash， and identify the likely culprit based on：**

【68】**(1) Known propensity of the drug to cause rashes： Especially beta-lactams， NSAIDs， sulphonamides (e.g.， bactrim)， allopurinol， antivirals and antiepileptics.**

【69】**(2) Temporal course： Usually a new drug initiated several days ago (not immediately). Exception： DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) is a delayed reaction 2 to 6 weeks after drug initiation. Drawing a drug chart helps.**

【70】**Viral exanthem： Itselfindistinguishable from drug rashes， but there may be accom-panying viral symptoms (fever， upper respiratory symptoms， etc.). The classic viral exanthems include measles， rubella， roseola (fifth disease， herpes virus 6)， enterovi-ruses and erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19)-but many other viruses can cause exanthems too. Viral exanthems are most common in children； take a vacci-nation and contact history.**

【71】**SSecondary syphilis： Consider especially if palms and soles are involved.**

【72】**Mainly erythema：**

【73】**Toxic erythemas： Generalised erythema with a sandpaper feel ± desquamation， fever and mucous membrane involvement. Each cause of toxic erythema has unique features：**

【74】**\- Scarlet fever： Sore throat and strawberry tongue (initially white exudate with red papillae， then beefy red). This is due to toxin secretion by erythrogenic strains of _Streptococcus pyogenes._**

【75】**Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome： Red， blistering skin (that looks like a scald) due to a local staphylococcus infection (abscess， cellulitis， otitis). Mucous membranes are spared.**

【76】**\- Toxic shock syndrome： Typically， a patient with cutaneous staphylococcus infection who abruptly develops fever， hypotension， diffuse erythroderma with subsequent desquamation， mucosal hyperaemia and multiorgan involvement(gastrointestinal， muscular， renal， hepatic， neurological and haematological).**

【77】**\- Kawasaki disease： A child with fever exceeding 5 days， bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis， mucosal erythema， cervical lymphadenopathy， truncal rash， ery-thema and oedema of palms/soles then desquamation. Not all features may be present but one clue is that children with Kawasaki disease are always irritable.**

【78】**This is a vasculitis and important to diagnose because of the propensity for coro-nary artery aneurysm formation (and medicolegal complications).**

【79】**· Erythroderma： Erythema and exfoliation affecting almost the entire skin (>90%)multiple causes： psoriasis， severe atopic dermatitis， drug (e.g.， vancomycin)， Sezary syndrome (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) and so forth.**

【80】**Localised Erythema**

【81】**These have unique morphologies and are spot diagnoses.**

【82】**Urticaria (hives) and angioedema： Urticaria is seen as pruritic oedematous wheals with red borders and pale centres. Angioedema also involves mucosa (e.g.， eyelids， lips)， and may be tender. Rule out anaphylaxis (stridor， dyspnoea or hypotension).**

【83】**\- Acute urticaria is transient (<24 hr， or <72 hr for angio-oedema) and triggered by acute viral infections， drugs (antibiotics， NSAIDs， opiates， CT contrast， etc.)， food allergy or insect stings. Ifurticaria is painful， resolves slowly (>24 hr)， or leaves a bruise or hyper-pigmentation， suspect urticarial vasculitis and do biopsy.**

【84】**\- Chronic urticaria (>6 weeks， each wheal <24 hr) may be due to physical (heat， cold， pressure， sunlight， exercise) or contact (e.g.， latex) triggers， occult infection(e.g.， Helicobacter pylori)， autoimmune disease (e.g.， thyroid) or idiopathic. Also consider urticaria due to ACE-inhibitors (bradykinin pathway) and hereditary angio-oedema (due to C1 inhibitor deficiency).**

【85】**·(Cellulitis： A febrile patient with an erythematous， warm， swollen and tender patch of skin (most commonly in the lower limbs). Watch out for necrotising fasciitis if pain is unusually severe， erythema progresses rapidly or the patient is toxic.**

【86】**Systemic autoimmune diseases： Photosensitive erythematous rashes characteris-tically occurring on sun-exposed areas (e.g.， face， neck and shoulders in a 'shawl'distribution， etc.)， with other characteristic features：**

【87】**\-Lupus： ‘Butterfly' malar facial rash sparing the nasolabial folds， oral ulcers， discoid rash and systemic involvement .**

【88】**\- Dermatomyositis： Violaceous macules around the eyelids (heliotrope rash)， hyperpigmented papules over the knuckles (Gottron’s papules) and proximal myopathy.**

【89】**Discrete Erythematous Nodules**

【90】**Erythema nodosum： Acute-onset tender nodules on bilateral shins. This has mul-tiple disease associations， including infection (streptococcal throat infection， viruses， mycoplasma， tuberculosis)， autoimmune disease (inflammatory bowel disease， sarcoidosis)， haematological malignancies and drugs (oral contraceptives， sulphonamides， NSAIDs).**

【91】**·IPrurigo nodularis： Intensely pruritic erythematous and firm nodules (1-3 cm)， often with excoriations and scratch marks. There will often be a history of the patient repeatedly scratching the nodule， which contributes to its persistence.**

【93】**Discrete Erythematous Plaques and Patches**

【94】**Lichen planus： Pruritic purple planar (flat) polygonal papules and plaques， with a reticulate pattern of white lines on its surface (Wickham's striae). This classically affects flexors of wrists and shins， but can involve any site， including mucosa (white patches with reticulated white lines) and scalp (scarring alopecia). Trauma aggra-vates lesions (the Koebner phenomenon)， and lichen planus can occur in streaks(it spreads along where the patient has scratched). Lichen planus is idiopathic or secondary to drugs (take a drug history). Most lesions resolve spontaneously in l to2 years but 10% remain chronic.**

【95】**Candidiasis： A confluent， beefy red eruption with indistinct borders， satellite papules and pustules. This usually occurs in a moist area， for example， the groin. Fungal scrapings are positive.**

【96】**Fixed drug eruption： Sharply demarcated red， violet or dusky plaques， appearing24 to 48 hr after exposure to an offending drug； the centre of the plaque can blister， fading when the drug is discontinued， and recurring at the same spot when re-exposed to the drug.**

【97】**Erythema migrans： This cutaneous lesion of Lyme disease is an erythematous patch that expands over days to weeks， giving a macular non-scaling border (fungal scrapings negative) and clearing centre. Consider in patients with a travel history to grassy areas in temperate countries-where ticks may be found.**

【1】#### 5.2.1.2 Plaque Stage

【2】Biopsies of plaque stage MF demonstrate more pronounced epidermal involvement by the neoplastic T cells, including prominent epidermotropism, tagging, and Pautrier microabscesses 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 11 \]</u>. The neoplastic infiltrate is typically superficial and bandlike, although the atypical T cells are usually present singly or in clusters in the epidermis. In rare cases they can replace nearly the entire epidermis. There may be overlying mild acanthosis, compact hyperkeratosis, or patchy parakeratosis, although significant epidermal hyperplasia or scale crust is not usually seen. Other possible findings include pigment incontinence, edema, fibrosis of the papillary dermis, and proliferation of postcapillary venules. Eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells may rarely be present 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 \]</u>.

【3】#### 5.2.1.3 Tumor Stage

【4】Tumor stage MF is characterized by a dense, diffuse, or nodular dermal infiltrate composed of sheets of atypical T cells, in some cases extending into the subcutis 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 17 \]</u>. Ulceration is common. Epidermotropism may be present or absent 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. In tumor stage MF cells can range in size from small to large 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. By definition large cells must make up less than 25 % of the infiltrate; a higher proportion would be considered LCT. Mitotic figures are readily apparent and often atypical.

【5】#### 5.2.1.4 Large-Cell Transformation

【6】When LCT of MF occurs, it is characterized by the presence of more than 25 % large T cells in the dermal infiltrate on cutaneous biopsy 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. The large cells may have prominent vesicular or hyperchromatic nuclei with conspicuous nucleoli; nuclear pleomorphism is common. Large cells not only have large nuclei but also may have apparent cytoplasm. There is typically prominent mitotic activity, and atypical mitoses are not uncommon. In one third of cases the transformed cells will be positive for CD30; the remaining two thirds are CD30-negative  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 9 \]</u>.

( b ) The neoplastic T cells are very large with irregularly shaped, crenellated, heterochromatic nuclei. Blastic cells have prominent nucleoli (H&E, 60×). ( c ) The majority of the large atypical cells express CD30 (CD30, 20×). ( d ) The large atypical cells are Alk negative, (Alk, 20×)</u>

【8】During any stage of the disease patients may develop dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, which is manifested histopathologically as lymph nodes with paracortical hyperplasia comprised of interdigitating dendritic cells, histiocytes, melanophages, and small reactive T cells; dermatopathic lymphadenopathy does not represent lymphomatous involvement of the node 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>.

【9】### 5.2.2 Immunophenotype and Molecular Findings

【10】The neoplastic CD4+ T cells of MF often stain positively for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, TCRbeta, and CD45RO. In the vast majority of cases of MF, the neoplastic T cells are CD4+ CD8−; only rarely is MF composed of CD8+ CD4− T cells 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. Neoplastic cells may show loss of pan–T-cell antigens including CD2 and CD5, a helpful diagnostic finding  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 11 \]</u>. CD7 is lost in one third of cases. However, because CD7 is frequently lost in reactive cutaneous T-cell infiltrates, it is not a useful marker of neoplastic T cells in the skin 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. CD25 is rarely present 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 \]</u>. As the disease progresses, loss of CD2, CD3, and CD5 becomes more common  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 \]</u>.

【14】Although these are generally true, there are always exceptions. Notable exceptions include hypopigmented MF, which is often CD8+

【15】a Often lost with disease progression

【16】Cells typically express CLA, a cell surface antigen involved in homing of lymphocytes to the skin. Cytotoxic granules are rarely seen early in disease progression but may be present in neoplastic cells of advanced lesions 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>.

【17】Clonal rearrangement of the TCR is nearly always detected 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. A concomitant loss of TCR diversity in the blood may contribute to deficiencies in immunity 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 11 \]</u>. Of note, the presence of the same TCR clone in multiple biopsies is correlated with a worse prognosis 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 18 \]</u>.

【18】The genetics underlying MF are poorly understood 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 19 \]</u>. Complex karyotypes are usually present, including recurrent loss of 1p, 17p, 10q, 13a, and 19 and gains of 4q, 17q, and 18 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 19 – 25 \]</u>. Constitutive activation of STAT3, CDKN2A/p16 INK4a , and PTEN has also been implicated in disease progression 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 24 \]</u>. There is some evidence that microsatellite instability may play a role in the underlying pathobiology of MF 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 26 \]</u>.

【19】5.3 Subtypes of MF
------------------

【20】Numerous subtypes of MF have been described. These include classic, erythrodermic, follicular, syringotropic, bullous, granulomatous, poikilodermatous, hypopigmented, hyperpigmented, unilesional (Pagetoid reticulosis), palmoplantar, hyperkeratotic, vegetating, ichthyosiform, pigmented purpura-like, and pustular, among others 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 \]</u>. Notably, the only subtypes of MF explicitly mentioned in the WHO guidelines are folliculotropic MF, pagetoid reticulosis, and granulomatous slack skin 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. Here, we will discuss the clinical presentation and histopathology of those three entities as well as hypopigmented, poikilodermatous, syringotropic, and granulomatous variants of MF .

【25】### 5.3.1 Folliculotropic MF

【26】Folliculotropic MF (also called pilotropic or folliculocentric MF) accounts for approximately 13 % of cases of MF 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 10 \]</u>. Most often presenting as grouped follicular papules on the head and neck  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 17 \]</u>, folliculotopic MF may be accompanied by alopecia, acneiform lesions, mucinorrhea, comedo-like plugs, epidermal cysts, follicular hyper-keratosis, erythematous patches and plaques, and severe pruritus 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 , 27 , 28 \]</u>. This form of MF is four to five times more common in men than in women 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 17 \]</u>. 【32】### 5.3.2 Pagetoid Reticulosis

【33】Pagetoid reticulosis is an exceedingly rare form of MF characterized by a single patch or plaque. These lesions usually occur on acral sites but may occasionally be present in a bathing-suit distribution. By definition, the lesions of pagetoid reticulosis cover less than 5 % of body surface area 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 17 \]</u>. Pagetoid reticulosis is indolent; extracutaneous spread has never been reported 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. Of note, most consider pagetoid reticulosis to be synonymous with unilesional MF, whereas others consider these to be distinct entities 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 30 \]</u>.

【34】The patches and plaques of pagetoid reticulosis are composed of a prominent epidermotropic intraepidermal proliferation of medium-to-large, hyperchromatic, cerebriform T cells, usually with more “pagetoid” distribution of the epidermotropic cells than is seen in classic MF . However, usually the pagetoid reticulosis is histopathologically indistinguishable from classic MF and requires clinicopathologic correlation for the diagnosis 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 17 \]</u>. The tumor cells may have helper (CD4+ CD8−) or cytotoxic (CD8+ CD4−) immunophenotypes and are often CD30+ 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>.

These are now believed to be distinct disease entities. Woringer-Kolopp is now considered synonymous with pagetoid reticulosis, while Ketron-Goodman is now thought to be more similar to the deadly CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic T-cell lymphoma (CD8+ AECTCL). Because pagetoid reticulosis and CD8+ AECTCL have such different prognoses and presentations, the terms Woringer-Kolopp and Ketron-Goodman are avoided in order to minimize confusion 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u> and are included here only because of their historical significance.

【37】### 5.3.3 Granulomatous Slack Skin

【38】Granulomatous slack skin (GSS) is an extremely rare but indolent variant of MF 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 \]</u>. Fewer than 50 cases have been reported in the literature 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 32 \]</u>. GSS typically presents with the slow growth of distinctive bulky skin folds in intertriginous areas  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 17 , 32 \]</u>. These tend to be particularly prominent in the axillae and groin and may be accompanied by poikilodermatous patches or plaques. 【14】#### Introduction

【15】A radiculopathy is a pathologic process affecting the nerve root within the spinal canal. It usually causes pain, paresthesias, and weakness in the distribution of the nerve root (myotomes and dermatome). Radiculopathy may be caused by compressive etiologies at the neural foramina or within the spinal canal (such as spondylosis or disc herniation) or rarely non-compressive processes (infections, infarction, avulsion, infiltration by tumor or granulomatous tissue, or immune-mediated inflammation).

【16】Radiculopathy may occur in any part of the spine, but is most common in the lumbar and cervical regions. Radiculopathies often present with limb pain with sensory manifestations, reflex changes, and weakness. Sometimes they are painless, presenting with sensory manifestations and/or weakness only.

【17】The diagnosis of radiculopathy is based on history and neurologic examination and is supported by diagnostic studies. The electrodiagnostic studies are important in establishing the diagnosis and localizing the location of the lesion. Two criteria are necessary to establish the electrodiagnosis of radiculopathy:

【18】1\. Normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) of the corresponding dermatome on nerve conduction studies. The lesion in radiculopathy is preganglionic (i.e. within the spinal canal) which results in normal SNAP since it does not interfere with the peripheral axon of the unipolar dorsal root ganglion. In contrast, postganglionic lesions (such as brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy) disrupt the peripheral axon and result in low amplitude or absent SNAP of the corresponding dermatome.

【19】2\. Denervation in a segmental myotomal distribution. Fibrillation potentials and/or reinnervation motor unit action potentials and/or reduced recruitment in at least two muscles innervated by the same root via more than one peripheral nerve, with or without denervation of the paraspinal muscles.

【20】Two provocative bedside tests are useful in the confirmation of radiculopathy:

【21】1\. Straight leg raise test: This is a maneuver that causes stretching of the L5 and S1 nerve roots, and also the sciatic nerve and sacral plexus. It is considered positive if the pain is reproduced between 30 and 70 degrees with passive straight leg rising while the patient is supine. A useful and as reliable test is a reverse straight leg raise test. This test stretches the upper lumbar roots (L2, L3, or L4), and also the femoral nerve and lumbar plexus. It is performed by passive hip extension while the patient is prone and is considered positive if pain is reproduced in the groin or anterior thigh.

【22】2\. Spurling maneuver: This test is useful in the diagnosis of cervical root compression. During this maneuver, the head is first slightly extended, rotated and laterally flexed, and then compressed downwards. This maneuver produces significant reduction of the surface area and shape of the cervical intervertebral foramina, particularly at the midcervical spine. A positive sign (reproducible radicular pain) is diagnostic of cervical radiculopathy.

【32】#### Case vignette

【33】A 53-year-old man in otherwise good health presented with a 3-week history of severe left buttock pain radiating to posterior thigh, lateral leg, and into the medial foot. He also had numbness predominantly in the left lateral leg and left big toe. A week prior to this, he worked in his garage and carried several heavy objects. He did not recall having back pain or other symptoms during the work. The pain is worse when he stands or walks a short distance. Coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva maneuver does not worsen the pain. He was taking ibuprofen 800 mg 3 times a day without any effect on the intensity of the pain. He had no bladder or bowel symptoms. He was treated with a course of oral steroids for 10 days with no change in symptoms.

【34】On examination, he was in modest distress and walked with an antalgic gait. Straight leg raise was positive at 60 degrees on the left and negative on the right. There was no muscle atrophy or fasciculations. He had slight tenderness in the left buttock. Manual muscle examination revealed weakness of the left ankle dorsiflexion (Medical Research Council scale (MRC) 5−/5), ankle eversion (MRC 5−/5), and great toe extension (MRC 4+/5). Plantar flexion was normal. There was no weakness of hip abduction, flexion, or extension, or knee extension and flexion. His deep tendon reflexes were +2 and symmetric throughout, including the ankle jerks and knee jerks. His plantar responses were both flexors. The sensory examination revealed decreased pin and touch sensation in the left lateral leg and the great toe. Vibration and position senses were normal.

【35】An electrodiagnostic study showed normal sensory and motor nerve conduction studies (NCS) including left sural and superficial peroneal sensory studies, left peroneal motor and tibial motor studies, and bilateral H-reflexes. 【50】#### Introduction

【51】The sixth (VI, abducens) cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle and is responsible for abduction of the eye. 【10】# Section 2 Differential Diagnosis within Specific Localizations/101 Radiculopathy

【11】### 101 Radiculopathy

【12】Amtul Farheen and Bashar Katirji

【13】Neurologic Differential Diagnosis , ed. Alan B. Ettinger and Deborah M. Weisbrot. Published by Cambridge University Press.  Cambridge University Press 2014.

【14】#### Introduction

【15】A radiculopathy is a pathologic process affecting the nerve root within the spinal canal. It usually causes pain, paresthesias, and weakness in the distribution of the nerve root (myotomes and dermatome). Radiculopathy may be caused by compressive etiologies at the neural foramina or within the spinal canal (such as spondylosis or disc herniation) or rarely non-compressive processes (infections, infarction, avulsion, infiltration by tumor or granulomatous tissue, or immune-mediated inflammation).

【16】Radiculopathy may occur in any part of the spine, but is most common in the lumbar and cervical regions. Radiculopathies often present with limb pain with sensory manifestations, reflex changes, and weakness. Sometimes they are painless, presenting with sensory manifestations and/or weakness only.

【17】The diagnosis of radiculopathy is based on history and neurologic examination and is supported by diagnostic studies. The electrodiagnostic studies are important in establishing the diagnosis and localizing the location of the lesion. Two criteria are necessary to establish the electrodiagnosis of radiculopathy:

【18】1\. Normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) of the corresponding dermatome on nerve conduction studies. The lesion in radiculopathy is preganglionic (i.e. within the spinal canal) which results in normal SNAP since it does not interfere with the peripheral axon of the unipolar dorsal root ganglion. In contrast, postganglionic lesions (such as brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy) disrupt the peripheral axon and result in low amplitude or absent SNAP of the corresponding dermatome.

【19】2\. Denervation in a segmental myotomal distribution. Fibrillation potentials and/or reinnervation motor unit action potentials and/or reduced recruitment in at least two muscles innervated by the same root via more than one peripheral nerve, with or without denervation of the paraspinal muscles.

【20】Two provocative bedside tests are useful in the confirmation of radiculopathy:

【21】1\. Straight leg raise test: This is a maneuver that causes stretching of the L5 and S1 nerve roots, and also the sciatic nerve and sacral plexus. It is considered positive if the pain is reproduced between 30 and 70 degrees with passive straight leg rising while the patient is supine. A useful and as reliable test is a reverse straight leg raise test. This test stretches the upper lumbar roots (L2, L3, or L4), and also the femoral nerve and lumbar plexus. It is performed by passive hip extension while the patient is prone and is considered positive if pain is reproduced in the groin or anterior thigh.

【22】2\. Spurling maneuver: This test is useful in the diagnosis of cervical root compression. During this maneuver, the head is first slightly extended, rotated and laterally flexed, and then compressed downwards. This maneuver produces significant reduction of the surface area and shape of the cervical intervertebral foramina, particularly at the midcervical spine. A positive sign (reproducible radicular pain) is diagnostic of cervical radiculopathy.

【32】#### Case vignette

【33】A 53-year-old man in otherwise good health presented with a 3-week history of severe left buttock pain radiating to posterior thigh, lateral leg, and into the medial foot. He also had numbness predominantly in the left lateral leg and left big toe. A week prior to this, he worked in his garage and carried several heavy objects. He did not recall having back pain or other symptoms during the work. The pain is worse when he stands or walks a short distance. Coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva maneuver does not worsen the pain. He was taking ibuprofen 800 mg 3 times a day without any effect on the intensity of the pain. He had no bladder or bowel symptoms. He was treated with a course of oral steroids for 10 days with no change in symptoms.

【34】On examination, he was in modest distress and walked with an antalgic gait. Straight leg raise was positive at 60 degrees on the left and negative on the right. There was no muscle atrophy or fasciculations. He had slight tenderness in the left buttock. Manual muscle examination revealed weakness of the left ankle dorsiflexion (Medical Research Council scale (MRC) 5−/5), ankle eversion (MRC 5−/5), and great toe extension (MRC 4+/5). Plantar flexion was normal. There was no weakness of hip abduction, flexion, or extension, or knee extension and flexion. His deep tendon reflexes were +2 and symmetric throughout, including the ankle jerks and knee jerks. His plantar responses were both flexors. The sensory examination revealed decreased pin and touch sensation in the left lateral leg and the great toe. Vibration and position senses were normal.

【35】An electrodiagnostic study showed normal sensory and motor nerve conduction studies (NCS) including left sural and superficial peroneal sensory studies, left peroneal motor and tibial motor studies, and bilateral H-reflexes. Needle EMG revealed fibrillation potentials in the tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior, extensor hallucis longus, tensor fascia lata, and low lumbar paraspinal muscles. Motor unit action potentials were normal in morphology and recruitment. An MRI of the lumbar spine showed a left intraforaminal disc herniation at L5–S1 interspace .

【10】# Section 2 Differential Diagnosis within Specific Localizations/101 Radiculopathy

【11】### 101 Radiculopathy

【12】Amtul Farheen and Bashar Katirji

【13】Neurologic Differential Diagnosis , ed. Alan B. Ettinger and Deborah M. Weisbrot. Published by Cambridge University Press.  Cambridge University Press 2014.

【14】#### Introduction

【15】A radiculopathy is a pathologic process affecting the nerve root within the spinal canal. It usually causes pain, paresthesias, and weakness in the distribution of the nerve root (myotomes and dermatome). Radiculopathy may be caused by compressive etiologies at the neural foramina or within the spinal canal (such as spondylosis or disc herniation) or rarely non-compressive processes (infections, infarction, avulsion, infiltration by tumor or granulomatous tissue, or immune-mediated inflammation).

【16】Radiculopathy may occur in any part of the spine, but is most common in the lumbar and cervical regions. Radiculopathies often present with limb pain with sensory manifestations, reflex changes, and weakness. Sometimes they are painless, presenting with sensory manifestations and/or weakness only.

【17】The diagnosis of radiculopathy is based on history and neurologic examination and is supported by diagnostic studies. The electrodiagnostic studies are important in establishing the diagnosis and localizing the location of the lesion. Two criteria are necessary to establish the electrodiagnosis of radiculopathy:

【18】1\. Normal sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) of the corresponding dermatome on nerve conduction studies. The lesion in radiculopathy is preganglionic (i.e. within the spinal canal) which results in normal SNAP since it does not interfere with the peripheral axon of the unipolar dorsal root ganglion. In contrast, postganglionic lesions (such as brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy) disrupt the peripheral axon and result in low amplitude or absent SNAP of the corresponding dermatome.

【19】2\. Denervation in a segmental myotomal distribution. Fibrillation potentials and/or reinnervation motor unit action potentials and/or reduced recruitment in at least two muscles innervated by the same root via more than one peripheral nerve, with or without denervation of the paraspinal muscles.

【20】Two provocative bedside tests are useful in the confirmation of radiculopathy:

【21】1\. Straight leg raise test: This is a maneuver that causes stretching of the L5 and S1 nerve roots, and also the sciatic nerve and sacral plexus. It is considered positive if the pain is reproduced between 30 and 70 degrees with passive straight leg rising while the patient is supine. A useful and as reliable test is a reverse straight leg raise test. This test stretches the upper lumbar roots (L2, L3, or L4), and also the femoral nerve and lumbar plexus. It is performed by passive hip extension while the patient is prone and is considered positive if pain is reproduced in the groin or anterior thigh.

【22】2\. Spurling maneuver: This test is useful in the diagnosis of cervical root compression. During this maneuver, the head is first slightly extended, rotated and laterally flexed, and then compressed downwards. This maneuver produces significant reduction of the surface area and shape of the cervical intervertebral foramina, particularly at the midcervical spine. A positive sign (reproducible radicular pain) is diagnostic of cervical radiculopathy.

【32】#### Case vignette

【33】A 53-year-old man in otherwise good health presented with a 3-week history of severe left buttock pain radiating to posterior thigh, lateral leg, and into the medial foot. He also had numbness predominantly in the left lateral leg and left big toe. A week prior to this, he worked in his garage and carried several heavy objects. He did not recall having back pain or other symptoms during the work. The pain is worse when he stands or walks a short distance. Coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva maneuver does not worsen the pain. He was taking ibuprofen 800 mg 3 times a day without any effect on the intensity of the pain. He had no bladder or bowel symptoms. He was treated with a course of oral steroids for 10 days with no change in symptoms.

【34】On examination, he was in modest distress and walked with an antalgic gait. Straight leg raise was positive at 60 degrees on the left and negative on the right. There was no muscle atrophy or fasciculations. He had slight tenderness in the left buttock. Manual muscle examination revealed weakness of the left ankle dorsiflexion (Medical Research Council scale (MRC) 5−/5), ankle eversion (MRC 5−/5), and great toe extension (MRC 4+/5). Plantar flexion was normal. There was no weakness of hip abduction, flexion, or extension, or knee extension and flexion. His deep tendon reflexes were +2 and symmetric throughout, including the ankle jerks and knee jerks. His plantar responses were both flexors. The sensory examination revealed decreased pin and touch sensation in the left lateral leg and the great toe. Vibration and position senses were normal.

【35】An electrodiagnostic study showed normal sensory and motor nerve conduction studies (NCS) including left sural and superficial peroneal sensory studies, left peroneal motor and tibial motor studies, and bilateral H-reflexes. Needle EMG revealed fibrillation potentials in the tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior, extensor hallucis longus, tensor fascia lata, and low lumbar paraspinal muscles. Motor unit action potentials were normal in morphology and recruitment. An MRI of the lumbar spine showed a left intraforaminal disc herniation at L5–S1 interspace .

【47】### 102 Sixth nerve palsy

【48】Scott Uretsky

【49】Neurologic Differential Diagnosis , ed. Alan B. Ettinger and Deborah M. Weisbrot. Published by Cambridge University Press.  Cambridge University Press 2014.

【50】#### Introduction

【51】The sixth (VI, abducens) cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle and is responsible for abduction of the eye. Palsy of the abducens nerve causes an incomitant ocular misalignment manifesting most commonly with diplopia. It is the most common of the isolated ocular motor palsies 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 2 \]</u>. The abducens nucleus serves as the ipsilateral horizontal gaze center and thus nuclear lesions cause ipsilateral gaze palsy and not pure unilateral abduction deficits. When the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) is involved the one-and-a-half syndrome results. The nucleus contains large motor neurons innervating the ipsilateral lateral rectus and smaller interneurons that ascend in the MLF to innervate the contralateral medial rectus sub-nucleus of the third nerve nucleus.

【52】#### Anatomic considerations

【53】Precise knowledge of the course of the sixth nerve and the structures it keeps company with at various locations frequently allows localization of the pathologic process in non-isolated sixth nerve palsies.

【54】The abducens nucleus is located in the lower pons, separated from the floor of the fourth ventricle by the genu of the facial nerve, in proximity to the vestibular nuclei and the MLF. The sixth nerve exits the brainstem anterolaterally at the pontomedullary junction, medial to the exit of the seventh and eighth cranial nerves.

【55】The nerve enters the subarachnoid space and ascends in the prepontine cistern and along the clivus. It travels over the petrous apex, beneath the petroclinoid ligament, through Dorello's canal entering into the substance of the cavernous sinus. Here it is the cranial nerve closest to the internal carotid artery. The third, fourth, and first two divisions of the fifth cranial nerves travel in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. 【9】KEY FACTS

【10】Clinical

【11】 FHN is much more common in woman (85%); they typically present in the third to fifth decade of life.

【12】 They are usually asymptomatic and therefore detected incidentally. Only 10% are symptomatic, presenting with an abdominal mass or pain.

【13】 FNH are not associated with oral contraceptives, although there is evidence that oral contraceptives increase the otherwise low propensity for intratumoral hemorrhage.

【14】 The alpha-fetoprotein level is normal.

【15】 FNH are benign tumors that do not degenerate into well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinomas.

【16】Radiologic

【17】 Histologically, FNH are composed of hepatocytes, bile ducts, and Kuppfer cells to a variable degree (there is a much higher population of Kuppfer cells compared to adenomas), laid along fibrous strands that coalesce centrally to form a scar. These features determine the imaging findings.

【18】 Although most FNH are solitary, 20% are multiple.

【19】 Classically, they are isoattenuating precontrast, hyper-attenuating during the hepatic arterial phase, and iso-attenuating during the portal venous phase.

【20】 A central hypoattenuating scar is present about 50% of the time, but this finding is not specific for FNH as it can also be seen in hepatic adenomas and hepato-cellular carcinomas, especially fibrolamellar types. On MRI, the scar tends to be of high signal intensity on T2-weighted images in FNH and of low signal intensity in HCC, although this signal intensity pattern is not reliable.
